G. SEAN METROKA
Grand Master
October 25, 2023 - October 27, 2024

ii

G. Sean Metroka
Grand Master
2023-2024
Brother G. Sean Metroka was raised a Master Mason in Table Mountain
Lodge No. 124 in Paradise on October 23, 1979. He is a past master of Nevada
Lodge No. 13 in Nevada City and the current Master of Harmony Lodge No.
164 in Sierra City.
Brother Metroka currently serves the Grand Lodge of California as Grand
Master and is a former Grand Orator, district inspector and chairman of the
Grand Lodge Committee on Leadership Development. He has served on all five
of the Grand Lodge constitutional boards.
Brother Metroka’s involvement in Masonry began when he joined Paradise
Chapter Order of DeMolay in 1972. He served as chapter master councilor in
1974 and Superior Division master councilor in 1977. He was honored with the
Degree of Chevalier and Legion of Honor. Sean continued his involvement in
DeMolay as an adult advisor and was awarded the Cross of Honor, the Grand
Master’s Youth Support Award, and the Guild of the Leather Apron for his distinguished adult service. Sean credits DeMolay with having the greatest positive
influence on his youth, second only to his parents.
In 1976, Sean enlisted in the United States Marine Corps, the start of what
would be more than 30 years of military service to his country. After graduating from California State University at Chico with a Bachelor of Arts degree in
geography, Sean was commissioned a Second Lieutenant. He received numerous
promotions during his career and was ultimately elevated to the rank of Colonel.
During his tenure, he served in both active duty and reserve capacities. He was
the commander of the 5th Battalion, 14th Marines in Seal Beach and served two
combat tours of duty in Iraq, where he planned long-range fire support for the
First Marine Expeditionary Force and was the Marines’ liaison to the Combined
Joint Special Operations Task Force, Arabian Peninsula.
Following his initial release from active duty, Sean entered the aerospace
industry as a systems engineer with McDonnell Douglas in Long Beach. Through
several promotions he ended up as a senior manager in finance and accounting.
After a stint in healthcare business management, Sean joined the finance department of Nevada County Superior Court in 2000. Returning from a tour of duty
in Iraq in 2003, Sean was selected to be the court’s chief executive officer and
served in that position for 15 years. As CEO, Sean was responsible for overseeing
iii

the management and administration of all non-judicial functions of the court,
including personnel, finance, facilities, technology, security, jury management,
long-range planning, and public relations. Sean retired from the court in 2018
to focus on other things he loves, especially his service in Freemasonry.
Sean is a Scottish Rite, York Rite and Shrine Mason, and is a member
of the Red Cross of Constantine, Holy Royal Arch Knight Templar Priests,
Sciots, National Sojourners, Heroes of 76, Allied Masonic Degrees and Golden
Compasses Research Lodge.
Sean has actively supported his community. He served as cub master and
scout master when his sons were young, and he coached youth football. He
was a member of the board of directors of Sierra Nevada Memorial Hospital
Foundation for 15 years, including four years as president. He has served several other non-profits and as a volunteer for Empire Mine State Historic Park.​
Brother Sean and his wife, Margaret, live in Nevada City. They’ve been
married 39 years and have three adult children and two grandchildren.

ONE HUNDRED SEVENTY FIFTH
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
Friday Afternoon, October 25, 2024
The 175th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master G. Sean
Metroka on Friday, October 25, 2024.
Worshipful Brother Robert R. Aunchman, master of Madison No. 23,
called the Grand Lodge to order using a gavel presented to the grand master
by Madison No. 23 at its installation.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The grand master welcomed the brethren and directed the grand marshal to
present the past grand masters of the Grand Lodge of California at the altar. The
grand marshal then introduced each past grand master, the grand master, and the
deputy grand master and personally greeted each one. The grand master asked
the brethren to join him in saluting our past grand masters by the battery of three
times three. The past grand masters were then escorted to seats reserved for them
in the auditorium. The grand master then directed the grand secretary to send to
each absent past grand master the usual letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The grand secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge officers, past grand
masters, and past grand officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional number
were present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following were
present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

The grand secretary announced that, according to the credentials report,
there were 833 Master Masons registered as of 12 p.m. Friday, with at least 20
percent of the lodges chartered by this Grand Lodge represented, and that
therefore a quorum was present as required for the transaction of business.
The grand secretary reported that all lodges had paid their annual per capita
assessment to Grand Lodge.

7

Grand Lodge Opening
The grand master then opened Grand Lodge in ancient form. The grand marshal
and the deacons retired to escort the flag of the United States of America into
the auditorium, which was followed by the Pledge of Allegiance.
Introductions
The following were asked to rise as groups for recognition:
Residents of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek, Diamond Jubilee Award
recipients, Golden Veteran Award recipients, Diamond Jubilee recipients, Hiram
Award recipients, worshipful masters, lodge secretaries and officers, constitutional board members, Grand Lodge committeemen, and district inspectors;
each group was greeted with a round of applause.
The grand master also recognized Grand Lodge officers visiting from other
jurisdictions.
Reception of Visiting Grand Masters
The grand master then directed the grand marshal to escort the visiting grand
masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The following were
received with private grand honors and introduced:

Communication of the Grand Lodge of California, with the fraternal wish that
they would take back to their grand lodges a full measure of brotherly love
from California. The grand master directed the grand marshal to conduct Most
Worshipful Jonathan Spence, pro grand master of the United Grand Lodge of
England, to a seat in the east.
The grand master then directed the grand marshal to escort the representatives of grand masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The
following grand officers were introduced:

Grand Master’s Message
The grand master then relinquished his chair to the deputy grand master for
the purpose of delivering the grand master’s message (Appendix A). After his
message, the grand master received a standing ovation and then resumed his
station.

Memorial Service
The grand master called on the Very Reverend Alan S. Rellaford, grand chaplain,
to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren. His remarks
were as follows:
Brethren, family, and friends, we gather here today to honor and remember the lives of our Masonic brothers who have laid down their working tools
since our last Annual Communication. In this moment of reflection, we pause
to recognize their contributions, their spirit, and the legacy they leave behind.
Freemasonry teaches us that life is a journey from darkness into light, and
while our brothers have completed their journey here on Earth, their light shines
on through the impact they have made on each of us and the work of the craft.
Though they are no longer physically present, their influence remains a guiding
force in our lodges, our communities, and our hearts.
As we reflect on the passing of time, I would like to share a familiar passage
from the Book of Ecclesiastes:
To everything, there is a season, and a time to every purpose
under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to
plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
These words remind us that life follows a natural order, and while we grieve
the loss of our brothers, we take solace in knowing that they have completed
their journey with grace and dignity.

12

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Our brothers gave of themselves to the craft, demonstrating the principles
of Freemasonry in their daily lives. Whether through acts of charity, leadership
in their lodges, or quiet, steadfast service, they embodied the core values of
brotherly love, relief, and truth. Their work within our fraternity was not merely a
responsibility, but a calling—a way to build a better world, one small step at a time.
Today, we reflect on the light they brought into our lives. Each of them
contributed to our shared journey, and in so doing, they have strengthened the
bonds of brotherhood that unite us. We honor their memory not just by speaking
their names, but by carrying their spirit forward in the work that we continue.
At this time, I ask that we observe a moment of silence in honor of our
brothers who have passed. In this moment, let us reflect on their lives, their
service, and the impact they have had on us all.
Though our brothers have departed from this life, we trust that they have
now entered the celestial lodge, that eternal home where the Great Architect
of the Universe welcomes those who have lived with integrity and compassion.
Their journey has led them from this world to one where the light of truth
shines ever brighter.
We, too, are reminded that life is precious and fleeting. Our time on Earth
is but a brief moment and the bonds we create, the work we do, and the lives
we touch are what endure. It is through service to others and the pursuit of
higher ideals that we give meaning to our existence.
As we conclude this memorial service, let us carry forward the lessons our
brothers have taught us. Let us strive to live with the same dedication, humility,
and integrity that they exemplified. May their memory inspire us to continue
the work they began, and may we find comfort in the knowledge that their light
will always be with us.
Though we mourn their passing, we celebrate their lives, knowing that
each of them played an essential role in the grand design of the universe. Let
us honor their memory by continuing to build, with care and with love, upon
the foundation they laid.
In closing, I’d like to share a poem written by Rabbi Roland B. Gittelson,
U. S. Navy chaplain during World War II, and the first Jewish chaplain assigned
to the United States Marine Corps.
In the rising of the sun and its going down,
we remember them.
In the blowing of the wind and the chill of the Winter,
we remember them.
In the opening of buds and in the rebirth of Spring,
we remember them.
In the blueness of the sky and in the warmth of Summer,
we remember them.
In the rustling of the leaves and in the beauty of Autumn,
we remember them.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

13

In the beginning of the year and when it ends,
we remember them.
When we are weary and in need of strength,
we remember them.
When we are lost and sick at heart,
we remember them.
When we have joys we yearn to share,
we remember them.
As long as we live, they too shall live,
for they are now a part of us,
as we remember them.
Thank you.

The grand master called on Most Worshipful Brother Russell E. Charvonia
to deliver the eulogy for Most Worshipful Brother Sherod. His remarks were
as follows:

Eulogy
Ronald A. Sherod
Most Worshipful Ronald Arthur Sherod entered the celestial lodge
above on April 1, 2024, at the age of 97, having been a resident of our Union
City Masonic Home. He was born on May 24, 1926, in Omaha, Nebraska, but
moved to California with his family in the 1940s.
Ron served briefly in the U.S. Navy at the end of World War II as a pharmacist mate in San Diego. After his Navy stint, he returned to school, where he
earned his college degree in accounting. While not exactly the Oracle of Omaha,
he did meet the love of his life, Theola M. Hennig, there while they were both in
college. Ron didn’t much care for the name Theola, so he dubbed her “Terry,”
and their marriage lasted 76 years until her death in September 2022, also at
age 97. They had lived in Long Beach, Sedona, and Roseville before moving to
Acacia Creek in 2021.
This eulogy is as much a memory of Terry as it is of Ron, as Terry was
always about love of family and relationships, whereas Ron focused more on
his career and being a good provider. However, both possessed hearts of gold,
each in their own particular way.
In 1953, Ron and Terry had their only child, Craig. Ron was also an only child,
as is his now 27-year-old grandson, Ryan. This may well explain his dedication
and reliance on family. He often referred to his son Craig as his best friend, and
he never missed any of his special childhood events. In fact, it was to be closer
to Ryan that Terry and Ron moved back to California from Sedona.
As an avocation, he loved golfing almost as much as he loved Terry.
Ron served in senior management roles in the aerospace industry from the
1950s through 1975. He worked on many programs, from early satellites to the
Apollo moon landing. He worked for TRW, Space Technology Laboratories, and
McDonnell Douglas during these years.
In 1975, he founded the Equitable Management and Consulting Corporation,
focusing on management for retirement homes and large condo and townhouse
developments. During this time, Ron also served on the Presidential Council
on Aging during the Reagan administration. He sold the successful company
in 1985, in part to focus on his new responsibilities as grand orator under Most
Worshipful John Driskell.
Most Worshipful Ron was initiated as an Entered Apprentice Mason on
March 18, 1953, passed to the degree of Fellowcraft on April 15, 1953, and raised
to the sublime degree of Master Mason on July 22, 1953, all in Bixby Knolls
Lodge No. 699 (now Long Beach No. 327).
He served as master of Bixby Knolls Lodge No. 699 in 1961. He later affiliated

16

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

with International City Lodge No. 389 in 1989 and with Siminoff Daylight No.
850 in 2012. Most Worshipful Ron served our craft as a district inspector for
three years. He further served our Grand Lodge as a member of the Lodge
Resources Development Committee, a trustee of the Masonic Homes, and
as a member of the California Freemason Magazine Committee. He was also a
member of the California Masonic Memorial Temple board for five years. He
served as our 125th grand master in 1990-91.
Most Worshipful Ron’s theme of “California Masonry…Working Together”
guided his term as grand master. He formed the council of Masonic leaders,
bringing together 35 heads of all the concordant and appendant Masonic organizations. Quiet reasoning, understanding, and compassion were the consistent
guides of his term. As evidence of such, he was gracious and endearing to John
and Heather Cooper when John was in the process of taking over as grand
secretary from Bob Klinger.
His grand master’s Recommendation No. 4 created the basis for requiring three recommenders from different lodges to bring a piece of proposed
legislation before this body. This was done with the intention of reducing the
high number of resolutions while still allowing the craft to continue to present
issues of concern.
Perhaps the brightest highlight of Most Worshipful Ron’s term as grand
master was his son Craig becoming a Mason in San Jose Lodge No. 10, with
many past grand masters and Grand Lodge officers helping in the cause.
Ron stayed connected to California Masonry and always cared about the
wellbeing of the craft, even as his eyesight and overall health declined in his
later years. He wasn’t afraid to verge on the controversial, as many brothers
may recall.
Ron spent his final months in Lorber at our Union City Masonic Home.
He was referred to as grand master! by the staff, and that would “wake him up,”
even without having his hearing aids in. I guess once a grand master, always a
grand master.
His ashes were interred next to Terry’s at Chapel of the Chimes, right down
the street from here.
When we leave this mortal Earth, we are measured by the difference we
make during the brief time allotted to us. There is no doubt that our beloved
Brother Ronald A. Sherod helped to repair our world through quiet reasoning,
understanding, and compassion during his 70 years as a brother of our beloved
craft. Soft and safe to Thee, my dear brother, be thy resting place.
The grand organist provided a musical selection, following which the grand
master thanked both the grand organist and Most Worshipful Brother Charvonia.

Grand Master’s Lifetime Achievement Award
At 11:30 a.m., the grand master called announced that at the grand master’s banquet that evening he would present the Grand Master’s Lifetime Achievement
Award to Most Worshipful Brother R. Stephen Doan. He then called on Most
Worshipful Brother Doan to share remarks, which follow.
Past Grand Master Doan’s Remarks
When John Cooper received the lifetime achievement award in the York Rite
this May, I shared a brief overview of John’s help as I was matriculating through
the Grand Lodge line. John remarked afterward that Masons today take for
granted what they have in Grand Lodge. They do not realize how bad things
were when I joined the line in 1989.
In my remarks today, I will discuss why I was selected in 1989 to join the
line, what I did while in the line, and my service as a past grand master.
Our membership began its decline in the mid-1960s when the number of
deaths and demits surpassed the number of men joining. By then, the largest

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

19

cohort of the “greatest generation” who would be interested in Masonry had
largely joined, although more were to come. There were not as many men born
during the depression, and Baby Boomers would never join Masonry in the
numbers that their fathers and grandfathers did. Nothing we did stemmed the
decline. There was a growing lack of confidence that we could do anything that
would work. Most voluntary organizations were in a similar decline. The seminal
study of this problem and its root causes is Robert Putnam’s groundbreaking
book, Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community, but this
book was not published until the year 2000, seven years after I was grand master.
Voluntary organizations faced another challenge. It was becoming increasingly difficult for large voluntary organizations to operate with volunteers
holding the same leadership roles they filled in the past. Grand Lodge had the
added burden of operating several ever-more regulated businesses, such as the
Masonic Homes. Hiring our brother Masons for key roles in our Grand Lodge
entities based on Masonic achievement rather than people who were best for
the job, even if not a Mason or a man, was becoming part of the problem also.
We also had a tradition in our Grand Lodge of past grand master kingmakers.
While there may have been times when this system worked, there were by 1989
several notable incidents when it failed. In the 1960s, the preeminent kingmaker,
as part of his dynastic planning, got his man as the recommendee for election as
junior grand warden. The inspectors saw the choice for what it was and rallied
the masters and wardens in their districts to support an assistant grand lecturer
who then defeated the kingmaker’s candidate. This assistant grand lecturer, as
grand master, tried to curtail the influence of this kingmaker and some of his
key supporters. He lost. When his term as grand master ended, he and his key
supporters were frozen out of Grand Lodge, beginning a rift that would widen
over the years between the executive and ritual sides of Grand Lodge—a rift
which impeded our progress and was not effectively addressed until I inserted
the AGLs in the chain of command between the inspectors and the grand master,
a seemingly common-sense change that had not been possible before then, and
which Grand Lodge added to our law by adopting my Recommendation No. 7.
The kingmaker model again failed in the late 1980s, when two aspiring
kingmakers made a series of bad decisions, compounded by what a then-senior
past grand master, Myron Smith, and other PGMs saw as an abuse of power.
Myron took this as a call to action and convened a meeting of other concerned
past grand masters at the Jonathan Club in Los Angeles to discuss this abuse
of power and the deteriorating condition of the Grand Lodge. Two non-past
grand masters were invited to at least two of their meetings: Grand Treasurer
John Sickenberger and me. Why me? Myron said I was there to take notes and
prepare any legislation that might come out of their deliberations. Those were
not the reasons. The past grand masters had been saying to me for some time
that I had a bright future in Grand Lodge—PGM-speak for “someday you can
be grand master, if you do not mess it up”—but that I had to wait probably until
I was in my 50s, then still 15 years or so away. In retrospect, I now understand

20

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

that these men were coming to the view that they could no longer wait.
Other than the abuse of power, I was familiar with most of the issues
raised during these Jonathan Club meetings. Interestingly, no action plan was
discussed while I was at these meetings other than the imperative of denying
the brother abusing his power further advancement in the craft, which Myron
Smith accomplished in a manner which to the best of my knowledge he never
shared, to prevent further embarrassment to the kingmakers responsible. There
were no other action plans discussed, no action plan to address the other issues
identified. I only later came to understand why. These PGMs were looking to
me to develop the action plan, and they saw to it that I was the recommendee
for election as junior grand warden in 1989, the next time a southerner was
chosen. I was 39 at the time.
At my first Executive Committee meeting, the Grand Lodge office staff
brought a financial issue to us. There was an unbudgeted expenditure of $25,000
for audio-visual at the just-completed Annual Communication which we were
told we would struggle to pay. I did not understand why this was so and asked
more and more questions until I finally had a report which showed me (but
really no one else) that Grand Lodge was technically insolvent. In another 12
months, we would be insolvent in fact, unable to pay our bills, and were forced
to borrow money to cover the deficit. Over the prior six years, the Grand Lodge
had spent $200,000 ($435,000 in today’s money) that was not budgeted. No
one was monitoring compliance with the Grand Lodge budgets. Our Grand
Lodge reserves were gone. Stan Cazneaux was immediately ahead of me in the
line, and this failure of leadership awakened Stan to the issues which Myron
Smith and the other PGMs had discussed at their Jonathan Club meetings a few
years before. Stan and I were thenceforth in lockstep addressing those issues.
To respond to the financial crisis at hand, he and I developed new budgeting
processes and fiscal controls and cut expenses, and the surpluses thereby generated brought us back to solvency with all the borrowings repaid by the time
I finished my term as grand master. A very high-level explanation of this crisis
and the procedures implemented to guard against a repeat of what had happened before I joined the line may be found in my Recommendation No. 3. This
recommendation was adopted, and these procedures have been followed since.
This financial crisis was just more evidence that new leadership was needed
in the Grand Lodge office. Resumes were solicited, and John Cooper was one of
the applicants. I was the only one on the Executive Committee who really knew
John. He had been master of one of my dad’s lodges when Dad was an inspector.
John had since been superintendent of schools in the district near his home and
was an established Masonic scholar. John was and is a team player. He brought
organizational skills to the Grand Lodge office, plus an added dimension. We
could begin to rely on a professional, paid staff in the Grand Lodge office for
leadership in Masonic education and training, something unheard of before
that. John was elected grand secretary at the next Annual Communication. The
Grand Lodge office today is part of the solution, not part of the problem, and

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

21

this paradigm shift began with John.
Despite the setbacks of the prior 25 years and the falling confidence in our
ability to right the ship, I was confident that someday many more young men
like me would be drawn to the craft’s timeless teachings, unfolded through a
deep brotherhood with other men on the same journey. To prepare for that day,
I proposed re-imagining the craft to something these men would want to join
and remain active members of. We needed to change some things that were
holding us back and train our masters and wardens to offer a lodge experience
that young men would find engaging.
That Black men were then not welcome in our lodges was a reason some
of my Baby Boomer brothers in DeMolay gave for not joining Freemasonry. In
1947, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts determined that the “origin, early procedures and subsequent development of the so-called Prince Hall Freemasonry
in Massachusetts have been and are regular and legitimate.” This determination
removed the fundamental objection to recognition of Prince Hall Freemasonry.
California was in the lead of pressuring Massachusetts to rescind its landmark
determination of legitimacy, which it did in 1949. In 1993, therefore, when I
was grand master, it was thought that California would need to be on board
with any change before many Grand Lodges would consider it. Attitudes on
race were evolving, but we were held back by what was known as the American
Doctrine: That there could be only one grand lodge in any one American state.
I reinterpreted that doctrine. In my view, if any grand lodge had the power to
exclude any other Masonic obedience from its territory, it also could waive that
power and allow Prince Hall to share its Masonic jurisdiction. This interpretation was affirmed by the adoption of my Recommendation No. 1, and the next
year, California started the Prince Hall recognition process. The momentum
continued with other Grand Lodges taking similar action. It also accelerated
changing attitudes in our local lodges, and men of color began joining.1
Our commercialism rules greatly restricted how lodges and other Masonic
organizations could raise funds to support fraternal operations. Declining
membership meant lower dues income. Traditional Masonic activities were
increasingly harder to hold, given that diminished dues income. There was a
Grand Lodge year when the grand master strictly enforced these commercialism rules against the Shrine, which would have bankrupted it had that grand
master’s successors not backed away from this strict enforcement. While many
recognized that these rules were no longer tenable as written, the old guard in
our Grand Lodge frustrated any reforms. Using a provision in the commercialism
rules which allowed the grand master to grant exemptions from these rules, I
drafted a blanket exemption available to any lodge, Shrine, or other Masonic
body if certain expanded fundraising rules were followed. These expanded rules
preserved the original intent of the commercialism prohibition: they maintained
the dignity of our craft, yet allowed fundraising meals and other such projects
1

Not all prospective Masons were comfortable taking their obligation on Christian Bible. My Recommendation No. 5 allowed for alternate Holy Writings. This recommendation was a carryover
to 1994 when it was adopted.

22

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

to cover the costs of our programs. Grand Master Cazneaux promulgated this
blanket exemption upon his installation, and I continued it upon my installation. With two years of successful operation under these new rules, the Grand
Lodge added these expanded fundraising rules to the California Masonic Code
by the adoption of my Recommendation No. 4.2
Updating these and other rules would make us more relevant and sustainable, but they did little to improve the lodge experience.When younger men
eventually returned to Masonry, as I expected they would, they would want
to find an inviting place they wanted to join and remain a part of. This change
could only start with better-trained lodge officers. Stan Cazneaux and I took the
then only recently introduced wardens retreats and completely revamped them.
We added state-of-the-art leadership training, which Stan had experienced as a
senior executive at Pac Bell. We added significant Masonic education material—
not repeats of the tired bromides which people had been saying for years, but
new ways of looking at what our teachings mean and how they apply in a way
that Masons both young and old would find engaging. My 1985 grand oration,
entitled Masonry for the Twenty-first Century, was my road map. Our reimagined
wardens retreats became the gold standard in American Masonry, with many
Grand Lodges imitating what Stan and I had developed. I can see the fruits of
our labors in the continued improvement of these programs under our Grand
Lodge staff and how the quality of our Masonic leaders and the lodge experience has improved over the 35 years since I was installed junior grand warden.
Our Masonic Homes, Memorial Temple, and Foundation are today strong,
state-of-the-art charities. Increased professionalism at these charities began
with strategic changes in board membership, including my appointment of Stan
Cazneaux to the Masonic Homes board. We can thank Stan for his contributions
on that board, including his years as its president, as well as those of presidents
and later board chairs who followed him, including those of my brother and
Larry Adamson, and similar contributions by our volunteer leadership over the
years. We have also attracted, hired, and empowered top-quality, paid executives
and staff at our charities and Grand Lodge office. John Cooper’s contributions
as grand secretary have been noted. Allan Casalou is in my view the premier
grand secretary in American Masonry today. Unlike the 1980s, today we hire
the best person for the job, even if they are not a Mason or a man.
This overview should not lead you to believe that these changes were made
without opposition. Some of the old guard did resist. Even after I was GM, they
tried to get my successors to reverse many things I had done. The old guard
failed because there was nothing I did while in the line on which a consensus
among the line officers was not in place before they were implemented—a
novel approach to Executive Committee problem-solving which has endured
to the benefit of our craft.
Larry Adamson once asked me who in my opinion was the best grand master
in our history. I asked: For his term of office or his entire Masonic career? As
2

These commercialism rules were reorganized, made permanent, and supplemented to address
some additional issues by the adoption of Grand Master Stovall’s Recommendation No. 2 in 1995.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

23

a past grand master, I probably could have taken on a kingmaker role, but that
would have been antithetical to my view of a healthy craft. By my actions, I
have modeled that the kingmaker role is not appropriate in our Grand Lodge. I
have been fortunate to have chaired the Jurisprudence Committee for most of
the years since I was grand master. I did a major rewrite and reorganization of
our California Masonic Code in 2006. More importantly, I modeled appropriate
behavior by this committee. Before I was grand master, Jurisprudence would
largely have only one answer to any question, and most times that answer
advanced the policy goals of those on that committee. The long struggle to
update our commercialism rules is just one example of how this approach frustrated progress in our Grand Lodge. If the law had only one interpretation, as
Jurisprudence generally opined, then there would never be a need for lawyers!
Nothing is black or white. My approach was radically different. I am a business
lawyer. Good business lawyers do not give their clients one choice, but multiple
choices and the risks inherent in each. It is not our job to tell a client or the
grand master what to do, but to give him the tools to make his own decision.
Mentoring has been a large part of my Masonic service. I have taught classes
on mentoring. I taught one at the grand masters conference we hosted some
years ago. I explained how the best mentors are those whom you do not even
know are mentoring you! One of our past Grand masters was in the room and
came up afterward to ask if I had been mentoring him. This was a man older than
my dad. I told him yes, and with humor in my voice that was clearly understood
by both of us, said, “Had you just listened more, it would have been easier for
both of us!” We both then had a good laugh.
We stand on the shoulders of the Masons who preceded us. Among these
men, I will mention just two. Earlier in my remarks, I told of the assistant grand
lecturer who, while serving as grand master, tried to curtail the influence of
the kingmaker whose candidate he had defeated for junior grand warden. As
I also explained, this brother lost and he and his key supporters were frozen
out, beginning a rift that would widen over the years between the executive and
ritual sides of Grand Lodge. One of the men forced out was the assistant grand
lecturer for the old Division 5, then located in the Los Angeles area, whence this
dispute first arose. The executive and ritual sides of Grand Lodge wanted my dad
to be the AGL of this division because they felt that Dad could bring the parties
together. Dad was charming. Everybody loved Dad. Like Tom Sawyer, he could
get the boys to paint Aunt Polly’s fence. When the AGL offer was pending, Dad
was also offered an important job promotion which required him to move to
Texas. General Telephone saw in Dad what our Grand Lodge saw. After great
thought, Dad took the job promotion and declined AGL, knowing he would
never be grand master. No one can know how the history of our Grand Lodge
might have been different had Dad said yes. Dad was then only 42, the same age
I was when I was installed grand master. I looked like Dad (except for the red
hair) and talked like Dad, which is why I got on the PGM radar so soon after I
became a member of Grand Lodge—just four years after Dad moved to Texas.

24

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

I am maybe 60 percent Dad in the charm department, but Mom was the brains
of the operation, and I am 120 percent Mom in that department.
The other Mason I will mention is Myron Smith, a prior recipient of the
recognition I am receiving now. Myron was one of my mentors. He accelerated my election to the line. When an attempt was hatching at a past grand
masters meeting to stop my progression through the line by those who felt
threatened by me, Myron warned me. I armed him with what I was uncovering
and the steps I was taking to bring change. Myron replied that he would have
my back. No more attempts were made to get me out of the line. The deputy
grand master and grand wardens are members of the Junior Grand Warden
Recommending Committee today because Myron was first to the microphone
and spoke eloquently in favor of my Recommendation No. 8.3 Many of the past
grand masters in the room that day opposed this recommendation, but none
of them would speak after Myron. Myron often said, “Speak of a brother to
praise him.” Now, that is something Dad would have said. Mom, not so much.
I have not always been true to Myron’s advice. I have probably broken many
more eggs than Dad or Myron would have, but the cake we have made is far
bigger and better as a result.
Success has many fathers and comes through hard work over many years,
and we now can see more clearly the fruits of our labors: a membership that
is about to grow again and the chartering of many energetic and creative new
lodges with young men I predicted in 1985 would eventually knock at our door
and stay, if we were ready for them. I am gratified by your recognition of my
contributions to this success.
At 11:56 a.m., the grand master called Grand Lodge from labor to refreshment, to be called on again on at 1:15 p.m.

Biography of the Junior Grand Warden Recommendee
Brother Christopher D. “Chris” Smith was initiated into Allen Lodge No. 81
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Oklahoma on October 23, 1995.
He was raised a Master Mason on January 26, 1996. Shortly after moving to
California in 2003, he affiliated with Peninsula Lodge No. 168. He served as
master of the lodge for three years from 2009 to 2012 and was presented the
Hiram Award from that lodge in 2013. Brother Smith is also a charter member
of Columbia Historic Lodge and Sonora Lodge U.D.
Smith has served as a district inspector for nine years. In 2018, he was
appointed as senior grand deacon by Most Worshipful Stuart A. Wright. He has
also served on several Grand Lodge committees, including the Grand Master’s
Special Task Force on Recognition, the Special Committee on Leadership
Development, and the Lodge Leadership Committee. He has also served on
the board of trustees for the Masonic Homes of California.
Smith became a Scottish Rite Mason in the Valley of McAlester, Oklahoma
in 1996 before affiliating with the Valley of Burlingame in 2011. He has been

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

29

coroneted as a 33° inspector general honorary of the Supreme Council Southern
Jurisdiction, USA. He is the assistant to the personal representative of the Valley
of Burlingame. He served on the boards of the Burlingame and San Francisco/
Burlingame Childhood Language Centers and is currently chairman of the board
for Burlingame. He is on the board of directors and the governance committee of
the California Scottish Rite Foundation. He is also a York Rite Mason, a Shrine
Mason, a member of the Royal Order of Scotland, the Grand College of Rites
of the USA, and the Red Cross of Constantine.
Smith grew up in Oklahoma and received a bachelor’s of science in physics
from East Central University, a master’s of science in electrical engineering from
Oklahoma State University, and a Ph.D in electrical and biomedical engineering
from Purdue University. While at Purdue, he was a bagpiper and pipe major
with the 42nd Royal Highlanders. He has had a 24-year career in technology;
for 13 years, he was a senior research engineer at SRI International. He was a
vice president at Mastercard and held senior technology roles at other financial
technology organizations. Since 2020, he has been the chief technology officer
for the Masons of California.
Brother Smith lives in Redwood City with his wife, Lynise, and their five
furry children: Charlie, O’Malley, River, Roberts, and Simon.

Grand Master’s Lifetime Achievement Award
The grand master announced that in the business session earlier that morning he shared that the recipient of the Grand Master’s Lifetime Achievement
Award was Most Worshipful Brother R. Stephen Doan. He then called on Most
Worshipful Brother John L. Cooper III, a recipient of the Grand Master’s
Lifetime Achievement Award, to share a biographical sketch, which follows.
It is a distinct honor to have been asked by our grand master to introduce a
brother Mason on this very special occasion and for a most meaningful purpose.
R. Stephen Doan served as grand master of Masons in California from 1992 to
1993 and is one of the most well-known Masons in our jurisdiction—and indeed,
throughout the Masonic world. It would be a trite comment to state that he
“needs no introduction,” but it is more true of Steve than anyone else that I
know. You know R. Stephen Doan, and you know what he has contributed to
Freemasonry in general and to our Grand Lodge in particular. Today, however,
I would like to share some background information about him that you may
not be as familiar with.
First, let me share some family background. R. Stephen Doan was born on
October 17, 1949, in Santa Monica, California, to Robert W. and Barbara Sebring
Doan. He is married to the former Donna Heederik and they have four children:
daughter Stephanie, son-in-law Brian P. Bezner, son Robert, and daughter-in-law
Erin. They also have two granddaughters, Brianna and Charlotte Bezner. His
father, Robert Doan, was an inspector when I was an officer for my home lodge,
Culver City-Foshay Lodge No. 641 in Los Angeles. I knew Steve and his family
before he became a Mason, and he and I both had our Masonic “beginnings” in
the Order of DeMolay. Among other things, Steve was Master Councilor of the
Jurisdiction of Southern California—an early promise of his success in elective
offices in Masonry. Steve’s family is also the only California Masonic family with
two grand masters. Steve was the first, but his brother, David Doan, also served
our Grand Lodge as grand master.
Professionally, Steve was—and is—a lawyer. After graduating from the
University of California, Los Angeles, with top academic honors, he pursued his
legal education at the UCLA School of Law. He is now in law practice with his
daughter, Stephanie. Incidentally, Stephanie’s husband, Brother Brian Bezner,
served as our grand orator when I was grand master and has had his own distinguished Masonic career.
It is difficult to single out the most significant of Steve’s public and civic
accomplishments, as there have been so many over the years. So I will only

34

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

mention one, which I think best represents Steve’s commitment to the principles
of Freemasonry. Since 1985, he has served as a board member of the Midnight
Mission in Los Angeles and has held the positions of president and chairman of
the board for many of those years. The Midnight Mission is the largest human
service enterprise in Southern California, helping men and women who have
fallen on hard times find the life they deserve as children of God. The Midnight
Mission is almost a Masonic enterprise because so many of its leaders are—and
have been—Masons. It is an institution that takes our Masonic obligations seriously, offering an example that, as our ritual says, is “worthy of all imitation.”
Steve has also found time in his busy life to be an active member of his
church. He is currently a member of St. John Fisher Church in Rancho Palos
Verdes and an extraordinary minister of Holy Communion, taking the sacrament
to those who are unable to attend church on a regular basis.
As an active Freemason, you would expect Steve to have been honored by
the many branches of our fraternity—and that is indeed the case. He is a 33rd
degree Scottish Rite Mason and has presided over some of the most prestigious
organizations associated with our gentle craft. Among others, he was the national
head of the Red Cross of Constantine and now serves as its national secretary.
Steve is also a respected Masonic scholar. He is a fellow of the Philalethes
Society, the oldest and largest Masonic research society in America, and was
its president from 2018 to 2020. He was recently the grand treasurer for the
Grand Chapter of California of the Order of the Eastern Star.
In our Grand Lodge, Steve is not only a past grand master but has chaired
the Grand Lodge Jurisprudence Committee for several terms of office. He is
the author of the fourth edition of the California Masonic Code, and his legal
scholarship underpins much of what we do in our Grand Lodge today. I had the
privilege of serving with Steve during the years I was grand secretary and again
through the years of the elective line in becoming grand master. I can confidently
assure you that I have never met anyone who more closely represents the ideals
we practice in Freemasonry than Steve does. Although he is younger than I am,
Steve has been a mentor to me for many, many years.
Thank you, grand master, for the privilege of sharing this with our Grand
Lodge!
The grand master then asked Most Worshipful Brother R. Stephen Doan
to share remarks, which follow.
In Grand Lodge today, I shared my perspective on my service to the Grand
Lodge. In 1989, when I was 39, I was asked to join the Grand Lodge line at a
time of great trouble in our craft, not just declining membership and leadership challenges, but a growing lack of confidence that we could right the ship.
I brought a skill set and a vision. I was confident that someday many more
young men like me would be drawn to the craft’s timeless teachings unfolded
through a deep brotherhood with other men on the same journey. To prepare
for that day, I worked to re-imagine the craft as something these men would
want to join and remain active members of, and I had a blueprint, my 1985

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

35

grand oration entitled Masonry for the Twenty-first Century. Success has many
fathers and comes through hard work over many years, and we now can see
more clearly the fruits of our labors: a membership that is about to grow again
and the chartering of many energetic and creative new lodges with young men I
predicted in 1985 would eventually knock at our door and stay, if we were ready
for them. I am gratified by your recognition of my contributions to this success.
The grand master then introduced Shaina Evoniuk and the Luminescent
Grand, who entertained the audience for the evening.

The Grand master called on the four youth leaders of the three Masonic youth
orders in California.
Miss Rylin Gamble
Miss California Job’s Daughters
Hello, worshipful grand master, grand officers, Masons of California, and distinguished guests! I am Rylin Gamble, your Miss California Job’s Daughter and
I am thrilled to be here today.
Job 42:15: “In all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of
Job, and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren”. This is the
verse upon which Job’s Daughters is founded.
In this verse, at a time when female children were seen as a burden, Job
demonstrated that he loved his girls equally to his boys… and he backed it up
with action. “...and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren.”
I believe that our founder, Ethel T. Wead Mick, chose this verse with purpose. The order we now know as Job’s Daughters International was founded
during a time when women were fighting for the right to vote; to be seen as
equals. She chose this verse because Job set an example of equality for women.
It became her great work to create an order that gives girls the skills that they
could apply to their careers and daily lives. Job’s Daughters was then, and is
now, over 100 years later, a place for young women to come together to learn
skills such as public speaking, communication, running meetings, and the
importance of community service that will build our members into the leaders
of today and tomorrow.
The final question at the Miss California Job’s Daughter Pageant this year
was: Imagine that you are Miss California Job’s Daughter. You have just finished giving a speech and are approached by a member of the Masonic family,
asking how they can support Job’s Daughters through ways other than giving
a monetary donation. How do you respond?
When I answered, I talked about the time our lodge’s worshipful master
attended our bethel meeting. It was my first term as honored queen, and his first
experience with Job’s Daughters. I don’t know who was more excited—him or
me! I have talked about that night more times than I can remember because it
had such an impact on me and all of my bethel sisters. The mere act of sitting

38

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

on the sidelines during a meeting gave all of us the opportunity to share our
hard work as well as a renewed sense of purpose. Someone was watching; they
cared and they wanted us to succeed.
As we enter the next 100 years of Job’s Daughters International, I would
like to challenge the Masons of California to attend a meeting at your local
bethel. Sit on the sidelines and watch the daughters practice their spoken work
and run their business meeting. Through your presence, you are supporting
the girls. I know from experience that even a single sideliner can get daughters
excited for their meeting.
My theme for this year is “Rattle the stars.” I am here today to ask you to
help me continue the great work that was exemplified by Job and inspired Ethel
T. Wead Mick to create our great order—to lift up the girls and help them not
only reach for the stars but to grab hold and rattle them. It sounds hard at first,
but the journey starts with taking a seat at the bethel.
I am the daughter ambassador for my order to you. It is my job to strengthen
our connection so that we may continue to thrive together and inspire future
generations. If you wish to know more about becoming involved with a bethel
in your area, please come talk to me. Thank you all for having me here this
afternoon. It has been my pleasure to be here this weekend. Thank you again
for this honor.
Mr. Nicholas Bonnin, Master Councilor

As I look around the room this morning, I see so many different faces,

However, above that all, I see the strength of our Masonic family. I see our
shared goals of creating better people and a better world, and most importantly

I see the impact it has had on all our lives.
Each of us here today has a unique story to tell, but we are united by our
values of brotherhood and service, and by our goals of being better leaders and
better men.
Today we find ourselves in a world filled with many challenges and hard
decisions. When you look around your communities you find hundreds if not
thousands of young men struggling to find themselves, struggling to become
the right-thinking men that this world needs.
These young men need role models, they need mentors to be a guiding light
to help them navigate through the complexities of life. They need someone to

I owe the fundamental features of my character to DeMolay and our Masonic

This year Northern California DeMolay’s theme is “Steampunk.” To put
that into context, think of our youth as an engine with the Job’s Daughters,
Rainbow Girls, and DeMolay as the pistons; our shared goals represented the
fuel; our virtues represented by the gears. And finally, you all—as mentors, as
role models, as Masons—are the mechanics. Greasing up the gears, fine-tuning
the machine, and giving it the right tweak so that the machine runs smoothly
to create the best results, and to produce the best leaders.
I encourage each and every one of you to invest in the youth orders. Invest
not only financially but invest your time, invest your effort into the youth orders.
Be the mentors and role models that the young men in DeMolay so desperately

Join us in our efforts to accomplish our shared goals and join us as we lead

It has been my sincere honor and pleasure to speak to you this morning,

International Order of Rainbow, California
Most Worshipful Grand Master Metroka, officers and members of the Grand
Lodge, distinguished and honored guests, and friends of California Rainbow,
hello!
I am honored to be with you today in gorgeous San Francisco to bring greetings on behalf of the youth leaders of California Rainbow. I am also delighted to

40

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

introduce to you some of my fellow grand officers, as well as our state parents
for Grand Assembly 2025.
When was the last time you stopped and watched the sunset—its pink,
orange, and purple hues giving one last show before retiring for the night?
How often do you watch the sun rise over the horizon? The golden rays of the
sun promising a new day full of opportunities. Have you ever watched a full
moon from the darkness of the wilderness, or been fortunate enough to see
the Northern Lights in person? Who here has been reassured by the gentle,
calming light of a thousand candles or fascinated by the consistent beacon of
light from a lighthouse?
Light is powerful. No matter the source, or purpose, light has the power to
brighten our days and light our pathways. Light really is essential in our lives.
Without it, our days would be dark, and there would be nothing to signal the
beginning of a new day. Yet, we often forget the power of light and assume it
will always be present. Even worse, we take light for granted and forget that
we would be lost without its warmth and bright rays. However, light is also a
promise. Just as the last bit of light vanishes from our sky, it is peaking up over
the horizon of the other side of the world. How beautiful is that?
For me, though, light is so much more than any of these things. On
November 7, 2018, the lives of my entire community changed. Borderline was
an establishment that was constantly full of happy people, dancing and singing and having fun in a very safe city where nothing really bad ever happened.
Then, one fateful night, everything changed. Shots rang out, and at the end of
the night, 12 happy people, with so much life left to live, were no longer with us.
Our community was rocked to the core by the angry, hateful act of one person.
For our family, this was an even bigger blow, as one of my dad’s co-workers and
mentors was one of the ones whose family would never again be able to say,
“Be safe and come back home to us.”
Our community, in a state of shock, was left wondering what to do. We
were at a loss with how to begin to recover from such a tragedy. So, we did the
only thing that could be done. We gathered to remember. We remembered the
love, the happy times, and most of all we remembered the light of those who
were now gone. It started with one candle to signify the light of their loved one.
They then shared that light with another, and then another, and another. Soon,
the entire town was filled with the light of thousands of candles. A single light
was all it took to start our journey of healing.
A few months later, my family and I celebrated the lives of many fallen
law enforcement officers throughout the United States at the National Law
Enforcement Memorial in Washington D.C. At one of the more touching ceremonies, each person is given a candle, and then they are all lit at the same time.
Imagine 50,000 beacons of hope lighting up the National Mall. The comfort and
peace of light has never been better demonstrated than during these two events.
Even in the darkest of days, one, small, seemingly insignificant light, shared with
many, can create a warm glow that will overpower sadness, anger, and despair.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

41

While this turn of events was tragic, it impressed me with a valuable lesson.
Every path toward resilience, healing, and new beginnings is initiated with a
single spark. The same can be said for our Masonic family. Our orders were
decimated due to Covid, however we did not let that stop us. Instead, all it took
was one person’s spark to begin the process of coming back. We could have
stayed in the darkness. We could have accepted our fate and our orders could
have dwindled to nothing, but they didn’t. We allowed ourselves to be driven
to create new opportunities and growth in our orders, and look at us now, we
are thriving. However, it doesn’t stop here.
Each of us has been given a unique light. It is our obligation and a very special gift to share that light with others. However, so many are afraid of sharing
their light, and still others aren’t really sure what light they have to share. Still
others think they have no light to share. But here’s the truth: We all have a light
to share! Many of you, right now, may be asking yourselves, “How do I find that
bright light?” The simple answer is, Share what brings you joy.
Telling a joke, woodworking, gardening, playing chess or card games, sharing
your love of a sport, or really anything can spark a light in someone. Sometimes
just sitting and listening can be your light. It takes very little effort to share
your light, and when you do, it will create a chain reaction that will light the
entire world.
As Masons, you have a unique opportunity to “Share the Light of
Freemasonry” with all the youth orders. Rainbow Girls love the support of
Masons. You may be surprised that the girls are truly interested in more than
just your attendance at a spaghetti dinner or an occasional meeting. They want
you to share your light. They want to partner with you at community events.
They want to learn how to do woodworking and want to go to a baseball game
with you. Many Rainbow Girls are not fortunate to have a father figure in their
lives and need you to be that example. Most of all, Rainbow Girls need you to
share your knowledge and wisdom in all aspects of life. Don’t take your light
for granted. Share your light. It has wisdom and power and love and can change
the world, one girl at a time.
Thank you once again, Most Worshipful Grand Master Metroka for inviting
me to speak to you today, and I cannot wait to share our light with all of you
at our When The Clock Strikes 12: Let Your Dreams Come Alive in 2025 Grand
Assembly Sessions, from April 5–8 in Visalia. Thank you!
Bro. Conner Bezner, Master Councilor,
DeMolay International, Southern California
This year, Southern California DeMolay is working under the theme of “Evolving
DeMolay.” As an early 2000s baby, I grew up playing Pokemon. I grew fascinated with the cute and scary monsters who could do fantastic things. When I
got older, I still loved Pokemon, but now it was about the fact that there were
strategies and synergies that make a team even stronger. Then I joined DeMolay

42

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

and couldn’t stop seeing the parallels between DeMolay and Pokemon. In both,
there is a story that you have to complete, but though the end is the same, the
journey is not. Growth is a key detail in both especially evolution. Evolution
is the natural process of the world and how we become better men and better
leaders.
Our order is going through an evolution. We are changing at an incredible
rate with a steep learning curve. Trying to lead a jurisdiction alone is like going
up against a Pokemon champion with only a level-five pidgey. However, that’s
why we don’t do it alone. Having my officers, advisors, leagues, and chapters is
like adding more Pokemon to my team. Now, it’s not the one pidgey; we have a
whole team. All we need to be ready to take on the elite four is a proper trainer.
That’s where you all come in. You, the Masons of California, are the trainers
of our teams. You are the advisors of our chapters, and if you aren’t yet, you
should find the chapter/bethel/assembly nearest you and see what you can do to
help. Or, to paraphrase John F. Kennedy, ask not what our youth can do for you,
ask what you can do for our youth. Or, to quote our grand master, “share the
light of Freemasonry” with those around you. Sharing the light of Freemasonry
isn’t just about getting people to join, it’s about sharing your experience, your
wisdom, and the teachings of Freemasonry.
There is no better time to share your light than yesterday, but the present
is a pretty close second. As the grand master reminded us at our conclave with
a beautiful piece of the DeMolay ritual from the closing paragraph of the ceremony of light: “Each of you holds within your heart a flame. A beacon to guide
you through the darkness. And if you can make this light shine upon another
if you can reach into the innermost depths of his soul and set his flame afire.
Then therein lies the purpose of the Order of DeMolay. And therein lies your
purpose for living.”
That’s all I ask of you. Share the light of Freemasonry with our members!
Become our friends, our mentors, our advisors. Be the trainers that help DeMolay
evolve to the next level. Be there to help us as we evolve into the Masons of
tomorrow!
Thank you.

Robert Lewis Pawneshing
Robert Lewis Pawneshing, affectionately known as Bob, has been a dedicated
member of Lakewood Masonic Lodge No. 728 since being raised to Master
Mason in 1999. His leadership and commitment to the lodge are evident through
his service as worshipful master in 2008, 2009, 2010, and 2023. In recognition
of his exceptional contributions, Bob was honored with the Hiram Award in
2011. His unwavering focus on brotherhood, fellowship, and service has been
the cornerstone of his Masonic journey.
Bob’s dedication extends beyond the lodge to his impactful work with Job’s
Daughters. He has served as associate bethel guardian and is a past associate
bethel guardian for Bethel No. 161 in Long Beach. Additionally, he has held the
role of guardian treasurer for Bethel No. 2 in Culver City, where he actively
engaged the daughters in bookkeeping and financial oversight. Bob’s philosophy of empowering young women through leadership and financial literacy
has helped many daughters gain confidence and take ownership of their bethel.
At the California Grand Guardian Council level, Bob has chaired the grand
bethel volleyball competition and currently co-chairs this esteemed event. He
also coordinates and hosts the annual Men of Job Luncheon at Grand Council,
fostering fellowship among the men and Masons who serve as advisors and
mentors. His outstanding service was further recognized in 2011 when he was
appointed as grand outer guard.
In his personal life, Bob is a retired executive from the grocery industry.
He is a dedicated husband to his wife of 40 years, Sherry, a proud father to his
daughters, Melissa and Amanda, and a devoted grandfather to his granddaughters, Abigail and Juliet. Bob exemplifies the spirit of an empowering advisor,
teaching Job’s Daughters to realize their potential and embodying the true
essence of Masonic brotherhood through joyful fellowship and selfless service.
Robert Lee Meyer
Robert Meyer has been a dedicated member of California Rainbow for over 20
years, making significant contributions both locally and at the state level. His
unwavering commitment to the organization has seen him serve in various
impactful roles.
As an active adult supporter, Rob has served as the chairman of the advisory
board for Camellia Assembly for over two decades. He has been instrumental in the success of the assembly’s annual fireworks booth fundraiser, often
taking time off work to ensure its smooth operation. His dedication extends to
California’s Northern Rainbow Camp, where he has worked diligently behind
the scenes.
At the Grand Assembly each year, Rob has played a crucial role on the
security team, eventually becoming the chairman. His efforts have ensured
a safe environment for all attendees. In recognition of his exemplary service,
Dana Regier, supreme inspector, appointed him as State Rainbow Dad for the

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Milestone Making Meerkats in 2022. His dedication and support of the grand
officers that year have fostered lasting relationships.
Rob’s commitment to supporting Masonic youth is further exemplified
through his involvement with California Rainbow. His daily interactions with

development and well-being.
Robert Meyer is a shining example of a Mason dedicated to supporting
Masonic youth. His selfless service and dedication to the values of the organization make him a deserving recipient of the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award.
Ever Edgardo Mendoza
Ever Mendoza, fondly known as DadMendoza to many young men, has been an
ardent supporter of DeMolay in Southern California and a shining example to
both the young men of DeMolay and their adult advisors. He became a Master
Mason and a DeMolay advisor in 2012, immediately emerging as one of the most
involved advisors in the Southern California jurisdiction.
Brother Mendoza was introduced to Masonry by his employer and mentor,
Albert Davidoo, whose dedication to the Shrine Hospitals and Masonic youth
orders inspired Ever to join Van Nuys Lodge No. 450. Motivated by this influence, he encouraged his sons to consider DeMolay membership.
Ever embraced the challenge of developing the fledgling Hollywood Chapter,
becoming chapter dad and guiding its growth. Under his leadership, Hollywood
Chapter quickly became a leading chapter in the jurisdiction, earning the Chapter
of the Year award multiple times. His mentorship nurtured many outstanding
DeMolays, including his son, who served as the Southern California jurisdiction
master councilor. Even after his sons reached majority, Ever continued to serve
DeMolay with unwavering dedication as a chapter and league advisor, ensuring
Hollywood remained exemplary.
In recognition of his commitment, Ever Mendoza has been honored as the
Southern California Jurisdiction Advisor of the Year and received the DeMolay
Cross of Honor and Honorary Legion of Honor. Known for his hard work and
humility, Brother Mendoza remains a beloved mentor to the young men of
DeMolay and exemplifies the support and encouragement California Masons
can and should provide to our Youth order members.
Steven Kolden
Brother Steven Kolden, a dedicated member of Crow Canyon Lodge No. 551, was
raised as a Master Mason in 1984 and served as marshal in 2019. In the Order
of Eastern Star, Steve has shown exceptional dedication, serving as worthy
patron five times and earning recognition as the Best Overall Ritualist in 2018.
