REPORT OF THE GRAND MASTER
My dear brethren and friends,
Greetings and welcome to the 175th Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of California.
As required by Section 404.130 of the California Masonic Code, I’m pleased to
present to you this message chronicling my official acts, the general condition
of Masonry in our jurisdiction, and the recommendations which I believe are
necessary for the future welfare of the craft. This oral presentation will not
include my entire report, but will focus on several important points which I
believe deserve the emphasis of a personal presentation here. The entire report
may be read in the published Proceedings of this Annual Communication.
Later in this communication, I will present to you my recommendations for
your consideration.
Official Acts
This year, as in nearly every previous year in the history of our Grand Lodge,
there has been a mix of positive and negative actions taken by the grand master.
At the beginning of this term, I continued my predecessor’s suspension of
the charters issued to Palm Springs Lodge No. 693 and Colusa Lodge No. 240.
I am pleased to report that Colusa Lodge subsequently met the conditions for
restoration of their charter, as set forth in the suspending edict, and that charter
has been restored. Palm Springs Lodge continues to struggle in correcting their
deficiencies and has not met the conditions for restoration of that charter. I
continue to hope that the lodge will ultimately overcome these challenges, and
I am recommending that my successor continue the suspension of this charter,
to allow the lodge more time to implement the necessary corrections.
On November 22, 2023, I ordered suspension of the charter of Angels Gate
Lodge No. 198 for various violations of the California Masonic Code, including
reducing our cipher ritual to plain language. During the ensuing investigation, I
received evidence that the Master of the lodge gave false testimony and coerced
other members of the lodge to do the same, in an apparent effort to impede
the investigation. Consequently, I suspended the Master from office, issued a
written reprimand to the former Master, ordered that the reprimand be read
during the June stated meeting of the lodge, and that it be entered into the
permanent record of the lodge’s proceedings. Despite the failings of the former

52

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Master, Angels Gate Lodge met the conditions for restoration of their charter,
which has been returned.
On July 5, 2024, I ordered the suspension from office of the master of
Harding San Juan Lodge No. 579 for allegations of inappropriate physical contact with the spouses of two other Masons and for his provocative response
to those complaints.
On August 1, 2024, I ordered the suspension from office of the master of
Destiny Lodge No. 856 for violating Section 806.000 of the California Masonic
Code regarding actions of the lodge’s Charity Committee and for his circumvention of the provisions of the Code regarding approval of disbursement of
lodge funds.
I received requests from two former lodge masters who were removed
from office, pursuant to the edicts of my predecessors, suspending their lodges’
charters, asking to be designated past masters under Section 805.020 of the
Code. I denied both requests because I believe they each failed to fulfill their
duties as master and those failures contributed to the suspension of the charters.
During the investigation which led to the suspension of the charter issued
to Angels Gate Lodge, a pattern of mistreatment and physical abuse of prospects, candidates, and members came to light. The evidence indicated that the
alleged abuser had engaged in this reprehensible conduct for more than 20
years, without any complaint being pursued. After reviewing the evidence, I
ordered the filing of Masonic charges under Section 1401.010 of the California
Masonic Code and suspended the alleged abuser from all the rights and benefits
of Masonry pursuant to Section 404.130 of the Code.
I have subsequently been informed that the practice of various forms of
humiliation and physical abuse of candidates exists in other California lodges.
Some of our members have suggested that this horrible “tradition” has been
imported to our lodges by Masons who were raised in other jurisdictions, where
the practice is or has been common. Some of these men believe that they must
perpetuate this crime because they were subjected to it when they joined—
something akin to a belief that “if I had to endure it, everyone should have to.”
Clearly, that approach is immature and cannot be sustained by true Masons.
To bring this potential problem into the light, I issued a letter to all lodges
and members in this jurisdiction, addressing the mistreatment of prospects,
candidates, and members. In the letter, I made it clear that such behavior constitutes unmasonic conduct in California, would not be tolerated, and would
be swiftly prosecuted. I also informed our members and lodges how best to
address cases of abuse, when discovered, how to root it out and take action to
ensure this abusive behavior is stopped. All good and true Masons know that
there is no place in our gentle craft for the mistreatment of anyone. There is
no safe haven in this jurisdiction for those who think otherwise.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

53

Making Masons at Sight
On January 16, 2024, I attended an Entered Apprentice degree at Madison Lodge
No. 23. This was a double degree and one of the candidates, Arlie Thompson,
was nearly 89 years old. Despite his best efforts, his limited hearing and mobility made it very difficult to fully participate in his initiation. The lodge took
appropriate steps to accommodate Brother Thompson, but the ordeal was still
unreasonable.
After the degree, I spoke with Brother Thompson and learned that his father
was a past master and very engaged in Masonry. I also learned that Brother
Arlie had an excellent opinion of Freemasonry and a sincere desire to join our
fraternity. He intended to apply to join for most of his adult life, but never
seemed to find a place to fit in, until he became acquainted with members of
Madison Lodge last year.
I later spoke with the master of the lodge and expressed my willingness to
make Brother Thompson a Master Mason at sight. On January 30, I convened
Madison Lodge No. 23 and, with the consent of all members present, I made
Brother Arlie Thompson a Master Mason at sight. Brother Thompson now
regularly attends lodge and is a very proud and grateful Mason.
On May 15, 2024, at the request of Nevada Lodge No. 13, I made Brother Brad
Robbins a Mason at sight. Brother Robbins had previously been a regular visitor
to Nevada Lodge and to Evangeline Chapter No. 9 of the Order of Eastern Star.
Though he had a longstanding desire to become a Mason, his physical condition
prevented him from participating in the Masonic degrees and he didn’t pursue
this dream. Brother Robbins is a rare survivor of cystic fibrosis, a disease which
has impaired his mobility and hearing. Since being made a Mason at sight, he
is actively participating in his lodge, has joined the Order of Eastern Star, and
will be installed as an officer in Evangeline Chapter next month.

General Condition of Masonry
in this Jurisdiction
New Lodges
We have instituted six new lodges and constituted five lodges this year, which
may be viewed as a good indication of the relative health of our Grand Lodge. I
issued dispensations to sundry brethren who have formed Sonora, Kapayapaan
at Pagkakaisa (a Tagalog phrase meaning “Peace and Harmony”), Wayfarers,
Royal Street, High 12, and Citlati lodges. As approved during our last annual
communication, charters have been issued in the appropriate constitution
ceremonies to the following lodges: La France, Mission Peak, Pilares Del Rey
Salomon, Palos Verdes, and Edwin Sherman Research.
I believe it is important that we continue to encourage and assist our

54

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

brethren in forming new lodges. Each one provides additional opportunities to
actively engage Masons in the work of the craft and in service to our communities. Through focused analysis, we have learned that most lodges can only truly
engage 30 to 40 members at any one time. Members in excess of that number
rarely participate and many simply stop showing up, because there isn’t any
reasonable way for them to contribute or engage. I recognize that a percentage
of our members live too far away from their lodges to regularly participate, and
others are advanced enough in age that attendance is not a reasonable option.
Still, there remain many others who can participate and do not.
We can and must develop a better and more effective model in California.
We have proven that we have a strong new lodge development program and the
forecast there is good, though probably not enough in the short term.
Member Retention and Restoration
We must improve the way we address those members with whom we have lost
contact. We can no longer simply cancel their membership by pretending to
have made a satisfactory attempt to contact them, and when we have failed in
the attempt, suspend them without any further effort.
This year we implemented a member retention program which is designed
to help lodges regain contact with their “lost members” who were in arrears for
more than two years. Our Member Services staff worked diligently to contact
the brothers included in this program and helped them to regain good standing.
While the program is still in its infancy, 45 percent of the members in the initial
group have been contacted and restored to good standing, and we will continue
our efforts to contact the others. I am hopeful that this initiative will grow and
become a regular part of our program of support for our members and lodges.
When a lodge has a much larger membership, they tend to lose contact with
some of their brothers and this often results in suspensions for non-payment
of dues, not because these brethren are unable or unwilling to pay their dues,
but often because they don’t receive dues notices or otherwise know how to
make remittance.
I was dismayed to discover details of membership actions undertaken in our
largest chartered lodge. The lodge began this year with a total membership of
584. During this year, they have suspended 76 Masons for non-payment of dues
and have issued an additional 118 notices of intent to suspend. How could this
possibly be good for anyone? It certainly is not good for those brothers who will
summarily lose their membership in our beloved fraternity, and it isn’t helping
the lodge who has lost those members. Think of the effort involved in making
Masons, the hours of degree practices and conferrals and the associated costs,
only to throw it all away by not maintaining contact or engaging with members.
During MW John Trauner’s term as grand master, we implemented a
member restoration program which continues to this day and has been very successful. Participation in the restoration program by lodges is voluntary and 167
of our lodges have agreed to participate. Of the remaining 160 non-participating

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

55

lodges, some have not suspended any members for many years and do not have
any reason to participate. Among those lodges who have suspended members
for non-payment of dues and choose not to participate in the restoration program, some have stated that it is more important to them to recover all the
dues in arrears, and not “settle” for the $100 restoration fee, than it is to have
these brothers restored to good standing. I think this approach is unfortunate
and callous.
In March, we received a letter from the secretary of one of our lodges
informing us that they will no longer participate in the restoration program
because they have only retained two of the 14 members who were restored to
good standing in their lodge in 2020. Among those who were restored and are
no longer members in their lodge, one died, one resigned, three demitted, and
seven were subsequently suspended again.
I am sharing this with you preparatory to asking a question. How much do
you value your membership in our fraternity? It should not surprise you to hear
that I value my membership greatly, and I imagine all of you do as well. If that is
the case, how can we presume that our brothers value their membership any less?
Why do we continually act as if we don’t need to help our brothers remain
in good standing with their lodge? Perhaps some of you believe that it is only the
individual’s responsibility to retain contact with their lodge and that payment
of dues is not something the lodge should have to assist its members with.
We all have times in our lives when the daily struggle of living consumes
our attention and things like paying lodge dues falls in our list of priorities.
That cannot be reasonably construed to mean that the non-paying brother
doesn’t care or otherwise value his Masonic membership. We have all promised
to help one another and I believe that promise extends to the preservation of
membership in Freemasonry. We can and must do more in this area. Let’s stop
looking for reasons to suspend our members and start helping one another to
maintain good standing in our fraternity.
I think it is important to note here that we would have seen a growth in
total membership in our jurisdiction in each of the last three years, had it not
been for the losses resulting from suspensions for non-payment of dues.
During the last four years, our lodges have suspended 4,757 Masons—that’s
more than 10 percent of our total membership. Shocking as this is, the statistics
are improving. Last year, we suspended 873 members. In the 10 years prior to
the pandemic, we suspended an average of 1,415 annually. Our membership
retention and restoration programs are working.
Most suspended members we have contacted report that they were not
previously contacted by their lodge. The certified letters our Code requires a
lodge to send, prior to suspending a member, are entirely ineffective. Phone
calls work. Do not shortcut the process. Expediency is not an excuse for failing
to personally contact your lodge members.

56

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Truth, Justice, and Harmony
During this year, I have been asked to help resolve disputes between Masons
and their brethren and lodges and to forgive brothers for their transgressions.
Perhaps I am naïve, but I think the distinction between right and wrong is generally clear. In fact, I believe that most of us instinctively know the difference.
Nevertheless, we have more than a few Masons among us who seem to think
that it is OK to willfully violate their Masonic obligations. Some who think they
can prioritize their cultural norms over their pledges to be good and true. Our
teachings and obligations transcend culture. That is one of the principal aspects
that separates our order from much of the rest of humanity.
As Master Masons, we have all promised to not cheat, wrong, or defraud
our brethren or our lodges. We have promised to conform to and abide by all
the laws, rules, and regulations of our lodge and to maintain and support the
constitution and edicts of the Grand Lodge. Nevertheless, we have some brethren who think they are justified in violating these promises for expediency or
because they have decided that these regulations or our Grand Lodge are no
longer valid.
For these brethren, the options are few. Either you keep your promises for
the sake of honor or resign your membership in our jurisdiction. If you are not
the honorable person you presented to us when you joined our ranks, at least
have the decency to move on without trying to make this beloved institution
conform to your mistaken sense of reality.
Lodges that decide that they are no longer beholden to the Grand Lodge
that issued them a charter are free to surrender that charter and form their own
tradition in Freemasonry—albeit an irregular one. If you aspire to share in the
benefits of our history and the resources accumulated by our predecessors, you
must abide by our regulations, without fail.
Quasi-masonic organizations that are exclusionary and hurtful to other
Masons have no place in legitimate Freemasonry. Organizations like the Snakes
and the Travelers Tambyan are not likely to gain legitimacy in this jurisdiction
if they engage in exclusionary tactics, threatening behavior, hazing, and cultural
segregation.
We are all obligated to do our part in the maintenance of peace and harmony
within our lodges and among our brethren. It is not enough to simply ignore
the shortcomings of our brethren. We must assist one another to improve. To
achieve this goal, we must be tolerant, forgiving, and compassionate. We must
acknowledge that we are all going to make mistakes, and we must do as we
have been instructed—whisper good counsel and, in the most friendly manner,
endeavor to bring about a reformation. We should be allowed to recover and
learn from our mistakes when we sincerely desire to do so.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

57

Youth Orders
At the beginning of this term, I asked our lodges and members to increase
their active support of Masonic youth orders by engaging more Masons in the
service of our chapters, bethels, and assemblies and by developing an internal
program for identifying and recruiting Masons to serve as mentors and advisors
for our youth.
I visited each of our youth jurisdictions this year and participated in several of their local meetings and events. While I continue to hold hope for their
future, I don’t believe we made much progress in our efforts to improve our
support of these important Masonic family organizations this year. They are still
struggling and still need more Masons to directly participate in their activities.
Additionally, we all should routinely look for young people who might benefit
from membership in these organizations, and help them to connect with a
bethel, chapter, or assembly.
We should do this because our efforts will result in more skilled and confident citizens and leaders, not just because they might eventually join our
Masonic institutions. Some do choose to join our orders, but most reach their
majority having simply gained from the positive influence of our teachings
and examples. That is reward enough for our efforts! Please don’t give up on
Rainbow, Job’s, and DeMolay. We must help them to succeed.
Veterans Support
I began this year encouraging greater support of military veterans in our communities. On November 11, 2023, Margaret and I participated in a visit to the San
Francisco V.A. hospital, to look in on veterans there and give them winter coats
as a token of our appreciation for their service. It was a wonderful experience
and very well received by the patients we visited. This effort was supported by
our Grand Lodge staff, the California Masonic Foundation, the masters of each
of our San Francisco-based lodges, and the masters of lodges under the George
Washington Union Grand Lodge, Grand Orient of France, and Le Droit Humain.
Many of our lodges regularly provide support to military veterans and their
families in California. Of note is San Dimas Lodge No. 428, which has partnered
with their local Rotary Foundation and American Legion post for several years,
providing direct support to active-duty military families serving at 29 Palms
and Camp Pendleton Marine Corps bases and the U.S. Army’s Fort Irwin. They
provide food, clothing, gifts, and household items and donate holiday meals
to these families. San Dimas Lodge provides an excellent example of lodge
engagement with other worthy organizations in our communities. Together
we have a much greater positive impact. Also, their work greatly increases the
positive awareness of Freemasonry in the communities they serve.
Though not a program aimed at providing support to veterans, Ione Lodge
No. 80 has partnered with their city fire department and occasionally with
the Ione Police Department to provide and distribute teddy bears to children

58

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

involved in accidents and other traumatic events as a way of giving them a bit
of comfort in trying times. They call this effort the Masonic Care Bear Program
and each stuffed bear sports a shirt with “Masons Care” emblazoned on it.
This is another wonderful way to foster goodwill and positive awareness in
the community.
This year, we began the process of joining the Masonic Service Association’s
veterans visitation program. I am grateful to Brother Matt Schrader of Saddleback
Laguna Lodge No. 672 and Worshipful Brother Ed Vandiver of Penrhyn Gold
Hill Lodge No. 32 for their willingness to serve as our representatives in this
important program. I got a late start on this, so we are in the early stages of this
endeavor. My special thanks to Most Worshipful Stu Wright for his encouragement and support in developing this program in our jurisdiction.
California Masonic Foundation
Our principal charity continues to grow and expand the reach of service to our
fellow man in California and outside our jurisdiction. This year, we increased our
support to our Major League Baseball partner organizations and surpassed the
$2 million mark in total support since the inception of Masons4Mitts. Thanks
to the hard work of many of our lodges, several California Prince Hall lodges,
and the extraordinary contributions of several of our brothers, we are increasing the impact of this important program for youth in the major metropolitan
areas of California. Margaret and I were able to attend all four Masons nights
this year, and we had a wonderful time at each game.
Masons know that education, especially literacy, is essential to the preservation and success of a democratic government. Citizens must be functionally
literate to be able to fully participate in the democratic process.
This year, our Foundation expanded its reach in Northern California by
initiating relationships with the Sacramento City Schools’ vocational and technical programs and with the Washington School District in West Sacramento
by supporting the introduction of Raising a Reader in the district.
This latter program now provides books and related program material
published in Pashto, Dari, and English to Afghan refugee children and their
families. We are helping a new generation of immigrants to more quickly adjust
to their new home and ensuring that none are left behind through an inability
to communicate effectively. This new phase in the Raising a Reader program is
an important step in fulfilling the promise of a better life for our immigrants.
We’re proving, by our actions, that we are committed to improving literacy for
all members of our society, regardless of their origin or native language.
Fraternal Relations
This year we strengthened our relationships with the Most Worshipful Prince
Hall Grand Lodge of California and the Grand Lodge of Iran (In Exile). This
effort was greatly enhanced as we implemented the new admissions policy

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

59

adopted by the Masonic Homes of California late last year. Through this action,
we have given clear evidence of our commitment of support to all Masons in
California.
Additionally, I established a practice of periodically meeting with the Grand
Masters of these two jurisdictions to discuss current issues and opportunities. The result has been wonderful! We have elevated our mutual trust and
understanding and are truly living the promise of treating all our members as
“California Masons,” without the traditional separation of jurisdictional boundaries. I am deeply touched by the warm welcome I received by hundreds of our
brethren in our Prince Hall and Iranian grand lodges. This endeavor has greatly
enhanced our ability to work together and better understand the beauty of each
other’s traditions. This is a shining example of the essence of brotherly love.
As has been our practice for many years, we attended the communications
of the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Grand Lodge of Iran, Grande
Loge Nationale Française, Grand Lodge of the Philippines, York Grand Lodge
of Mexico, Gran Logia de Estado de Baja California, and the grand lodges of
Alaska, British Columbia and Yukon, Washington, Oregon, Nevada, Arizona,
and Hawaii. We also attended the annual Conference of the Three Californias
which was hosted this year by the Gran Logia de Estado de Baja California Sur,
in La Paz, Mexico. Our relationships with these grand lodges remain strong
and important to all of us.
We know that there are many other Masonic traditions practiced in our
state. Among them, we currently recognize the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of
California and the Grand Lodge of Iran. The fact that we don’t recognize any
of the other Masonic traditions in this territory doesn’t necessarily mean that
they are not practicing a regular form of Freemasonry. Generally, we make
recognition decisions based on what is commonly referred to as “legitimacy
of origin,” exclusive territorial jurisdiction (except by mutual consent and/
or treaty), and adherence to the Ancient Landmarks—specifically, a belief in
God, the volume of the sacred law as an indispensable part of the furniture of
the lodge, and the prohibition of the discussion of politics and religion. These
standards are not consistently or universally applied.
Much like our brethren in the United Grand Lodge of England, we have
learned that there are other Masonic traditions in this state which practice
a regular form of Freemasonry. In the last decade, we have been cultivating
relationships of association with some of the lodges and members of these
“unrecognized” traditions and have begun collaborating in our education,
charity, service, and social activities. For many of these lodges, we also provide
them a place to meet.
Recognizing that progress in these relationships will naturally be slow as
our understanding and trust of one another grows, I am hopeful that we can
find a way to acknowledge the inherent goodness of many of these other traditions and embrace them as our brothers and sisters in Freemasonry. I do not
propose that any of us should merge our traditions or change our membership

60

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

standards—doing so would certainly diminish the diversity, beauty, and usefulness of the whole of Freemasonry. I merely suggest that we can more fully
expand the good influence of our craft by working together than we would
otherwise if we remain at a perpetual distance.
Gratitude
I give my sincere thanks to the officers who have so well and faithfully served
our grand lodge this year. The members of our grand family have far exceeded
my greatest hopes and desires, and I am grateful to you all. Especially to our
elected officers, whose advice and counsel has helped keep me focused on the
best path forward when it wasn’t always clear to me.
I am thankful to many of our past grand masters for their assistance and
wise counsel, particularly to Most Worshipful Brothers John Cooper, Steven
Doan, Art Weiss, and David Doan. Also, to Most Worshipful Brother John
Trauner who, in many ways, paved the way for me to have this opportunity to
serve our Grand Lodge.
And finally, I express to you that I am most grateful to my wife Margaret
for her encouragement and support on this journey. She has walked beside me
every step of the way and has helped to make this year enjoyable and successful
in many unexpected ways.
To you, my dear brethren, I am sincerely grateful for this honor you have
given me. Thank you!
Respectfully submitted,

G. Sean Metroka, Grand Master

75

REPORT OF THE
DEPUTY GRAND MASTER
2024–2025 GRAND LODGE BUDGET

Dear masters, wardens, and esteemed members of the Grand Lodge,
I want to extend my heartfelt gratitude for your trust in me to craft
the budget for our upcoming fiscal year, November 1, 2024, through October
31, 2025. This budget reflects our collective commitment to the future of our
fraternity, building on the per capita proposal you endorsed last year.
As we navigate a 2.5 percent decline in membership this fiscal year, it’s
crucial to understand the broader context. While inflation is easing, its lingering
effects pose challenges. Our total budgeted revenue is slightly over $4.4 million, a 3 percent decrease from last year. Notably, per capita accounts for $2.3
million, covering about half of our expenses. This year, we anticipate a record
dividend of $507,000 from the Nob Hill Masonic Center, alongside $664,000
from investments and a generous $331,000 grant from the California Masonic
Foundation for leadership and education programs.
This budget supports vital initiatives, including:
• Masonic Education: Supporting programs like the International
Conference on Freemasonry and our Candidate Learning Center.
• Membership Management: Utilizing iMember to streamline operations across lodges.
• Financial Services: Offering accounting, dues collection, tax preparation, and support for lodges and halls.
• Leadership Training: Retreats and programs to equip our leaders for
success. These programs include the in-person retreats for lodge and
district leaders and the Lodge Management Certification Program.
• Membership Development: Connecting prospects to our lodges and
resources like the Simple Guide to Freemasonry.
• New Lodge Development: We’ve successfully established over 35
new lodges in California since 2016.

76

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

• Public Relations: Enhancing awareness of Masonry and encouraging
members to share their experiences.
Economic pressures have prompted us to enhance efficiencies across our operations, programs, and services. We successfully reduced fraternal expenses by
over 10 percent compared to last year, while appropriations have remained flat.
Additionally, we managed to limit the increase in general and administrative
expenses to just 3.5 percent despite rising insurance and other costs.
I sincerely appreciate the efforts of our grand treasurer, grand secretary,
finance staff, and Finance Committee in shaping this budget. I also want to
thank our masters and wardens. Your feedback during our spring leadership
retreats has been invaluable.
As we move toward completion of our 2025 Fraternity Plan, I humbly ask
for your support in adopting this budget. Together, we can inspire our members,
strengthen our lodges, and make a meaningful impact in our communities.
Thank you for your dedication and commitment to our fraternity.
Sincerely and fraternally,

Arthur L. Salazar, Jr., Deputy Grand Master

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED
MASONS OF CALIFORNIA
Fiscal Year 2024/2025
Art Salazar, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue sources have been Per
Capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates income
from the investment returns. To better manage the income from the Endowment, a 4.5% spending policy has been
instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year market value average to protect the fund principle. The Grand Lodge has other
finance income, such as investment and interest income. The Grand Lodge receives dues from the Grand Master’s Lodge.
In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included in its mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership
training programs and now provides a grant for such purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual
Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by all applicants for the degrees of Masonry
and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge provides services throughout the state and receives reimbursement for
certain expenses incurred from the Masonic Services Bureaus funds. The Grand Lodge manages the investments of its
related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of providing those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole
shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc. and receives dividends on the profits of this Corporation. The Grand
Lodge also receives support from reserves generated from prior fiscal years' surplus/operating reserves to balance its
budget.

GRAND MASTER’S
INSTALLATION SPEECH
Thank you for being here on this beautiful Sunday morning to celebrate an
historic moment for the Grand Lodge of California. Not only are we celebrating
175 years of Masonry in California this year, but also, for the first time in those
175 years, we have had a Latino serving as grand master. And, at the age of 49,
I am also the youngest California grand master in modern history. I would like
to take a moment to reflect on this particular intersection of history and what
it means for our path forward. When we look at the state of California, we see
people coming from all over the world to enjoy the promise of a better life
and making this great state the most diverse in our country. When we look at
California Masonry, we see that diversity reflected in the faces of the 38,000
Masons who call our lodges home.
Within those lodges, we learn to see past the external characteristics of
mankind and witness the beauty of the divine that lives within each of us. It
doesn’t matter what language you speak, the color of your hair, the color of your
skin, your ethnicity, who you love, or whether you’re male or female. Masonry
teaches us that we are all children of the Great Creator and members of the
same family. With that divine inspiration, we can come together as brothers
and take the time to really get to know one another, to learn to appreciate each
other’s traditions, cultural celebrations, languages spoken, and for many the
incredible foods we each enjoy. Quite simply, we learn to appreciate and celebrate our differences as something that bring us closer together rather than as
something that divides us.
As I reflected on my journey in preparation for this next chapter, I realized
that it was important for me to embrace who I am. I’m a fourth-generation
Mexican descendant born in California who grew up with Spanish in my ears but
not on my tongue. I had to navigate learning about my cultural heritage while
being considered not Mexican or American enough, even though I carried both
in my heart. From these experiences, I learned that remembering where you
come from and celebrating that heritage does not take away from loving where
you are and the freedoms and opportunities that we are blessed with. I am an
American, I am from California, my family is from Mexico, and I am a Mason.
And today I honor that with a representation of my theme, which embraces
the influences on my cultural heritage. The color, style, border, and face within
the square and compass celebrate Aztec and Mayan culture which are at the

86

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

heart of Mexican culture today. The face is a representation of Quetzalcoatl, the
serpent god, who is the Aztec god of creation, light, and wisdom. And moving
in the direction of that light and wisdom is the California bear. This is who I
am as a California Mason. And at the center of it all is the single word of my
theme and a call to action for every Mason: Inspire
My hope is that my logo will inspire you to embrace who you are and be
willing to share your experiences and perspective with your brothers. But on
the other side of that is my hope that you will also be willing to open your
minds and hearts to learning about one another. When we as Masons learn to
embrace one another and truly exemplify our tenets within our lodge, we will
inspire one another to work toward becoming that better version of ourselves.
And when we achieve that, we will have created true friendship and harmony
within the walls of our lodges.
This year, there will be a number of projects you will see undertaken by our
Grand Lodge on your behalf. The details of those will be shared with you over
time through the leadership retreats as well as through your district inspectors.
These projects include developing the next evolution of our Grand Lodge’s
strategic plan, rolling out a plan to migrate lodges and hall associations from
Intacct to the accounting system available through Grand View, expanding
our member restoration program, assisting lodges with dues notices and dues
collection, and offering more online educational opportunities for lodge officers on topics relevant to lodge governance. These programs are essential to
helping lodges remain healthy from a financial and compliance perspective. I’m
asking you here today for your cooperation in implementing these programs
and your patience in working through the hiccups which we will inevitably face
along the way.
It’s important for all of us to remember that it is the responsibility of
our Grand Lodge to respond to the needs of our lodges and our members. All
of these administrative programs are the result of your requests for help to
lighten the administrative burden so that you can focus on what really matters:
practicing Masonry. It’s spending time coaching your candidates so they have
the opportunity to more fully understand the lessons of each degree, working
with your officer’s coach to learn to deliver the ritual in a meaningful way for
each candidate, and taking the time to explore the different forms of ritual used
throughout the world of Masonry.
As we begin our 175th year as the Grand Lodge of California, I’m asking all
California Masons to join together in service to our communities. Seek out your
local schools, first responders, veterans’ organizations, and youth organizations
and ask, “How can we help?” Be bold in showing them that, “We’ll get it done.”
On April 15, 1850, brethren from lodges originating from the District of
Columbia, Missouri, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Louisiana met in the city of
Sacramento to convene our first Annual Communication. This year on Thursday,
April 15, 2025, I’m asking all California Masons to make a special effort to engage
beyond their lodge and participate in a community service project on that day.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

87

Let’s show each of our communities that we care and are willing to step up
and be the hero.
Remember that you are not alone. Come together as a lodge. Come together
as a district. Come together with all of the members of the Masonic family in
your community. Lead the way in your community as the shining example of a
hero. Inspire them through your actions to join in the efforts to serve our fellow
man and lift one another up. Inspire them through your commitment to seek
out your lodge as a place where good things happen. Our communities will learn
about Masonry by how we communicate our values. But more importantly, they
will remember Masonry by how we made them feel with our actions.
I would like to leave you with this story. In 2011, our Grand Lodge initiated
a partnership with Raising a Reader. The incoming master of my lodge in Orange
County wanted us to participate in a meaningful way. He urged the members
of our lodge to work with a local elementary school to volunteer once a week
in an after-school reading program. Our members were so committed to this
program that for several years, we changed our work schedules to be there
every Tuesday afternoon. Over time, we began hearing from the teachers and
parents that the children were not only catching up with their classes, but that
they were actually falling in love with reading. The parents and teachers would
excitedly announce to the kids as we were walking up that “the Masons are here.”
After several years, the after-school reading program ended due to changes in
the school curriculum, but its impact lives on. In 2022, one of the graduating
seniors reminded me that we used to read with her after school for a couple of
years and that she was excited to be attending San Diego State that fall. That
young woman’s life was changed because a Mason asked “how can we help?”
and his brothers responded to the need with a resounding “we’ll get it done.”
Now imagine what the world would look like if we were able to live this
example and inspire all those around us to see what we see and to do what we
do. It starts to look like a world in harmony.
With our example of working together in harmony with those from all walks
of life and our desire to be of service to our community and be the hero who
gets it done, not only will the world know we have each become a better man
by becoming a Mason, but they, too, will be inspired by our actions, seeking out
Masonry and leading us into that next evolution of a world in harmony. Y por
eso los grandes amores de muchos colores me gustan a mi.
Thank you!
Respectfully submitted,

Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Grand Master

REPORT OF THE
SENIOR GRAND WARDEN
2025–2026 PER CAPITA PROPOSAL
Garrett S. Chan, Senior Grand Warden
Dear masters, wardens, and esteemed members of the Grand Lodge,
As senior grand warden, it is my duty to present to you the per capita proposal
which will fund the Grand Lodge budget during the fiscal year of November 1,
2025, through October 31, 2026. This per capita will be collected next summer
based on the number of Masons on the rolls of each lodge on June 30, 2025.
As the deputy grand master shared in his report, we are still being impacted
by lower membership and persistent inflation, but our opportunities for growth
and success are greater than our challenges. We know there is significant interest
in membership in Freemasonry. The thousands of prospects who have sought
us out are proof that Freemasonry is not only relevant and respected, but
greatly needed in our communities today. In drafting a budget for our Grand
Lodge, I have relied upon the best available data on membership trends and
various financial indicators to anticipate the trajectory of our challenges
and opportunities.
Through your efforts in working with prospects to become friends and then
brothers, I am optimistic that our membership will stabilize and could even
grow over the next few years. This will help offset the impact of post-pandemic
inflation across goods and services that all organizations must now face. In
Fiscal Year 2026, our plan accounts for just a 1.4 percent increase in expenses
over Fiscal Year 2025, including a slight 1.5 percent increase in general and
administrative expenses. This plan requires a $3.00 increase in per capita.
Therefore, the per capita I propose for the Fiscal Year 2026 is $68.50.
I am confident that this plan will serve the best interests of the fraternity.
With your support of this proposal, we will be able to continue delivering to
our lodges those important programs and services they have requested, such
as leadership training and education, communications, technology, financial
and administrative services, and the initiatives to increase positive public
awareness and membership growth.
Working together, I am confident that we can continue to create more

92

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

positive awareness of our fraternity, continue to improve the organization,
and grow our membership so that our lodges may prosper in harmony. I
look forward to being on this journey with you!
Sincerely and fraternally,
Garrett S. Chan, Senior Grand Warden

Revenue Analysis
PER CAPITA

Per capita provides approximately 53% of the Grand Lodge revenue. Applications, background
check revenue, and dues from the Grand Master's lodge make up roughly 3%. Investment Income,
Nob Hill dividend, transfers from prior years' operating surplus, Grant from the California Masonic
Foundation, and reimbursements from investments make up most of the remaining revenue. Total
per capita anticipated to be collected for FY25 is 5.1% more than what will be collected for FY25.

REPORT OF THE
GRAND TREASURER
Most Worshipful Grand Master and brethren all,
Serving as your grand treasurer for the third term, I am pleased
to report on the financial health of our Grand Lodge and its related entities.
We continue to benefit from the efforts and expertise of our brethren who
continue to volunteer their time as board members and committee members,
to include the expertise of our entire Grand Lodge financial services team led
by Carol Hunter, our CFO; Maribel Pasamic, our vice president of finance; and
ControllerKhalil Sweidy, our director of financial planning and real estate; and
of course, Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, our grand secretary.
The Audit Committee, led by Worshipful David Griffiths, continues to
work closely with Moss Adams, as our outside auditor, and ensures that our
financial statement audits for all of our Grand Lodge entities continue to go
smoothly. As of our last fiscal year, ending October 31, 2024, each of our entities
once again received a clean audit opinion and were informed that our internal
controls remain effective and that our model for shared service costs is not only
appropriate but consistent with best practices and within industry standards.
This fiscal year, ending October 2024, we will be audited by a new audit firm,
Armanino LLP.
The Finance Committee, led by Worshipful Steven Yeffa, continues to
bring its vast corporate experience to our budgeting process in working with
our deputy grand MMaster and senior grand warden to provide wise and timely
counsel in the preparation of their annual budgets and per capita calculations.
The Insurance Committee, led by Worshipful David M. Anderson, continues its untiring work in its detailed review of our vast and complex insurance
needs not only for our Grand Lodge entities but also for our lodges and hall
associations. Those members have been diligent in negotiating the premiums
of our insurance needs. As most of us are aware, the price of insurance has
escalated. This year we had a 7.55 percent average increase in premium costs
to our business entities due to rate increases and valuation adjustments. This
includes an ongoing review of claims to ensure a premier result for the benefit
of the craft and to find ways to deliver its services in the most cost-efficient
method possible.
The Investments Committee, led by our new chair, Bro. Fadel Lawandy, is

100

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

deeply immersed in itsongoing efforts to monitor the economic factors which
impact our portfolio. In their ongoing evaluation of our investment policies,
they recommend that 4.5 percent of our investment portfolio be distributed to
fund the Grand Lodge operating budget, aligned at preserving and growing our
overall portfolio for future use. The relationship with NEPC as our investment
advisory firm, which began seven years ago, continues to bring forward important discussions with our fund managers and to provide an in-depth analysis of
our asset allocations.
The following financial highlights are based on the unaudited results for the

from October 31, 2023. The audited financial statements for the current fiscal

upon publication.

Overall, our current Master Trust total as of July 31, 2024, is equivalent
to $1.05 billion, or a positive gain of $32.4 million from last year. The return
on investment for the year ending July, 31, 2024 was 3.2 percent and since the
inception of our Master Trust in January 1995 it remains at a healthy 7.5 percent.
While our Master Trust has gained a respectable size, we all must remember
that these funds are not available to simply withdraw to cover the expense needs
of the several entities. For best practices, we are limited to draw 4.5 percent up
to 4.75 percent of the 20-quarter average of the market value portfolio for the
investments of each entity to support their operations. The Masonic Homes and
Acacia Creek received a 4.75 percent distribution for fiscal year 2024. What this
means is that in the example of our Masonic Homes, with a current operating
budget of approximately $76 million each year and an investment distribution of
approximately $43 million, we have a delta of approximately $33 million that needs
to be made up from other sources such as fees for certain services and each of
our annual contributions in fulfillment of our ongoing obligations to each other.
In 1992, our Grand Lodge created an endowment funded by the budget
surplus of each grand master. Since that time, the Endowment Fund has grown
to $2.96 million as of July 31, 2024, from $2.82 million in July 31, 2023. This
allowed us to normalize our budgets and per capita assessments specifically
dealing with the economic impact brought about by the recent pandemic on our
operations at Nob Hill Masonic Center and the California Masonic Memorial
Temple. We have accrued these surpluses as deferred assets for our operating
reserves. This same Endowment Fund will now provide $177,627 for the budget
of Right Worshipful Salazar in the fiscal year ending October 31, 2025, compared
to the amount of $263,841 for the current fiscal year.
Participation in the Grand Lodge Life Membership Funds and the Grand
Lodge General Investments Fund has increased over the last year, allowing
lodges more flexibility in their investment strategies. As of July 31, 2024, we
have 64 lodges participating in the Life Membership Master Fund with a value of

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

103

$3.2 million from $2.9 million, and we have 37 lodges participating in the Lodge
Investments Master Fund with a value of $35.8 million, up from $31.4 million.
Our Grand Lodge financial services team continues to assist our lodge
officers and hall association directors in planning their budgets, bank reconciliations, administering their payroll needs and tax filings, addressing real
estate issues and needs, reconciling their month-end investments, and providing general accounting solutions in their day-to-day operations. We have
purchased Grand View together with other three other Masonic jurisdictions
not only just as an investment but as a tool to move and transfer the accounting
operations of our participating lodges to this platform, and at the same time
save on subscription costs with Intacct, our current provider. We have encouraged lodges and hall associations at all our retreats to take advantage of their
expertise and services, which allows our lodges the opportunity to focus their
attention on practicing Masonry and creating meaningful relationships with
the communities they serve.
I request the leadership of all our lodges to begin their budget discussions
as early as possible and present to your brethren a balanced, granular, and
transparent budget. Also, submit your year-end financial statements early so
we can accomplish the preparation of your hall and lodges tax returns in a
timely manner and avoid penalties. Allow us to assist you in unraveling some
of the mysteries in your lodge. It is always advantageous to obey the laws of
the country in which you reside!
I would like to thank Most Worshipful Metroka and all of you for allowing
me the opportunity to serve as your grand treasurer. I am honored working
with so many devoted and caring individuals. Once again, a special thank you
to my brother, colleague, and friend, Very Worshipful Allan Casalou. My three
years working with you has tremendously impacted my focus and enthusiasm
for serving the jewel of our craft, our Masonic Homes.
Finally, allow me to share a manifesto which was developed by a collaboration of our in-house team, outlining who we really are as Masons, why we
exist, and how we accomplish things. “Masons are builders. Where once we built
magnificent structures, today we build character. Steeped in tradition and ritual,
our values are based on a bedrock of friendship and philanthropy. We believe
that harmony between diverse individuals is a powerful force for good. And
just as ancient stonemasons perfected their craft, we employ timeless lessons
that create meaningful change in ourselves, stronger communities around us,
and a better world for all.”
Let harmony prevail!
Respectfully submitted,
Charles P. Cross, Grand Treasurer

REPORT OF THE
GRAND SECRETARY
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to present this, my 17th annual report as your grand secretary.

Membership Information
Current Membership Statistics
As of June 30, 2024, we had 37,240 active Masons, including 2,722 Entered
Apprentices and 864 Fellow Crafts. Our Masonic family also includes 12,011
widows. Please refer to my written report for detailed membership activity,
by-law amendments, life memberships, and veterans’ awards.

Priorities for 2024
As the facilitator of the administrative systems and programs at our Grand
Lodge, the Grand Secretary’s office prioritized five key areas in 2024: brand
awareness, membership and new lodge development, leadership development,
hall assessment and insurance, and technology enhancements. I am pleased to
report that we successfully achieved nearly all our objectives in these areas.
Brand Awareness: Freemasons globally have a well-established brand. Our
latest market research revealed that awareness of Freemasonry surpasses that
of any other adult membership organization in California, including Rotary and
Kiwanis. However, we identified the need to communicate our brand in a way
that resonates with both our current members and the public, while remaining
true to our values as Freemasons. Our team collaborated effectively with leadership and members to define our brand identity. The outcome is a refreshed brand
identity and manifesto, which we will widely disseminate in the coming year
and incorporate into all our communications and decision-making processes.
Membership and New Lodge Development: Over the past three years,
we’ve made remarkable progress in assessing interest in Freemasonry. What

116

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

have we discovered? The challenge is not attracting interest. In fact, we’ve
identified tens of thousands of qualified prospects eager to join our fraternity.
During this time, we’ve successfully connected some 10,000 of these prospects
with lodges. However, we’ve also learned that some lodges are better prepared
to handle these new inquiries than others.
In the first two years, only about 55 percent of lodges reached out to any
of the prospects. I’m pleased to report that this year, more than 70 percent
of lodges have engaged with potential members. To support this momentum,
every lodge now has a designated prospect manager responsible for overseeing
engagement with prospects. If no other brother has been assigned, the junior
warden will take on this role. Lodges that actively engage and maintain regular
communication with prospects are thriving in ways that others are not.
New lodge development remains crucial to our growth and future. Since
launching this initiative in 2016, our grand lodge has instituted 37 new lodges,
and today over 12 percent of our lodges were established through this program.
In this past year alone, we constituted six new lodges and instituted another
six under dispensation. These efforts are expanding Freemasonry into new
communities and enhancing opportunities in areas where lodges already exist,
ensuring a strong and vibrant future for our fraternity.
Leadership Development: We have significantly strengthened leadership
within the fraternity through extensive officer training and ongoing support. The
introduction of a lodge officer vacancy dashboard, along with comprehensive
updates to leadership resources has provided officers with valuable tools and
insights. Our high-level leadership retreats have also been highly successful,
enhancing skills and leadership capabilities across the organization. In 2024
alone, more than 800 officers participated in these retreats.
Looking ahead to 2025, we will take our progress further by merging the
Masters and Wardens Retreats with the Secretary and Treasurer Retreats. This
will allow the entire executive committee of elected lodge leaders to attend
together, collaborate, and develop action plans to bring back to their lodges. Stay
tuned for more details about the 2025 Lodge Leadership Retreats. Registration
opens this weekend.
Halls Assessment and Insurance: Our real estate holdings are among
our most valuable financial assets. Together, the Grand Lodge and our lodges
own property valued at over $1 billion. Like any asset, however, real estate can
either appreciate or depreciate. We risk losing value when we neglect regular
maintenance or defer essential upkeep for years, even decades. Market research
shows that the public’s perception of Freemasonry is shaped more by what
they see than by what they hear or read. Our buildings, as visible symbols of
Freemasonry in the community, must be maintained as vibrant, attractive, and
inviting community resources.
This year, we made significant progress in assessing and improving our
Masonic halls across the state. We launched a robust hall improvement grant
program to support much-needed refurbishments and enhance insurance

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

117

coverage for Masonic properties. The grand lodge allocated $300,000 for these
efforts through the adoption of the 2024 budget. We received 30 applications
requesting nearly $2 million in funding. After a thorough review, 16 halls were
selected, and the $300,000 was disbursed to fund their projects.
Maintaining our halls in good condition and ensuring compliance with
government standards is crucial for securing affordable property insurance.
Due to the extreme wildfires and other natural disasters California has faced
over the past decade, AIG is currently the only carrier willing to insure our
properties. Our Chief Financial Officer, Carol Hunter, along with the Insurance
Committee, is actively exploring alternative insurance options to provide more
reliable coverage, greater flexibility, and more favorable financial terms.
In addition to these efforts, we added the Masonic Hall in Sonora to the
list of Grand Lodge-owned properties this year. The building, which now hosts
new commercial tenants and generates positive cash flow, has been refurbished,
and a new lodge is meeting there. We also preserved and maintained four other
historic buildings across the state, including the oldest Masonic structure in
California, located in Benicia, and the historic halls in Columbia State Park,
Malakoff Diggins State Park, and Quincy.
Technology: Situated near Silicon Valley, it’s no surprise that the Masons
of California have embraced technology to enhance efficiency and member
services. This year, we completed critical upgrades to the iMember system in
partnership with Grand View and made the strategic decision to join other
grand lodges in acquiring Grand View. While the company was previously
owned by non-Masons, today, it is owned by the fraternity. Currently, nearly
80 percent of grand lodges in the U.S., along with several Eastern Star Grand
Chapters, Job’s Daughters Grand Councils, and other Masonic organizations
use the Grand View platform.
In 2025, we will launch a new accounting system within iMember, eliminating the need for Intacct. Designed to be more intuitive and user-friendly,
this new system is tailored for non-accountants, making the role of treasurer
accessible to almost any lodge member.
In 2024, we began exploring ways to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)
to free up resources and provide members with better access to information.
We’ve developed an AI-based model that will allow members to ask questions
directly about the California Masonic Code. Instead of paging through the document, members will soon be able to ask a chatbot questions like, “What are
the procedures for electing officers,” “What are the rules around alcohol in
a lodge,” or “How does a lodge amend its bylaws?” In our latest tests, the AI
delivers succinct and accurate responses. We are also exploring additional AI
applications to further support lodge leaders and members.
I believe this impact of these achievements will aid in our immediate and
future progress and together we will leverage them to our best advantage.

118

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges
It is my responsibility to inform the grand master of matters pertaining to
foreign grand lodge recognition and to present to you, in the form of a motion,
the recognition of certain grand lodges that meet our criteria. The Grand Lodge
has received the following requests for recognition by foreign grand lodges:
Brazil: In Brazil, there is a national grand orient, a separate confederation
of 27 state grand lodges, and independent state grand orients, which are separate and sovereign from the national grand orient. Our grand lodge currently
recognizes the Grand Orient of Brazil, all 27 state grand lodges, and several of
the independent state grand orients. We have received a request for mutual
recognition from three of the independent state grand orients.
Grand Orient of Rio Grande North: The Independent Grand Orient
of Bahai was founded on August 25, 1969. This grand lodge is a member of
the Brazilian Masonic Confederation and the Inter-American Masonic
Confederation. It enjoys mutual recognition with the two other grand lodges
in the same territory whom we recognize.
Grand Orient of the State of Mato Grosso: This grand lodge was founded
on October 12, 1972. This grand lodge is a member of the Brazilian Masonic
Confederation and the Inter-American Masonic Confederation. It enjoys mutual
recognition with the two other grand lodges in the same territory whom we
recognize.
Grand Orient of Paraíba: This grand lodge was founded on April 21, 1980.
This grand lodge is a member of the Brazilian Masonic Confederation and the
Inter-American Masonic Confederation. It enjoys mutual recognition with the
two other grand lodges in the same territory whom we recognize.
The Commission on Information for Recognition confirms that these grand
lodges meet the recognition standards of the Conference of Grand Master
of Masons of North America and we find that they meet the requirements in
California.
The Grand Lodge unanimously entered into agreements of mutual recognition with the Grand Orient of Rio Grande North, Grand Orient of the State
of Matro Grosso, and the Grand Orient of Praiba.
Reflecting on the past several years and considering the opportunities ahead,
I firmly believe that every Masonic lodge must concentrate on two essential
areas to thrive and grow in the coming years. First, we need to actively engage
with potential members and those interested in Freemasonry. It is important
that we discuss our fraternity with pride and confidence, utilizing resources
like the “Simple Guide to Freemasonry” to clearly articulate our identity and
values. Second, lodges must fulfill the promise of Freemasonry. Newer members,
in particular, seek a transformative experience from their Masonic journey.
Our messaging, such as “Discover Freemasonry, Discover Yourself ” and “Be
the change you want to see in the world,” reflects this aspiration and must be
matched by our lodge practices. As we plan for the future, we should critically

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

119

assess both new and traditional practices, prioritizing those that advance our
fraternity and eliminating any barriers that hinder our progress. It’s crucial that
we move beyond merely performing rituals; we must strive to deeply understand, teach, and share their wisdom with others. By investing in the education
and exemplary behavior of our leaders, we can nurture a strong and committed
future for our lodges. As leaders, our unwavering dedication is vital if we are to
inspire the next generation to embrace the same level of commitment.

Appreciation
As I conclude my report, I want to express my heartfelt gratitude to our lodge
secretaries and assistant secretaries, whose unwavering dedication serves as
the backbone of our jurisdiction. I also extend my thanks to our assistant grand
lecturers and district inspectors, whose ritual contributions are greatly enhanced
by their invaluable administrative support throughout the year.
It has been an honor to work alongside Very Worshipful Brother Charles
Cross, our grand treasurer, as he diligently completes his third term. Serving
with our grand lecturer, Very Worshipful Brother Ricky Lawler, who is wrapping up his tenure, has been a true privilege. His friendship and commitment
to Masonry have deeply enriched my experience.
I am sincerely grateful to the dedicated professionals in our Grand Lodge
office. Their passion for our fraternity ensures our mission is upheld. I commend
them all for their exceptional work and unwavering commitment. I would like
to give special recognition to Assistant Grand Secretary Jordan Yelinek for
his exemplary leadership in membership and program services. Many of our
advancements can be attributed to his efforts, and I am truly thankful for his
contributions.
Lastly, I want to express my appreciation to our grand master, Most
Worshipful Brother G. Sean Metroka. It has been a pleasure to collaborate with
you. Your leadership and vision have greatly benefited Freemasonry in California.
Thank you for your outstanding service and for your true and lasting friendship.
And thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

By Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

having been complied with, authorization is requested to properly endorse the
charters of these lodges as follows:

consolidated as Roundtable No. 329.

consolidated as Phoenix Rising No. 178.
