139

REPORT OF THE
GRAND LECTURER
Good afternoon, brethren.
This is my sixth report to you as your grand lecturer.
This has been a difficult year for me. My 35-year career in agriculture, environmental health, and consumer protection came to an end a few months ago.
When I started, I replaced a man who had himself put 35 years into his work
when he retired. When I began my career, I had only been married for two years
and been a Master Mason for four years.
I started my career in 1989 inspecting the dairies of Tulare and Kings
counties, and I remember asking farmers questions about their crops and the
timeframe for planting and harvesting. I would watch the trees in the area, particularly the almond trees, in their various stages as I drove past them through
the seasons. If you are willing to take the time, you can discover that so many
of life’s lessons come from watching animals, nature, and people. What may be
interpreted as orchard trees bending under the effects and stresses of a great
storm may actually be trees overladen and bearing fruit. I was given a great
blessing some time ago when my friend and inspector for our Masonic district,
Jon Humphreys, convinced the assistant grand lecturer that I may be a good
candidate to replace him as inspector for the district. Little did I know that it
would start me down a long path to serve you as your grand lecturer. The only
tools I possessed were a love of our ritual and a heart from my creator with the
gifts to support and encourage. From my time as officers coach to inspector
to assistant grand lecturer to your grand lecturer, this journey and work have
never been a burden to me.
I began to learn the value of praying for wisdom and opportunities.

California Visits
We began the ritual year by performing the constitutions at La France Lodge
on November 2; a cornerstone at San Ramon Fire District on November 5; a
constitution on November 18 at Pilares del Rey Solomon Lodge in Long Beach;
Palos Verdes Lodge constitution on February 4; and the Edwin Sherman Research
Lodge constitution on March 18.
In my travels this year, I made my rounds to visit Masonic districts to watch

140

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

our inspectors conduct their schools of instruction and ensure consistency
throughout the state, and also to make sure the inspectors are meeting the needs
of their district and serving our lodge officers. I start each year with a request
for each district calendar, for the purpose of review and consistency. I remind
the brethren that the instruction and rehearsing of the ritual must be performed
within each of our lodges with the lodge officers and officers’ coach. The work
learned within our lodges should then be exemplified with greater efficiency
in front of each district’s brethren, as well as the other officer coaches and the
inspector for fine-tuning and discussion. I use the submitted district calendars
to plan my visits for the year. On my way to events in Southern California, on
March 21, I had the opportunity to visit Wor. Bret Hart and the brethren of the
701st Masonic District at Palmdale Lodge No. 769. I continued my travels and
attended the 652nd Masonic District School at Whittier Lodge on March 25, and
the Stan Salter School at Bellflower Lodge and the 636th Masonic District at
Gardena-Moneta Lodge with Wor. Alan Ergina on March 26. I was particularly
interested in watching Wor. Alan conduct his school. It was refreshing to see a
different perspective on how our schools are conducted and the reaction of the
brethren to each format. Thank you Wor. Bret, Wor. Max Rush, Wor. Alan, and
your respective district officers for your generous hospitality and fellowship.
For our Master Mason seminars this year, I requested that the work be
exemplified in the entire third degree, including the second section. Our Division
VIII MMS was located at Hemet-San Jacinto Lodge on March 16, Division VI at
Simi Valley Lodge on April 20, a return to Division I and Francis Drake Lodge on
June 15, Division V at Santa Barbara on June 29, and Division IV at Natoma Lodge
on July 20. Brethren, you impressed me with the quality of your exemplifying
work, your questions, and your comments on recent ritual events. It doesn’t
always happen, but this year your excellent work was consistent throughout the
state. Thank you, brethren, for all your fellowship and hard work.

Research Trip To Alabama
A few years ago, when the question of the Scottish Rite degrees first came up,
a treasured friend recommended that I talk to the brethren in Louisiana. Wor.
Bobby Brandsetter, the traveling degree coordinator for the Grand Lodge of
Louisiana, recommended that I attend one of their degrees. At the time, the
only degree that had been scheduled was in April, in Alabama. Bobby and I chose
to wait and see if another would be scheduled that might be closer for me to
attend. None presented themselves, so I called Bobby in January and told him
I would see him and Reggie in April in Alabama.
On April 27, my wife and I flew back to Birmingham, Ala., for the Scottish
Rite third degree at Metro East King Solomon Lodge No. 932. I was met at the
door by the lodge secretary, who informed me that he had received the documents of my travels from the Grand Lodge of Alabama and said he appreciated
the observance of the formal protocols. I met Wor. Brandsetter and Wor. Reggie

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

141

McCue, the assistant grand lecturer for District XIV for the Grand Lodge of
Louisiana, before I took my seat. I was introduced to the deputy grand master of
Georgia, a past grand master of Alabama, the grand master of the work for the
Grand Lodge of Louisiana, and Most Worshipful Larry J. Playsance, the newly
installed grand master of Louisiana. It is worthy of note that Most Worshipful
Playsance, Wor. Reggie McCue, and Wor. Bobby Brandsetter all received their
original three degrees from lodges working in the Scottish Rite. There were
90 brothers in attendance from Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee,
Georgia, Texas, and Alaska, in addition to me from California. After the degree,
I spoke to the delegation from Louisiana and asked many of the same questions I asked Wor. Sergio Soto of Panamericana No. 513 and Wor. Sina Tabesh
of La Parfaite Union No. 17. The brethren of Louisiana reminded me that their
Etoile Polaire Lodge gave La Parfaite Union its original charter. Throughout our
conversations, Wor. McCue and Wor. Brandsetter gave insight issues including
candidates’ advancements, officer proficiencies, and their system of district
management with different languages and two rituals.
Wor. Brandsetter and Wor. McCue further spoke with me about the condition of the ritual in Louisiana and the state of their lodges, particularly the
older lodges in New Orleans. Of the 10 lodges that constitute the 16th Masonic
District, five are English-speaking, with the other five divided into Spanish,
French, and German. As with all Masonic bodies, membership is waning. The
German-speaking lodge was transitioning to English because of the declining
number of brothers who speak the language. The Spanish and French lodges
were experiencing similar challenges, but at present, were holding their own.
Of the 10 lodges, at least four are practicing the Scottish Rite ritual. A resolution that passed some years ago allowed for one Scottish Rite ritual lodge per
district to accommodate those brethren wishing to practice and participate
while recognizing the demand placed on district resources. To date, only eight
of the 16 districts have at least one Scottish Rite ritual lodge.
Most of the degree I observed was performed from memory, except for
portions of the Master’s ritual that were read. My conversations with Wor.
Brandsetter had prepared me for the differences in the Scottish Rite degree. It
was slightly shorter in length than our California ritual, with only a few participants moving about. The lesson at the end is quite different. When I returned
home, I consulted again with Wor. Tabesh and Wor. Soto for their insight into
what I had observed and asked their assistance in forming my recommendations for California.
With the approval of the craft to allow La France to conduct the Scottish
Rite ritual in their lodge, I am inclined to extend that approval so both La
France and La Parfaite Union can perform all three degrees in the Scottish
Rite ritual, not just the first degree, provided they can show proficiency in the
work by memory. Also, since both constituent lodges are making Masons via
the Scottish Rite ritual, it in fact became the ritual of the Grand Lodge F. & A.
M. of California at the close of business after the 2023 Annual Communication,

142

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

regardless of language.
Wor. Brandsetter later asked me if I remembered my Scottish Rite degrees.
I told him that I did. He asked if any of them particularly bothered me, and I
confirmed that I found one degree a bit distressing. He asked what bothered
me, and I told him it was finding out that the ruffians were still alive. Bobby
said, “Wor. Ricky, in the Scottish Rite third degree, the three ruffians are not
killed. They remain alive and at large.”
My visit to Birmingham to watch the Grand Lodge of Louisiana’s traveling degree team was the high point of my year. With brethren from six grand
jurisdictions attending, it was standing room only in this lodge in the woods
southeast of Birmingham, all watching a unique third degree together. I felt
that this was the best of Freemasonry—what I wish each of our lodge brethren
could experience in their own lodges. I am especially grateful to Wor. Reggie
McCue, the District 16 assistant grand lecturer, and Wor. Bobby Brandsetter for
their kind assistance in answering all my questions, providing copies of their
Scottish Rite ritual, and sharing their method and framework for administering
the ritual quality in Louisiana.

Wisdom And Opportunities
Many of you have heard me talk about learning the ritual, about brothers in
my life who have encouraged and mentored me, and events that have been
significant, meaningful, and even humorous. I remember telling some attendees at a Saturday morning Music School of Instruction event at Marin No. 191
about being invited to hear Wor. Nolan Parisimo, a past master at Gen. Douglas
MacArthur No. 853 in Sacramento, deliver the staircase lecture for the first time
during a candidate’s degree. Several months later, I received an email from one
of the brothers who’d heard me mention that, and he asked if I would come and
see him deliver the same lecture. Again, I readily said yes. And shortly thereafter,
it was my pleasure to visit Mill Valley No. 356, sit in the north, close my eyes,
and listen to Bro. William Ross deliver his staircase lecture for the first time.
Thank you, Bro. Ross and Worshipful Bransgrove, master of Mill Valley No. 356,
for inviting me and allowing me to observe your work in our ritual.
I have nothing in my heart but gratitude for the 26 brothers who have served
with me as assistant grand lecturers, for the inspectors who have learned the
importance of serving their districts (and not being served), and for all the
Grand Lodge officers who have learned what an honor it is to come through
those doors and sit in these chairs. And also for the friends I have made who
refuse to let me walk by without saying hello.
We had to say goodbye to one assistant grand lecturer this year, and will be
saying goodbye to three more after the Annual Communication. Our Division
V assistant grand lecturer, Wor. Robert Beeson, resigned and moved to Texas.
We will miss Bob and Cindy, and we hope they have found happiness in their
new home. Thank you, Bob. It was a joy working with you. We welcome Wor.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

143

Christian Marano, who has been selected to serve the brethren in the middle
of our state as our new Division V AGL. The three others are Gary Quintrell
from Division I, Mike Edwards from Division II, and Alberto Casanova from
Division VII. Thank you, my brothers, for your service to our craft. Thank you,
Wor. Alberto, for bringing to light the needs of our brethren and lodges performing the ritual in Spanish, French, and Armenian. I am reminded of a series of
events several years ago in which a call went out to the four northern divisions
for assistance. It was answered by our brother inspectors. Tony Cimarra, Mike
Edwards, and I, with help from Gary Quintrell, were able to muster the inspectors in a very short period to ensure that not one but two separate events were
successful. I have never been prouder of working for our fraternity than I was
then. Thank you Gary for always being there. Mike, we have shared 19 years of
ritual service together, an experience that can never be replaced. It has been
a tremendous honor to serve our craft with all three of you. I wish you every
success in all your future endeavors.
I am reflecting on two other events that greatly impacted my work in our
ritual. One came as a result of a phone call I received from the inspector of the
143rd Masonic District a few years ago, informing me of a degree that would take
place in Vallejo, where the Grand Master was going to make a Mason at sight.
The second event was a third degree I happened to be attending at Washington
No. 20 in Sacramento.
The first event, I attended unsure of what to expect. That evening, I witnessed some of the most heartfelt ritual I had ever seen. The brother receiving
this distinction had been diagnosed with inoperable cancer the year before,
after receiving his first degree. The lodge and brethren were prepared when
they wheeled him in, without the tubes he had been connected to. I watched
Most Worshipful David Perry stand in front of this man and declare him first
an Entered Apprentice Mason, and then, as the ceremony continued, a Fellow
Craft. It was after the Grand Master proclaimed him a Master Mason that I
observed our brother leaning forward in his wheelchair, burying his face in
his hands, and weeping. That is the power of what we do. That is the power of
our ritual. How can we expect our brothers to come to us for the privilege of
obtaining our degrees and place a value on what they receive, if we are unable
or unwilling to value the ritual ourselves? There were no dry eyes in Vallejo
Lodge that evening. I asked the inspector, Wor. John Wasson, if the ritual had
been written down somewhere. He wasn’t sure, but we agreed that the two of
us would go home and write down everything we observed. After we finished,
we met again and reconciled our versions. This beautiful ceremony, written
by our Most Worshipful David Perry, is preserved in the written observations
made by Wor. John Wasson and me and is now in the Resources section of our
website for future use.
At the second event, I arrived at the Sacramento Masonic Temple to visit
Washington No. 20 and was met in the tiler’s room by a smiling candidate, trying
to balance himself on a set of crutches, who proudly proclaimed to me that he

144

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

was being made a Master Mason. The lodge had taken great care in making
preparations for our brother that evening, just as they had done for his previous
two degrees. The degree was outstanding. The brethren were commended for
making such careful accommodations. Afterward, he left the lodge room with
an even bigger smile than he had come in with. I have since learned that we
have made Masons in this jurisdiction who are deaf and blind, in addition to
those who have other physical limitations. The ritual will accommodate. And
it fills in nicely where other means of inclusion fall short.

Ritual Competition
Two years ago, Most Worshipful Micheal D. Johnson of the Grand Lodge of
Kansas told me that he would be in touch to discuss a ritual competition for
his grand lodge. A few months later, we started communicating, and I shared
some materials with him related to the administration and judging of the ritual
competition in this jurisdiction. The Grand Lodge of Kansas has now had two
successful ritual competitions. It gives me great pride and pleasure to have
shared our resources and the lessons we have learned with the Grand Lodge
of Kansas and to observe their successes.
In our own jurisdiction, we tried something new this year. Because of the
large response last year from brothers seeking to participate, we opened a
portion of the competition for 2024 to current Entered Apprentices and Fellow
Crafts, and we framed it so as not to interfere with our competitors’ natural
progression through the degrees.
The winners of our Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft proficiency ritual
competition are Brothers John P. Paradis and Darryl T. Cunningham from
Redding-Trinity No. 27.
Many of those brethren who asked to participate last year as Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts showed up in great numbers as Master Masons
this year. The ritual competition for Master Masons was a return to the senior deacon’s work in the staircase lecture of the second degree. Our division winners are:
• Division I: Bro. Garry Fontillas, San Francisco No. 120
• Division II: Wor. Rick Hodkin, Eureka No. 16
• Division III: Bro. Mark Zevanove, Pleasanton No. 321
• Division IV: Wor. James Wise, Gen. Douglas MacArthur No. 853
• Division V: Bro. Mike Cummins, King David No. 209
• Division VI: Bro. Peter Parsons, Conejo Valley No. 807
• Division VII: Bro. Wes Bozard, Granada Hills No. 378
• Division VIII: Bro. Emmanuel Butiu, Widows Sons No. 869
• Division IX: Wor. Jeffrey Powell, Consuelo No. 325

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

145

Competitors with the four highest divisional scores were invited to attend
the final competition at Lodi No. 256 on Saturday, August 31. After that morning’s competition, the scores were sealed. It is my pleasure to announce that
the winner of the 2024 ritual competition is Wor. Jeffrey Powell from Division
IX and Consuelo No. 325.
To all the brethren who participated this year, thank you! Personally, it
has given me great joy to hear the ritual and to observe the caring heart of a
brother at work participating in these competitions. Your efforts to make the
ritual better and set this example of excellence within your lodges and districts
is greatly appreciated.

Gratitude
I wish to close my remarks with an admonishment given to me by Wor.
Brandsetter from the Grand Lodge of Louisiana. He said, “Remember, Ricky,
the ruffians are still out there. They are still at large. It is up to you to be vigilant
and not let them take control of you or take your life. Always remember their
names: Ignorance, Falsehood, and Ambition.”
Brethren, if I have ever been a light to you, if you have found encouragement
in my words and actions, please return that support to your lodge leaders. Please
give encouragement to your fellow brethren working to improve their ritual and
be an example to candidates coming into your lodges. Be the reason our candidates are smiling after their degrees and give them a reason to return to lodge.
I do not require a position or title to do what is right for my brethren. God
has given me a great gift, and He has been generous in offering opportunities
to practice it.
Respectfully submitted,
Ricky Lawler, Grand Lecturer

MESSAGE FROM THE
GRAND CHAPLAIN
Brethren, family, and honored guests,
It is my privilege to stand before you today as we celebrate the culmination of a year filled with remarkable service, dedication, and growth. Together,
we’ve journeyed side by side, not just as members of an ancient and honorable
fraternity, but as a united family—one that has embraced the grand master’s
theme of “Sharing the Light of Freemasonry.”
Scripture reminds us time and again the significance of light. In the Hebrew
scriptures, Genesis Chapter 3: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there
was light. God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the
darkness. God called the light ‘day’ and the darkness he called ‘night.’”
From the parable in the Gospel of Luke, we read, “No one lights a lamp
and hides it in a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he puts it on a stand, so that
those who come in can see the light.”
The light of Freemasonry is more than a metaphor; it is the guiding principle that illuminates our path and leads us in the work we are called to do. In
Freemasonry, our search for light is the search for understanding, truth, and
wisdom. The work we do, the lives we lead, and the examples we set are reflections of that light. And this year, we have been asked not just to seek that light
for ourselves, but to share it with the world.
The Nature of Light
Let’s first reflect on the nature of light. Light has no physical substance of its
own, yet it illuminates everything. It allows us to see what is true and what
is real, to distinguish between right and wrong. It is essential for growth, for
clarity, and for life itself.
In Freemasonry, light represents knowledge, enlightenment, and spiritual
awakening. But it is not a light meant to be hidden or kept for ourselves. It is
a light that must be shared. If we think about the light of a single candle, we
know that its flame can ignite hundreds of others without diminishing. Each
of us, in our own way, carries a light within us, and when we share it, we are
not diminished—we are made brighter by the collective illumination of our
brotherhood and our actions.

150

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Sharing the Light with Others
What does it mean to share the light? Each of us will have our own interpretation, but let me offer a few reflections of my own.
First, to share the light is to live by the values we espouse as Masons: brotherly love, relief, and truth. It is not enough to speak of these values; we must
live them every day in our interactions with our families, our communities, and
our brethren. When we practice brotherly love, we build stronger connections
with others and spread warmth and kindness. When we offer relief, we show
compassion and charity to those who need it most. And when we commit ourselves to the pursuit of truth, we challenge ignorance, prejudice, and injustice,
shining a light where darkness hides.
Second, sharing the light means mentoring and guiding others. As Masons,
we are called to bring others to light, not only through the ritual, but through
example. Our Masonic youth orders exemplify this beautifully. Today, we will hear
from the leaders of our youth orders, who have not only embraced the teachings
of Masonry but have been beacons of leadership, integrity, and service. Their
light is growing, and it is our responsibility to nurture and support that growth.
When we mentor and guide those who come after us, we are ensuring that
the light of Freemasonry continues to shine brightly into the future. Each of us
has the opportunity and indeed the obligation to pass on the lessons we have
learned, the values we uphold, and the light we carry.
I believe it is the goodness—the divine, the pure, the noble, the dignified,
the very best of what Freemasonry teaches us. When we are doing our very best,
we share the light of Freemasonry.
When we do our finest ritual work or visit another lodge, we share the light
of Freemasonry. We know the light is not bound by the physical limitations of
a lodge room or building. The light of Freemasonry shines brightest when we
wash dishes, or move chairs, or practice degrees, or extend a helping hand to
a brother in need.
A Light That Transforms
As we share the light of Freemasonry, we also transform ourselves and the world
around us. There is a beautiful truth in the idea that when we act selflessly,
we ourselves are changed. When we share our light, our capacity for empathy,
compassion, and love expands. And as we light the way for others, we also
illuminate the path ahead of us, making it easier to see where we are going and
who we are becoming.
In the words of St. Francis of Assisi, “All the darkness in the world cannot
extinguish the light of a single candle.” This is the transformative power of
Freemasonry. Even in a world that may at times seem divided, uncertain, or
challenging, we possess a light that can overcome those obstacles. The darkness cannot stand against the light of a compassionate heart, a wise mind, and
a spirit of integrity.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

This transformative light has been seen in the work of countless brothers this year. We have witnessed acts of charity, leadership, and unity across
California, each one a spark that keeps the flame of Freemasonry burning bright.
We celebrate those who have gone above and beyond, not for personal recognition, but for the good of the craft and the betterment of society. It is in these
moments and these acts we see the true spirit of sharing the light.
Light as Legacy
Sharing the light of Freemasonry is not only about the present, but also about
the legacy we leave behind. We are all part of a continuum—those who came
before us, those who walk with us today, and those who will come after us. Our
work is not solely for our own benefit, but for the benefit of future generations.
What we do today matters not just to those around us but to those who will
one day look back and see the impact of our actions.
As we prepare to install the next officers of this grand lodge, we are
reminded of the importance of continuity and leadership. The officers who have
served with Grand Master G. Sean Metroka have been remarkable stewards of
Freemasonry’s light. Their dedication has left a lasting imprint and their efforts
will be felt for years to come. But as they step down and pass the torch to the
next generation of leaders, we see the light being shared, passed from hand to
hand, guiding the way forward.
For ages, our craft has existed not for our own benefit, but for the world’s.
Through centuries, our fellow craftsmen have labored to make this fraternity
stronger and more vibrant. We have seen the impact of culture wars on our
beloved craft and other organizations with noble purposes. We have seen membership decline with the advent of technology. But we have also seen the embers
of devotion be rekindled in our members. We have seen new lodges emerge and
grow. We have seen the impact of brothers working together.
When the Grand Master and I were growing up in Paradise, we attended
Paradise High School, where I took an English class taught by Mr. Smith, a
long-haired self-described hippie. Unlike the rest of the faculty, he was considered the cool teacher who read poetry and played the guitar. He would
regale us with tales of his adventures and get us to think about life beyond our
hometown. One day, he introduced us to the Hindu word Namaste and told
us it meant “I honor the light within you.” I’ve since learned that the actual
translation is, “I honor the divine within you.” Nonetheless, for a kid growing
up in a small town, it was an exotic word. Several months ago, in my work as
a hospital chaplain, I ran into Mr. Smith. I hadn’t seen him since high school.
I introduced myself and told him I still remembered that lesson from so many
years ago. He teared up and thanked me for reminding him of the gift he had
given to so many students. Today, I say to you, Namaste, because I see—and
have seen—the light within you. I have seen the light of Freemasonry shine
through the people I’ve met throughout the state. It has been a privilege to
share that light, and I know I can speak for my fellow Grand Lodge officers

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

when I say that we have all experienced a great outpouring of brotherly love,
friendship, and hospitality.
Challenge for the Future
As I come to the close of this message, I want to issue a challenge to all of you.
Sharing the light is not a one-time act; it is a way of life. Each of us, every day,
has the opportunity to share the light of Freemasonry with the world around
us. Whether through small gestures of kindness, acts of charity, or by standing
up for what is right, we have the power to make a difference.
As we journey home today, let us carry the grand master’s theme with us.
Let us commit ourselves to sharing the light wherever we go—in our homes,
in our workplaces, in our communities, and in our lodges. Let us be the light in
the darkness, the spark that ignites positive change in the world.
And as we share the light, may we remember that the more we give, the
brighter the world becomes. The more we act in the spirit of brotherhood, the
stronger our bonds grow. The more we live the values of Freemasonry, the
closer we come to realizing our true potential as individuals and as a fraternity.
Brethren, family, and friends, may we leave this weekend renewed in our
purpose, committed to our work, and inspired to continue sharing the light of
Freemasonry for all to see.
Respectfully submitted,
Alan S. Rellaford, Grand Chaplain

MESSAGE FROM THE
GRAND ORATOR
“Share the Light of Freemasonry,” our grand master’s theme this year,
is centered on the concept of “light,” the most important and quintessential
symbol of Freemasonry. Light is the very essence and fabric of speculative
Masonry. For that reason, there are numerous references to and a great deal of
emphasis on light in our ritual.
In all three degrees of our jurisdiction, the candidate is brought into the
bodge blindfolded so that he can personally and vividly experience the transition
from darkness to light. The only question asked from a candidate in all three
degrees is, while he kneels at the altar, “Being in the condition of darkness (or
being again in the condition of darkness), what do you most desire?” And the
answer is “light.” In every degree, the first objects presented to the candidate
after being brought from darkness are the “three great lights of Masonry.”
Perhaps the most dramatic and beautiful reference to light is in the first
degree. Right before the candidate is brought to light, the Master recites the
first few lines of the Bible, “the Great Light in Masonry.”
“In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And
the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon
the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the
face of the waters. And God said, Let there be light: and there
was light.” And the Bible continues, “And God saw the light,
that it was good.”
We all have heard these words in lodge, and many of us have solemnly
recited them. But how do we know what that “light” mentioned in the Bible is?
It is understandable that one may think this light refers to the sun, moon, the
stars, or the physical illumination. But according to the Bible, the sun, moon,
and stars were created on day four of the creation. The “light” referenced in our
ritual comes on day one! What, then, is the light that symbolizes the Masonic
initiation? We will come back to this question.
“Share the Light of Freemasonry”
Whether one is a Freemason or not, when they hear the phrase, “Share the Light
of Freemasonry,” some questions may come to the mind:

156

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Why is light the symbol of Freemasonry?
How is that light shared?
Why should we share that light?
What is the Masonic light?
My oration today will address these four questions in that order. It will
then conclude with a short story which is very much related to sharing the
light of Freemasonry.
Why is light the symbol of Freemasonry? In our culture and language, light, as
opposed to darkness, symbolizes several ideas and concepts. Light is a symbol
of hope. The expression, “light at the end of the tunnel,” signifies hopefulness.
Light is a symbol of understanding. When someone sees the light, he understands. Light represents intellectual advancement and freedom. When Europe
came out of the Dark Ages, what followd was called the Enlightenment. Light is
a symbol of safety and comfort. People are afraid of the dark; no one is afraid of
the light. Light represents insight and wisdom. We call someone wise an enlightened person. Light can be a sign of salvation. Lighthouses are to save sailors at
night. But more importantly, the Bible, in the books of Job and Proverbs, uses
light as a symbol of morality.
So if light represents and embodies hope, understanding, intellectual
advancement and freedom, safety and comfort, insight and wisdom, salvation,
and morality, then it is very fitting and appropriate that light should be the
symbol of Freemasonry. Because we stand for all these principles and ideas,
and because that is what we should represent.
How is the light of Freemasonry shared? This is an easy question. The light
of Freemasonry can be shared on different scales and levels. It can be shared
at an institutional level, by a group, or even by an individual. The examples are
countless.
When Shriners Hospitals help a physically challenged child take their first
steps into their parents’ arms, the light of Freemasonry radiates. When the
Scottish Rite Children’s Language Center helps a child with a speech impediment communicate, the light of Freemasonry shines brightly. When the Knights
Templar’s Eye Foundation gives the gift of sight to those who are visually
impaired, the light of Freemasonry illuminates their world.
Masons4Mitts, the Masonic Homes, the California Masonic Foundation,
the Midnight Mission, and Public Schools programs are all examples of how
we perpetuate the light of Freemasonry. Individually, you have probably shared
the light of Freemasonry. Outside the walls of our temples, when you show
compassion, humility, respect, and dignity, and when others know you are a
Freemason by seeing the ring that you proudly wear or the pin that you wear
with honor, you spread and share the light of Masonry.
My favorite example is this: When a good man applies for membership in
a lodge and receives our degrees, he undergoes the transformative journey of

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

157

Masonic initiation and “by the influence of the pure principles of our institution,” becomes a better man. Then, the light of Freemasonry shines most
brilliantly.
Why should we share the light of Freemasonry? This is a very important
question. Why should we share the light? I submit to you, my brothers, that
sharing the light of Freemasonry is not a choice or an option; it is a duty, a
responsibility, an imperative. Because today, more than ever, the world needs
the light of our institution.
Today, our society is fractured! Economic, political, racial, and religious
differences have divided us. In fact, these divisions have often been the cause
of wars, crimes against humanity, and atrocities in human history. Sadly, today,
people are even more obsessed with wealth, politics, race, and religion.
The principles of our institution transcend all these superficial differences.
Wealth is never a factor in our fraternity, as “Masonry regards no man on account
of his worldly wealth and honor.” It is the “internal not the external qualities
which recommend a man to be made a Mason.” Our bond is much deeper and
more fundamental than politics and political differences. Masonry unites men
of every country, sect and opinion. Race and ethnicity do not divide us; they
give us the chance to enjoy and celebrate our diversity. We welcome men of
all backgrounds and ethnicities. And finally religion is never a factor for us. If
a man believes in the Supreme Being, the manner, place, time, and form of his
worship are of no concern to us.
Differences are inevitable, but Freemasonry helps us rise above these differences by teaching equality, respect, and meritocracy. Those principles render
other differences immaterial, insignificant, and inconsequential. It is the dissemination and sharing of these principles that hold the potential for unity
and reconciliation among humanity. Hence, our duty and responsibility to go
beyond our differences and share our light!
What is the Masonic light? As promised, I would like to return to the question
about Bible’s first symbolic reference to darkness and light. The second verse
of the first chapter of Book of Genesis says, “And the earth was without form,
and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep.” What is this symbolic
darkness that would be defeated by the symbolic light? Many Bible scholars
believe the answer is in the same sentence!
The word “darkness” follows immediately the phrase “without form and
void.” The symbolic darkness refers to a situation in which there is no form—
chaos—and there is a “void” or emptiness. That symbolic darkness is where
there is chaos and emptiness. And if chaos and emptiness define symbolic
darkness, then the symbolic light that would defeat that darkness will be order
and purpose.
To us Freemasons, order and purpose are not unfamiliar or strange ideas.
Order and purpose are beacons of our light. For us, order is achieved by brotherly

158

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

love, relief and truth, and there is no better purpose in life than faith, hope and
charity. To me, that is the true Masonic light—that is the light we receive, that
is the light we confer, and that is the light that should lead our lives.
A touching story about light: Today, the oration will conclude with the touching story of seven brothers who, almost 80 years ago, during the darkest days
of our fraternity and under the most difficult and dangerous circumstances,
courageously chose to share the light of Freemasonry. They knew this could
put their lives in danger and in fact most of them lost their lives because of
what they chose to do. The story of their sacrifice has been captured in many
books and articles. One of these books, published in 2020, is very appropriately
titled A Light in the Darkness.
Beginning in 1933, when Nazis became empowered in Germany, Masons
and Masonic lodges faced immense difficulties. As the grip of Nazi oppression
tightened around Freemasonry, lodges were closed, their books and records
were confiscated, and Masons were identified and arrested. Most were executed,
and some were taken as political prisoners. It is believed that about 80,000
German Freemasons were killed during the reign of the Nazi regime. In other
European countries occupied by Germany (such as France, Belgium, Spain),
another 110,000 Freemasons were killed.
Those brothers who were not killed became political prisoners and were
housed in different prisons and labor camps. One of these camps was in the city
of Esterwegen in Germany. The Esterwegen prison, a forced labor camp, was
known for its extremely harsh living conditions. The camp officers intentionally and methodically starved the prisoners and used food, the basic necessity
of life, to force them to work harder. After being liberated at the end of the
war, one of the prisoners from Esterwegen was taken to an army hospital and
examined. His medical records show that while he was six feet tall, he weighed
only 75 pounds.
Yet under those difficult and inhumane circumstances, on November 15,
1943, seven brothers from Belgium, who were imprisoned for the crime of
being a Freemason, dared to form a Masonic lodge inside the camp and called
it Liberté Chérie, meaning “beloved liberty.” We have the names of the seven
brothers who founded the lodge. Later, two other prisoners in the camp joined
the Liberté Chérie lodge.
But that is not the best part of the story. The most beautiful and touching
part of their story is that on February 20, 1944, under those most difficult and
perilous conditions and unimaginable hardship, the brothers of Liberté Chérie
initiated a candidate. His name was Fernand Erauw.
Sadly, the Germans discovered the existence of the lodge in the camp. They
separated the members and sent them to different concentration camps. Of
the 10 members of lodge, seven died after being sent to other concentration
camps. Only three survived. The prisoner who weighed only 75 pounds was in
fact Brother Fernand Erauw, the only Mason who was initiated in a German

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

159

concentration camp. The last living witness of the Liberté Chérie, Brother Erauw
died in 1997, at the age of 83.
Today, in the city of Esterwegen, there is a monument dedicated to the
memory of the courageous brothers of Liberté Chérie. It is a cubical stone, or
an ashlar, sitting on a Mosaic pavement, breaking through a metal fence. In the
Museum of Freemasonry in Brussels, there is a sculpture commemorating the
original seven brothers of Liberté Chérie lodge.
The story of these brothers, the epitome of love, commitment, and dedication to our fraternity and its principles, serves as a beacon of inspiration. In
the face of adversity, they chose not silence, not complacency, but action. Their
act of defiance and their commitment to our craft stand as a beacon of light in
a world consumed by darkness.
When I first learned about their story, I asked myself, why? At that time, as
starving prisoners, their only goal must have been to survive. In the face of all
that danger, they could have abandoned their fraternity, or at least remained
silent. But they chose to fight back. Why did they decide to practice our craft
under those exceedingly difficult circumstances? Why did they decide to risk
their lives?
Was it because they were bored and had nothing to do in the evenings? Did
they want to just hang out with their friends? Did they want to prove to each
other that they knew the floor work and the ritual? Or because they wanted
to show they could recite perambulations, lectures, or charges by memory?
Obviously not! They did it because they remembered their responsibility and
found an opportunity to share the light of Freemasonry. “An example, my Brother,
worthy of all imitations.”
My brothers, it is in darkness that people feel lost and lose their way, and
it is the light that saves them. As we conclude our Annual Communication and
go back to our homes, work, friends, family, and our lodges, let us remember
who we are. Let us symbolize the light, let us be the “ambassadors of light.”
Let us remember our responsibility, feel the inspiration, and share the true
light of Freemasonry.
Respectfully submitted,
Narbeh Bagdasarian, Grand Orator

2024 GRAND LODGE LEGISLATION

GRAND MASTER’S DECISIONS
AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 1
Simplifies and Modernizes Service and Notice Requirements
Under Part 14 of the California Masonic Code
The California Masonic Code (the “Code”) provides detailed protections
to ensure members are
(1) informed that they have become the subject of charges of unmasonic
conduct (“Service”); and
(2) properly notified throughout the Masonic trial proceedings (“Notices”).
These provisions are designed to ensure that our members are aware
of the allegations, given an opportunity to respond, and receive adequate notice before any consequences are imposed upon them. While
well intentioned, the methods mandated by the Code have become
outdated, expensive and impractical, hindering the efficiency of our
Masonic trial system.
For instance, the Code requires the Trial Master first attempt to find a
disinterested Mason to personally deliver Service to the Accused at his home.
This is an unpopular volunteer task and can take weeks to arrange. If personal
delivery fails, the Trial Master must then resort to sending Service via certified
mail, return receipt requested, to the Accused’s last known address, which is
both expensive and time-consuming. This delay continues until the return
receipt card is returned, further stalling the process.
Regardless of the effectiveness of Service, other Notices throughout the trial
proceedings require similarly complex and costly methods. These methods do not
enhance members’ protections but do impose significant burdens on efficiency,
increase costs, and cause delays in a system dependent on volunteer efforts.

164

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Email and regular mail are modernly accepted as sufficient methods for
important notifications and provide a more practical and timely solution without sacrificing effectiveness. The personal service requirement is outdated and
cumbersome, while certified mail is costly and inefficient.
To streamline the Service process, I propose amendments to allow Service
to be effective if sent electronically (via email with read receipt requested) and
by USPS mail, eliminating the need for personal delivery and certified mail.
These changes will reduce time and costs, avoid the burden of home visits, and
provide quicker, more private, and less embarrassing notifications to members.
Supplementing email Service with USPS mail ensures our members are properly
notified charges have been filed against them.
Upon completion of Service, subsequent Notices by email should be sufficient to ensure members stay informed. The Trial Master, Accused, and Accuser
are aware of the parties’ contact information, making reliance on outdated
methods unnecessary. Simplifying these requirements will prevent unnecessary
burdens on the system and reduce costs.
These changes will not prejudice an Accused member. To the contrary, the
member will receive notice faster, more reliably, and in a manner more private
and less likely to cause needless embarrassment or animosity. With these
amendments, our brothers will receive all the same notifications just by different
methods and have the same opportunities to explain circumstances in which
they may have not received required notices. By enacting these amendments,
our Masonic trial system will operate more quickly and efficiently.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 1404.325 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.325. SERVICE OF CHARGES ON THE ACCUSED.
Upon receipt of the Grand Secretary’s notification of the Trial Master’s
appointment with a copy of the charge or charges, the Trial Master shall
cause a true copy of the notification of the Trial Master’s appointment and
each such charge to be served upon the Accused, as provided in Section
1404.330 of this Code, together with the following statement, printed in
no less than 12-point type:
You are hereby notified that the enclosed charge or charges of unmasonic conduct have been filed against you. If you are found guilty of any
charge of unmasonic conduct, the penalty may be fixed at reprimand in
open lodge or suspension or expulsion from Masonry.
Within 30 days from your receipt of this notice, if personally delivered, or within 30 days from the date of mailing of this notice to you, you
must file with the Trial Master a statement in writing that you are either
guilty or not guilty of each charge against you or that you are pleading no
contest. If you plead guilty or no contest or you fail to enter a plea, there
will be no trial and you may be found guilty and a penalty may be imposed

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

165

without further notification. If you enter a plea of guilty or no contest, you
may submit with your response to this notice any evidence of mitigating
or extenuating circumstances which you wish the Trial Master to consider
in determining the verdict and penalty.
You have the right to have your trial held before either a Trial Master
sitting alone or a Trial Master sitting with Commissioners. You must designate in your statement whether you request a trial by a Trial Master alone
or before a Trial Master sitting with Commissioners. If you fail to make
such a designation, the trial shall be held before a Trial Master sitting alone.
You have the right to be present at any hearing on this matter. You are
entitled to represent yourself. You also have the right to be represented by
counsel of your choice. Your counsel, if any, must be a Master Mason in
good standing in this Jurisdiction but need not be an attorney. You are not
entitled to the appointment of counsel to represent you at Lodge expense
or to reimbursement of your legal expenses. You are entitled to present
any relevant evidence and call witnesses. You are entitled to the issuance of
notices to compel the attendance of Masons to testify at trial. You will be
given full opportunity to cross-examine all witnesses testifying against you.
You must comply with those provisions of Part 14 of the California
Masonic Code applicable to this matter. A copy of Part 14 of the California
Masonic Code is enclosed.
Section 1404.330 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.330. TIME AND MANNER OF SERVICE.
Service of any charges and notices upon the Accused shall be made personally by any disinterested Master Mason authorized by the Trial Master.
If personal service cannot be effected upon the Accused after reasonable
attempt, as determined by the Trial Master, the The Trial Master shall serve
the Accused by sending the applicable charges or notice(s) via electronic
mail (with a read receipt requested) and via United States Postal Service
regular mail certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid,
addressed to his last known electronic mail address and his last known
mailing address as shown in the Grand Lodge’s records, in which case the
date of mailing shall be the. The date of mailing shall be the date of service.
The service of any charges and notice is mandatory, and in its absence, the
Trial Master has no authority to proceed. The foregoing notwithstanding,
after the initial service of charges and notice upon the Accused is made as
provided in this Section 1404.330 of this Code, subsequent notices to the
Accused may be sent by the Trial Master via electronic mail (with a read
receipt requested) to his last known electronic mail address as shown in
the Grand Lodge’s records.
Section 1404.335 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:

166

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

§1404.335. CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE.
A Certificate of Service of a true copy of the charge and specifications, and
the notice to the Accused, shall be executed by the Trial Master confirming
that Master Mason making the service showing the method by which it
was accomplished in accordance with Section 1404.330 of this Code. The
Certificate shall be filed with maintained by the Trial Master for the trial
record.
Section 1404.410 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.410. PROCEDURE IF THE ACCUSED FAILS TO PLEAD.
If the Accused fails, within 30 days as required, to file a statement in writing
containing a plea of guilty, not guilty or no contest, the Trial Master shall,
without further notice to the Accused:
A. Complete such investigation, as he shall deem appropriate;
B. Determine in his discretion whether the charge and specifications
are true;
C. Make a finding as to the guilt or innocence of the Accused; and
D. If the Trial Master makes a finding of guilty, fix the penalty under
Section 1404.620 of this Code. No other penalty may be imposed.
The Trial Master shall prepare a written report of his investigation,

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 2
Eliminates the Certification Requirements for Certain
Documents Under Part 14 of the California Masonic Code
The California Masonic Code (the “Code”) requires that Grand Lodge
obtain certain court documents certified by the clerk of court for Masonic
trials. The Code also requires that we obtain certain court documents that are
certified by the court clerk before a Mason can be expelled for pleading guilty
to, pleading no contest or being convicted of a crime of moral turpitude. While
well intentioned, these requirements have become outdated and impractical
and need to be changed.
As courts have automated many of their file retrieval systems, the manual
certification of documents by court clerks has become harder and slower for
us to obtain. Short-staffed, California courts can now take months to manually
certify individual documents from their court files. Recently enacted California
privacy legislation also makes obtaining such court documents more time-consuming as these new laws require court clerks to redact certain personally identifiable information from their records systems. We can safely rely on documents
that are provided by the court but are not certified by the local court clerks.
Therefore, I recommend we modify certain provisions of Part 14 of the
Code that require the use of certified court documents.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 1404.555 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§1404.555. RULES OF EVIDENCE.
A. The following rules of evidence shall be followed at a Masonic trial as
nearly as the circumstances permit:
1.

Any evidence shall be admitted if:

2.

The evidence has some tendency in reason to prove or disprove a
fact or issue in dispute; and

3.

It is the sort of evidence on which responsible persons are accustomed to rely in the conduct of serious affairs, regardless of the
existence of any common law or statutory rule which might make
improper the admission of the evidence over objection in civil
actions;

174

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

4.

Admissions or confessions of the Accused that would be admissible
in the courts are admissible in a Masonic trial;

5.

Hearsay evidence may be used for the purpose of supplementing
or explaining other evidence but shall not be sufficient in itself to
support a finding of unmasonic conduct;

6.

The rules of privilege shall be effective to the extent that they are
otherwise required by statute to be recognized in civil actions; and

7.

The Trial Master has the discretion to exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by its prejudice to the
Accused, or its admission will necessitate undue consumption
of time;

B. The records and reporter’s transcripts of testimony made in state and
federal courts, properly authenticated, may be allowed in evidence.
The certified court-provided record of final conviction in criminal
proceedings, including a conviction based on a plea of nolo contendere
(or no contest), unless rebutted, is conclusive evidence in a Masonic
trial of guilt of the offense covered in the criminal proceedings;
C. A witness shall not be examined, nor shall any testimony be taken,
without an opportunity given the Accuser and the Accused to be present
and cross-examine the witness. Affidavits, interrogatories or depositions taken without notification to the Accused or the Accuser may
not be received;
D. Technical objections as to form shall not be permitted;
E. The Accused or his counsel has a right, as a part of his presentation,
to introduce testimony which explains his actions and has the further
right to introduce evidence in extenuation and mitigation; and
F.

Where guilt is sought to be proven by one witness, great caution is to
be exercised.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 3
Suspensions of Members Who Fail to Plead to
Charges of Unmasonic Conduct
As I have progressed through the Grand Lodge line, I have been
distressed by the number of disputes resulting in Masonic trials and the time
and talent invested in the trial process. Many Grand Masters before me have
expressed similar concerns with respect to the extensive use of our Masonic
trial system.
One common strain on our volunteer Trial Masters and our system is when
an Accused brother fails to plead to the charges filed against him. Despite the
Accused’s refusal to participate in his defense or comply with the California
Masonic Code (the “Code”) requirements to submit a response, the Code requires
the Trial Master make a complete investigation, determine the Accused’s guilt
or innocence based on the facts before him, set a penalty, if appropriate, and
issue a report to the Committee on Trial Review for review, recommendation,
and vote at Grand Lodge each year. This places tremendous responsibility, time,
and commitment from our Trial Masters, our Committees, and staff while the
Accused retains the rights and privileges of Masonry without engaging in the
process. In essence, the Trial Master, our Committees, and staff are punished
more than the Accused by these tasks.
It is essential that our members show respect for our system and for our
Trial Masters. Pending the withdrawal or dismissal of all charges, a finding of not
guilty on all charges or the notification to the Grand Secretary of the penalty,
if any, fixed by the Trial Master, the Grand Master may suspend the Accused
member under Section 1404.340 of the Code. My suggested amendments to the
Code would relieve the Trial Master of his duties while the Accused member
is suspended and prohibit the Accused member from participating in Stated
Meetings, holding Masonic Communication, and affiliating with other Lodges
until they plead to the charges against them and are restored to good standing. The Code’s current provisions requiring the Trial Master to complete his
duties would apply if the Grand Master decides not to suspend the Accused
for failing to plead.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 1404.410 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

§1404.1000. RESTORATION OF A SUSPENDED MASON.

unmasonic conduct filed in this Jurisdiction shall be restored to the
rights and privileges of Masonry upon the last to occur of (a) the
expiration of the term of his suspension and (b) the payment of any
dues and the performance of any other obligations required for his
restoration in this Jurisdiction.
1.

suspended for an indefinite period as a result of any charge of
unmasonic conduct filed in this Jurisdiction may be restored to
the rights and privileges of Masonry as follows:

2.

A suspended Mason may apply in writing for restoration to the
rights and privileges of Masonry to his Lodge in this Jurisdiction.
If his Lodge is not in this Jurisdiction, his application shall be
made to the Constituent Lodge selected by the Grand Master.
His application may be filed at any time 60 or more days after
the penalty of suspension has been affirmed by Grand Lodge. His

his restoration in this Jurisdiction. The Secretary shall promptly
notify the applicant of the Lodge’s action on his application. In the
case of restoration, the Secretary shall promptly notify the Grand
Secretary of the action taken.

Stated Meeting taking place 90 days or more after the penalty of
suspension has been affirmed by Grand Lodge, by an affirmative

If the suspended Mason is restored, the Secretary shall promptly

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 4
Updates Required Applicant Contributions
and Contribution Amounts
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) requires that:
• Applicants for the degrees and each applicant for affiliation whose
Demit or Certificate is from a Lodge of another Jurisdiction contribute $30 for the use and benefit of Grand Lodge and $25 for the use
and benefit of the Masonic Homes of California (unless the applicant
has paid such contribution with a former application); and
• Applicants for the degrees contribute $15 for the George Washington
Masonic National Memorial and $9 for the California Masonic
Memorial Temple (unless the applicant has paid such contribution
with a former application).
The dollar amounts of these required applicant contributions have not
been adjusted in a long time. The $25 contribution to the Masonic Homes has
not changed for nearly 100 years, and the $9 contribution to the Memorial
Temple has not changed in 70 years. The George Washington Masonic National
Memorial contribution was last changed in 2010. It is well past time to adjust
these amounts to reflect current economic reality. Between 2010 and 2024,
the U.S. dollar lost more than 30% of its value due to inflation. The buying
power of $100 in 2010 is less than $70 today. It is also time to amend the Code
so that these contributions can be more routinely adjusted to keep pace with
economic realities.
We should also take this opportunity to include in the Code the California
Masonic Foundation as a recipient of applicant contributions. Requiring applicants to contribute to the Foundation will strengthen this great charitable institution. Perhaps more importantly, a required contribution to the Foundation will
send a strong message to our applicants of the value we place on our Fraternity’s
charitable mission and activities.
Thus, I recommend that the Code be revised to state that applicants
must make contributions to Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes, the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial, the California Masonic Memorial
Temple, and the California Masonic Foundation. I also recommend that the
contribution amounts for these entities be established and adjusted as necessary with the adoption of the annual Grand Lodge Budget, beginning with the
budget for our 2025-2026 fiscal year. By using the Grand Lodge Budget process,

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

183

we can ensure that contribution levels keep pace with economic reality without
being onerous to applicants. I note that the Code currently calls for applicant
background check fees to be established and adjusted through the Grand Lodge
Budget process and that this process has worked well and without controversy
for more than decade.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 407.030 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§407.030. LODGE CONTRIBUTIONS ON APPLICATIONS.
Each applicant for the degrees and each applicant for affiliation whose
Demit or Certificate is from a Lodge of another Jurisdiction shall accompany his application with a contribution of $30 for the use and benefit of
Grand Lodge, unless he shall have paid such contribution with a former
application to a Constituent Lodge. The amount of such contribution shall
be established from time to time with the adoption of the Grand Lodge
Budget. All such contributions shall be transmitted to the Grand Secretary
at the time and in the manner specified on forms provided for that purpose. If the application is rejected or withdrawn, the Lodge shall return
any such contribution paid to the applicant. Such contributions shall be
non-refundable upon such applicant’s election to receive the degrees or
to membership.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 5
Lengthens Restoration Repayment Period Provided
to Masons Suspended for Non-Payment of Dues and Dues
Grace Period for Members on Active Military Combat Duty
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) states that a Mason suspended for
non-payment of dues shall be automatically restored if, within two years from
the date he was suspended, he pays the due owed at the time of his suspension,
together with dues that would have accrued had he not been suspended.
I recommend that we lengthen the Code’s two-year automatic restoration
window provided to suspended Masons to three years.
Lengthening the two-year window for automatic restoration to three years
will increase the efficiency of the dues repayment process and decrease the
administrative burden on Lodges. As Lodge Secretaries well know, automatic
restoration for non-payment of dues is far more easily managed than restoration
requests that require consideration and consent of the Lodge. In addition, we
know from experience that members may need more than 24-months to turn
things around. Members who are having trouble paying their dues are likely also
facing difficult family, medical, economic, or professional issues. Resolving these
issues takes time. Often, the resolution of such matters does not immediately
improve one’s financial position. It can take time for significant life changes to
bear fruit. In this light, the Code’s 24-month automatic restoration period is, in
some cases, too short a time for even well-meaning Masons to take advantage of.
A related section of the Code prohibits a Lodge from suspending a Mason
for non-payment of dues if the Mason has been on active military combat duty
at any time during the preceding 24 months. I recommend that this two-year
period also be extended to three years for the reasons set out above.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 809.370 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§809.370. SUSPENSION FOR NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
A. If a Mason has not paid his dues during a period of 12 months, the
Secretary shall notify him that he will be suspended for non-payment
of dues unless at the Lodge’s next Stated Meeting either his dues have
been paid or sickness or inability to pay is shown as the cause for the
failure to pay. The notice shall be given either by certified mail, return
receipt requested, postage prepaid, addressed to his last known address,

186

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

or by actual service of notice, duly certified by the Tiler. If all dues
due and payable have not been paid by the time of the Lodge’s next
Stated Meeting, he shall be declared suspended by the Master, unless
for special reasons shown the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant him
further time for payment.
B. No worthy brother who is unable to pay his dues shall be suspended
for non-payment of dues.
C. No Mason who has attained the age of 80 years or who has attained
an aggregate number of years in age and years as a Mason in good
standing equaling 120 or more shall be suspended for non-payment of
dues without a written report to the Lodge from the Member Retention
Committee evidencing when and where the committee interviewed the
delinquent Mason, why the delinquent Mason has not paid his dues and
whether the delinquent Mason has the ability to pay his dues. A copy
of this report shall be provided to the Grand Secretary at least thirty
days before the vote may be taken on the suspension.
D. No Lodge shall suspend a Mason for non-payment of dues if the Master
or Secretary of the Lodge has knowledge that this Mason has been on
active military combat duty at any time during the preceding 24 36
months.
1.

Active military combat duty is defined as having been military
personnel serving in an active capacity including but not limited
to active duty personnel, reservists and National Guard personnel
in a combat zone for a named United States military conflict. A
combat zone for a named United States military conflict is any
area which the President of the United States by Executive Order
designates or has designated as an area in which U.S. Armed Forces
are or have engaged in conflict.

2.

If a Lodge finds that a Mason of the Lodge was on active military
combat duty, as defined in Section 809.370.D of this Code, at any
time during the 24 36 month period preceding the date on which
the Lodge suspended him, then the Lodge shall remove such suspension from his record as if such suspension had not occurred
and the Secretary of the Lodge shall immediately notify the Grand
Secretary thereof.

3.

A Mason may request his Lodge to remove a previous suspension from his record if he was on active military combat duty, as
defined in Section 809.370.D of this Code, at any time during the
24 36 month period preceding the date on which the Lodge so
suspended him, and if his Lodge then finds that he was on active
military combat duty at any time during such 24 36 month period,

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

187

then his Lodge shall remove such suspension from his record as if
such suspension had not occurred and the Secretary of the Lodge
shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary thereof.
4.

Once 24 36 months have elapsed since a Mason’s service on active
military combat duty, he may be suspended for nonpayment of dues
as provided in this section, including suspension for unpaid dues
for the period during which he was on active military combat duty.

E. A Mason shall not be expelled from Masonry for non-payment of dues.
Section 809.380 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§809.380. RESTORATION OF A MASON SUSPENDED FOR NONPAYMENT OF DUES.
A Mason suspended for non-payment of dues:
A. Shall be automatically restored if, within two three years of his suspension, he pays any arrearage due at the time of his suspension, together
with such further dues as would have accrued against him had he not
been suspended, to the date of his payment, unless such arrearage and
dues have been remitted by his Lodge; and

or had them remitted by his Lodge for the period of within two three

Meeting after the request for restoration is presented. As a condition

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 6
Modifies Lodge Vote Required to Restore a Mason
Suspended for Non-Payment of Dues
A Mason suspended for non-payment of dues for two or more years may
make a request to his Lodge for restoration. Under the California Masonic Code
(“Code”), the suspended Mason shall not be restored except by a two-thirds
vote by ballot of all Lodge members present at the next Stated Meeting after his
request for restoration is presented. As a condition of his restoration, the Lodge
may require the suspended Mason to pay some portion of his outstanding dues.
I recommend that we reduce the required two-thirds vote of Lodge members to a simple majority vote. Except in very limited circumstances, our Code
sets a simple majority as the threshold for deciding Lodge matters. In matters
relating to Lodge finances, for example, a simple majority of Lodge members
carries the day. The Code’s few exceptions to the simple majority rule involve
issues of greater importance than the potential restoration of a member suspended for non-payment of dues. For example, the Code requires a unanimous
vote when balloting on an application and a two-thirds vote on changes to Lodge
Bylaws. These high thresholds are warranted as they relate to issues fundamental to the governance and character of the Lodge. Restoration of a particular
member who has failed to pay dues does not rise to this level of fundamental
or “core” importance.
The stringent two-thirds voting threshold might be justified if restoration
in all cases necessarily led to the forgiveness of all past dues. But it does not:
the Code gives Lodges the discretion to condition the suspended Mason’s
restoration on payment of a portion of his outstanding dues.
Given this discretion, it is appropriate that the will of a simple majority of
Lodge members present carries the day on this matter, as it does on so many
other matters of equal or greater importance to our Lodges.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 809.380 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§809.380. RESTORATION OF A MASON SUSPENDED FOR NONPAYMENT OF DUES.
A Mason suspended for non-payment of dues:
A. Shall be automatically restored if, within two years, he pays any arrearage due at the time of his suspension, together with such further dues

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

189

as would have accrued against him had he not been suspended, to the
date of his payment, unless such arrearage and dues have been remitted
by his Lodge; and
B. May make a request to his Lodge for restoration if he has not paid them
or had them remitted by his Lodge for the period of two years. The
Mason shall not be restored except by a two-thirds majority vote by
ballot of all the members present at the next Stated Meeting after the
request for restoration is presented. As a condition of his restoration,
he shall pay such amount of any arrearage due at the time of his suspension and such amount of dues as would have accrued against him had
he not been suspended, to the date of his payment, as his Lodge may
require, except such arrearage and dues that have been remitted by his
Lodge. A petition denied may be renewed at any future Stated Meeting.
The Secretary shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary of the
restoration. Amendment to the Ordinances.
5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 7
Allows for a Plain Language Text Ritual that Does Not
Reveal the Secrets of Freemasonry
For centuries, Masons around the world have used printed documents
as memory aids when studying and memorizing portions of our degree ceremonies. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, many Grand Lodges around
the world permitted their members to use “plain language texts” of the Ritual.
By “plain language text,” I mean a text of the Ritual that does not make use of
a cipher or other device to obscure its meaning. A significant number of Grand
Lodges publish their approved plain language ritual texts for their members. For
example, the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California authorized a plain language
ritual in place of a cipher in the 1960s.
There are sound reasons to permit members to use plain language texts
when studying the Ritual, provided that such texts do not reveal in plain language the signs, words and modes of recognition in our Ritual. First, it is widely
acknowledged that using a plain language text makes the Ritual significantly
easier to teach to new members and applicants. Second, and related, I’m sure
our members agree that the Ritual would be easier to understand, memorize
and benefit from with the aid of a plain language text. Third, allowing the use of
plain language texts avoids the disharmony that can arise in Lodges when their
“illicit” use is suspected or alleged. Fourth, the trend permitting use of plain
language text reflects their increasing general availability. With the Internet
and its explosion of information, and with more Grand Lodges self-publishing
their ritual, a Mason, or curious member of the general public, can already read
Masonic rituals for themselves.
The use of plain language rituals is not a new concept for our Grand Lodge.
As you may know, our Ritual is performed in various languages, including French,
Spanish, and Armenian. These rituals have long been taught using a plain language ritual. Experience with these practices has shown that concerns about
the efficacy of plain language rituals compared to ciphers are manageable. For
instance, a concern from the late 1980s—when our Grand Lodge first approved
the use of ciphers—was that using the cipher would weaken the relationship
between a candidate and his coach. I’ve heard the same concern expressed about
plain language rituals. However, with at least five of our lodges and many Grand
Lodges already using plain language rituals, it’s clear that the candidate-coach
relationship remains strong regardless of the instructional method. The quality
of this relationship is influenced more by the commitment of both the candidate
and the coach to work and learn together than by the specific instructional tool
used. In fact, employing a plain language ritual might even enhance the quality

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

191

of coaching, as it allows more time to focus on the meaning of the work rather
than on merely learning the cipher.
It is time we recognize the significant educational advantages of permitting
plain language texts. It is time to give coaches and candidates the best tools
available for a successful learning experience. It is also time we acknowledge
that our refusal to permit widely available texts no longer serves any particular
purpose. Accordingly, I recommend that we amend the California Masonic Code
(the “Code”) to eliminate the required publication of an “official” cipher and
permit Grand Lodge to publish a plain language text of the Ritual, so long as
that plain language text does not reveal in plain language the signs, words and
modes of recognition in our Ritual. The Grand Lodge may still make available
a cipher to those who wish to have one.
A few clarifying points:
First, our Code refers to the “esoteric and secret portion of the Ritual” but
does not define the phrase. To remove any uncertainty, my proposed amendment
defines this phrase to mean the signs, words and modes of recognition in our
Ritual. My amendment prohibits Grand Lodge’s plain language text from revealing in plain language the signs, words and modes of recognition in our Ritual.
Second, my recommended amendment generally retains the Code’s limitations as to the use of memory aids during a tiled meeting. These limitations
and protections remain important.
Third, under my recommended amendment, reducing to writing the signs,
words or modes of recognition in our Ritual (in other words, the esoteric or
secret portions of the Ritual) continues to constitute unmasonic conduct sufficient to support the filing of a charge of unmasonic conduct against a Mason.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code.
Section 100.085 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§100.085. RITUAL:
The work and lectures in the three degrees (composed of the esoteric or
secret portion, the portion in the approved plain language text of the Ritual
and the portion in the approved Grand Lodge Monitor), the Candidate’s
Lectures of each of the three degrees, the Installation Ceremony for
Constituent Lodges and the Funeral Service, each as has been and may be
from time to time adopted and modified by Grand Lodge. Grand Lodge
Ceremonies, although ritualistic in nature, are not part of the Ritual. The
signs, words and modes of recognition in the Ritual are referred to in this
Code as the “esoteric or secret portion” of the Ritual.
Section 402.030 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
