Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 8
Clarifies Process by Which Lodges May Use
Alternative Ritual
The Ritual, including the lectures in our three degrees, is central
to our practice of Freemasonry.
Grand Lodge has adopted a version of the “American Rite” for our lodge
ritual uses. The American Rite is commonly called The York Rite. Developed
over many decades, the American Rite’s last significant formulation occurred
in the early 1800s. The American Rite is just one of several major sets of rituals
(including the York and Scottish Rites) commonly used by Masonic lodges
around the world.
The California Masonic Code (the “Code”) generally requires our Lodges
to use the American Rite as modified by our Grand Lodge. There is a long-time
exception, however. The Code allows Lodges whose “long-established ritualistic
work” departs from the Ritual adopted by Grand Lodge to perform an alternate
ritual, unless doing so has been disapproved by the Grand Master and Grand
Lecturer. As a result of this exception, several Lodges under our Jurisdiction
have practiced alternative rituals, some for over a century, and still today we
have Lodges in our Jurisdiction that perform versions of the Scottish Rite. La
Parfaite Union No. 17 has done so since the 1850s, and in 2023, La France Lodge
No. 885 was granted authority to perform a version of the Scottish Rite.
The Code does not define the term, “long-established ritualistic work.”
It also does not set out any principles by which the Grand Master and Grand
Lecturer should evaluate ritual that departs from the Ritual of this Jurisdiction.
The Code’s ambiguity and backward-looking focus has generally not been an
issue for our Fraternity. The use of alternative ritual declined in the second
half of the 20th Century in California. In the instances where Lodges sought
permission to use alternative ritual, Grand Masters and Grand Lecturers exercised their discretion under the Code reasonably and without controversy. I am
confident future Grand Masters and Grand Lecturers will do the same.
That said, the issue of alternative ritual may arise more frequently in the
future. We see the interest growing. As California continues to become more
diverse, so too does California Freemasonry. For example, a number of both
young and old lodges in California but outside our Jurisdiction use ritual from
other major rites. While they depart to some degree from our Ritual, their
practice of Freemasonry is no more or less pure, correct or wise than ours.
I believe that we should continue to allow future Grand Masters and Grand

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

197

Lecturers to exercise discretion when considering lodge requests to use alternative ritual. It would be beneficial, however, to clarify the Code’s ambiguous
language on this topic and provide guidance to our Grand Lodge officers facing
such requests.
With respect to alternative ritual, I believe that there are three key principles
upon which we can agree. First, all ritual used by our Lodges should contain
the same obligations as the Ritual adopted by Grand Lodge. It is crucial that
all of our members, regardless of their Lodge memberships, be committed to
the same obligations and personal commitments to themselves, their Lodges
and their brothers. Second, all of our Lodges should use ritual that shares the
same signs, words and modes of recognition. Third, all of our Lodges should
perform ritual that adds to, rather than detracts from, the culture, integrity
and ideals of our Fraternity. Alternative ritual that does not reflect the culture,
integrity and ideals of our Fraternity does not have a place in our Jurisdiction.
My recommendation reflects these principles by granting the Grand Master
and the Grand Lecturer the discretion to grant lodge requests to perform alternative ritual if the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer determine that the use of
the alternative ritual: (1) includes the same obligations contained in the Ritual
adopted by Grand Lodge; and (2) includes the same signs, words and modes
of recognition contained in our Ritual; and (3) is consistent with the culture,
integrity and ideals of our Fraternity.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 402.010 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§402.010. RITUAL.
All work in this Jurisdiction, including each degree conferred and all lectures, must be in conformity with the Ritual, and such must be adhered to
by all Lodges and Masons in this Jurisdiction, except as otherwise provided
in this Code. Upon request by a Constituent Lodge, the Grand Master and
Grand Lecturer may consent to a Constituent Lodge’s use of an alternative
ritual that departs from the Ritual provided that such alternative ritual (a)
includes the same obligations as those contained in the Ritual, (b) includes
the same signs, words and modes of recognition as those contained in the
Ritual, and (c) is consistent in all material respects with the culture, integrity
and ideals of our Fraternity, as determined by the Grand Master and Grand
Lecturer. The language of the obligations in the alternative ritual need not
be exactly identical to the language used in the Ritual. Unless otherwise
determined by the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer, Constituent Lodges
who have used an alternative ritual since at least January 1, 2024 that was
not disapproved by the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer may continue
their use of such alternative ritual without the affirmative consent of the
Grand Master and Grand Lecturer required by this Section. Constituent
Lodges whose long-established ritualistic work is in part a departure from

198

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

the Ritual of this Jurisdiction may continue to perform such ritual, for so
long as the same has not been disapproved by action of the Grand Master
and the Grand Lecturer. The right to perform the long-established ritualistic work of Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 has been transferred to and
assumed by La France Lodge with the requisite approval of Grand Lodge.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 9
Requires Submission of Grand Lodge Officer
Nominations and Biographical Sketches at Least
Sixty Days Prior to Annual Communication
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) requires that the Grand Master,
Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and
Grand Lecturer be elected by written ballot at each Annual Communication.
Under the Code, recommendees for election to Grand Lodge offices must
provide biographical sketches to the Grand Secretary no less than two weeks
prior to the start of Annual Communication. Any other member desiring to be
nominated for election as a Grand Lodge officer may, but is not required to,
provide his biographical sketch to the Grand Secretary no less than two weeks
prior to the start of Annual Communication. If the Grand Secretary does not
receive a biographical sketch for a nominee by the required date, the vote at
Annual Communication shall be taken without reading a biographical sketch
for that nominee.
As we saw at last year’s Annual Communication, the Code’s differing treatment of recommendees and other members seeking nomination effectively
allows nominations from the floor, minutes before the scheduled secret ballot,
without prior notice to Grand Lodge and its voting members. The “snap” or
“floor” nomination of a member, without prior notice, undermines our officer
elections both substantively and procedurally.
First, it is not fair to require our members to vote only minutes after a
nomination from the floor. Some members may have no prior knowledge of
the nominee(s) just presented to them. None of our members will have more
than a few minutes to consider the choices just presented to them. Nominations
without prior notice deprive our members of their rights to be informed and
thoughtful when casting their ballots.
Second, last minute nominations from the floor create procedural challenges that could undermine our elections. The Code requires that the election
of Grand Lodge officers be conducted by written ballot. Producing valid written
ballots without prior notice of even the names of all candidates is unwieldly
and prone to delay and/or error.
There’s a simple fix, of course: require recommendees and potential nominees to play by the same rules and provide their biographical sketches and
nominations prior to the start of Annual Communication, and distribute them
to the membership. This fix gives voting members the opportunity to inform

200

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

themselves of, and reflect upon, the candidates. It also ensures that our most
important annual election — which includes the election of the Grand Master
— is conducted in an orderly manner that inspires the requisite confidence of
our members.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 404.410 of the Code would be
amended as marked:
§404.410. ELECTED OFFICERS.
The Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens, Grand Treasurer,
Grand Secretary, and Grand Lecturer shall be elected by written ballot as
the final item of business before the installation of said officers at each
Annual Communication. A majority of the votes cast shall be necessary
for an election. Grand Lodge, by unanimous consent, may permit any
designated officer to cast the ballot for Grand Lodge.
Each recommendee for election to any Grand Lodge office shall provide his biographical sketch to the Grand Secretary no less than two weeks
sixty days prior to the start of Annual Communication. Any other member
desiring to be nominated for election as a Grand Lodge officer may shall
provide his biographical sketch and a written statement of his nomination
signed by another voting member of Grand Lodge to the Grand Secretary no
less than two weeks sixty days prior to the start of Annual Communication.
Nominations of members who have not provided a biographical sketch and
written statement of nomination by the required date shall be rejected. No
less than twenty-one days prior to the start of Annual Communication, the
Grand Secretary shall provide to all Lodges and such other members of
Grand Lodge as he determines the name, current title, and facts contained
in the biographical sketch of each recommendee and valid nominee for each
Grand Lodge elected office. Immediately prior to the election of Grand
Lodge officers at Annual Communication, the Grand Orator shall read the
names and biographical sketches of all recommendees and valid nominees.
Nominations for election to any Grand Lodge office shall include only the
name and current title of the nominee. At the conclusion of the nomination
process for each elective office, if there are multiple nominees, the Grand
Orator shall read the biographical sketch submitted for each nominee, if
received by the Grand Secretary at least two weeks prior to the start of
Annual Communication, in the order of their nominations. The biographical sketch of the Junior Grand Warden shall be read by the Grand Orator
whether or not there are multiple nominees. The Grand Orator shall read
only the facts from each biographical sketch. If the Grand Secretary did
not receive a biographical sketch for a nominee by the required date, the
vote shall be taken without reading a biographical sketch for that nominee.
Each elective officer shall be installed before the close of the Annual
Communication and shall serve until the installation of his successor,

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

201

subject to Section 404.510. This installation may be public or private at the
option of the incoming Grand Master.
If an elective officer is unable to be present, due to circumstances
beyond his control, he may be installed by the Grand Master at an appropriate place, with such ceremony as deemed proper by the Grand Master,
as soon as practicable not to exceed 60 days. If the elective officer is not
installed within 60 days, the office shall be declared vacant and the Grand
Master may appoint any member of Grand Lodge to fill the vacant elective
office temporarily or for the remainder of the Grand Lodge year.

5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 10
Removes Requirement That an Assistant Grand Lecturer Be
a Past Master of a Lodge in the Division He Serves
Under the California Masonic Code (“Code”), Assistant Grand Lecturers
(“AGLs”) must be members of Lodges in the particular divisions they serve as
AGLs. The Code also requires that the AGL of a division must be a Past Master
of a Lodge from that particular division. This second requirement is unduly
restrictive and should be eliminated.
We want our AGLs to be members of Lodges in the divisions they serve as
AGLs. We also want our AGLs to be Past Masters (“PM”). It should be far less
of a concern, however, from where our AGLs acquired their PM titles. Requiring
the PM experience to have occurred in a particular division places too much
weight on division boundary lines, which each Grand Master may change. It
arbitrarily limits our Fraternity’s pool of qualified AGL candidates without
providing any particular benefit.
For example, consider a brother who resided and served as a Master in
Division I, relocated to Division II, and then served faithfully for over a decade as
a member, Secretary and Treasurer of a Division II Lodge. As currently worded,
the Code prohibits this brother from serving as an AGL in Division II. How is
the Fraternity better off by that arbitrary result?
This Code requirement assumes that our division boundaries do not change
over time. That is not the case. The Code gives each Grand Master the power
to redraw divisions within Grand Lodge’s jurisdiction, and for good reason. As
populations shift and other geographic factors change, so too must our division
boundaries. How are we to meaningfully apply this Code restriction in the event
that divisions have changed? Consider Brother A who is a PM from a Lodge
that had been, but is no longer, in the division in which he is now a member.
Consider Brother B who is a PM from a Lodge that is now, but was not at the
time, in the same division in which he is now a member? As currently written,
the Code would prohibit Brother A from serving as an AGL in the district in
which he is currently a member -- but would allow Brother B. Again, how is the
Fraternity better off by these results?
My suggested Code amendment frees us from these strange results and
arbitrary limitations. It removes the requirement that the AGL’s past experience
geographically match today’s divisional boundaries. Instead, my proposed amendment concentrates our inquiry on what really matters: is the AGL a member in
the jurisdiction he will serve as AGL? And, does he have experience as a PM?

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

203

If you adopt this recommendation, Section 404.315 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§404.315. ASSISTANT GRAND LECTURERS.
The Grand Master shall divide this Jurisdiction into general divisions and
shall appoint for each such division an Assistant Grand Lecturer who shall
be a Past Master and member of a Lodge in such division and a Past Master
of any Constituent Lodge, and who shall, before entering upon his duties,
produce a certificate from the Grand Lecturer that he is sufficiently proficient in the Ritual to act as an Assistant Grand Lecturer.
It shall be the duty of each Assistant Grand Lecturer to:
A. Assist the Grand Lecturer in the discharge of his duties;
B. Examine and instruct the Inspectors within his division in the performance of their duties with respect to Ritual and assist the Grand
Master as and to the extent that he may direct in the supervision of such

representative to the Lodges in their respective districts;
C. Exercise general supervision over the ritual work in the Lodges under
their care;
D. Attend meetings of the Committee on Ritual whenever required by
the Grand Lecturer;
E. Arrange and conduct an annual conference for the Inspectors within
his division, subject to the approval of the Grand Lecturer;
F.

Oversee arrangements for Ceremonial Communications of Grand
Lodge in his division when directed by the Grand Master;

G. Attend at each Annual Communication any school of instruction held

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 11
Permits a Secretary to Serve as Master, Warden
or Secretary of Another Lodge
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) prohibits a member from serving
as the Master, Warden or Secretary of one Lodge while simultaneously serving
in any of those three positions at another Lodge.
I recommend that we continue this prohibition with one change with
respect to Lodge Secretaries. I recommend that we allow a brother serving
as a Secretary at one Lodge to also serve as a Master, Warden or Secretary
of another Lodge. This modest relaxation of the Code recognizes the many
dedicated members of our fraternity who maintain multiple affiliations. It also
recognizes and addresses the continuing need of our Lodges to identify and
select qualified candidates to fill their officer ranks. I believe that our smaller
Lodges will particularly benefit from my recommendation.
In the past, it might have been fair to suppose that a member would have
difficulty dedicating the time and energy necessary to serve as Secretary of a
Lodge while also serving as an officer of another Lodge. As a result of, among
other things, technological enhancements and the many services now provided
by Grand Lodge to our Lodge Secretaries, I have no concern in this regard now.
We all know many members who are both able and willing to competently perform the duties of Lodge Secretary while also serving as an officer of another
Lodge. We should stop denying our Lodges the opportunity to avail themselves
of these men.
I note that the Code also prohibits a member from holding more than one
office in one Lodge at the same time. I do not recommend any change to this rule.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 805.010 of the Code would be
amended to read as marked:
§805.010. OFFICERS.
The officers of a Lodge are Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden,
Treasurer, Secretary, Chaplain, Senior Deacon, Junior Deacon, Marshal,
Senior Steward, Junior Steward, Tiler and other officers as the Lodge may
deem proper to appoint. The Master, Senior Warden and Junior Warden,
Treasurer and Secretary shall be elected in conformity with this Code. The
other officers shall be appointed by the Master. Any Master Mason in good
standing, whether or not a member of the Lodge, may be appointed Tiler or

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

205

Organist. All other officers shall be members in good standing of the Lodge.
A member may not be Master, or Warden or Secretary, or any combination thereof, of two or more Lodges (other than Research Lodges and
Historic Lodges) at the same time. No one may hold more than one office
in a Lodge at the same time.
The title of Master applies not only to him who has been elected and
installed as Master, but to either of the Wardens while acting as Master.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Grand Master Metroka’s Recommendation No. 12
Shortens the Process Required by the California Masonic
Code for Lodge Consolidations
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) sets the process by which a Lodge
and its members consider, reach agreement, and approve consolidation with
another Lodge. Fulfilling the Code’s consolidation requirements can take a
Lodge no fewer than four Stated Meetings. As Lodges may have Stated Meetings
less frequently than monthly, this could mean that a year or more can pass
before the consolidation issue is settled one way or another.
We need to amend this process so that those Lodges that will benefit from
consolidation receive those benefits without undue delay.
In order for Lodges to consolidate, the Code requires each Lodge at an
initial Stated Meeting to adopt written resolutions forming a consolidation
committee. Once formed, this committee’s task is to meet and negotiate the
terms of consolidation with the other Lodge’s consolidation committee.
If agreement is reached between the consolidation committees, each consolidating Lodge at a subsequent Stated Meeting shall receive a report from its
consolidation committee describing the terms of consolidation. At that Stated
Meeting, Lodge members vote on the terms of consolidation. To pass, the vote
requires a majority of votes of those present at the Stated Meeting.
After an affirmative vote on the consolidation terms, the Code requires
that the Lodge collect signatures of at least three-fourths of the members of
the Lodge consenting to the consolidation (the “Consents”). (If the Grand
Master finds it impracticable for the Lodge to secure the required number of
Consents, he may approve the consolidation upon consent of not less than a
majority of the members of the Lodge.)
Once the Consents are received, the Code requires the Master to perform
another step before consolidation may occur. Pursuant to the Code, at a Stated
Meeting not earlier than the third Stated Meeting after adoption of the initial
resolution, the Master must examine the Consents and determine whether
a sufficient number of valid Consents was received. If the requisite number
of valid Consents was received, the Master shall declare consolidation to be
approved by his Lodge.
Fulfillment of these Code requirements requires the passage of no less
than four Stated Meetings.
I recommend that we amend the Code so that the timeline for consolidation need not stretch out over four or more Stated Meetings. My recommended

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

207

amendment to the Code changes the requirement that the Master wait until the
third Stated Meeting after the adoption of the resolution to form the consolidation committee to inspect the consent signatures and declare consolidation
approval to the second such Stated Meeting. In addition, my recommended
amendment allows the Master to call a Special Meeting in order to inspect the
consent signatures and declare approval of consolidation if sufficient signatures
have been submitted. Under my recommended amendment, this Special Meeting
could not be held until two Stated Meetings have occurred after the adoption
of the resolution to form the consolidation committee. This will continue to
ensure plenty of time for deliberation by the Lodge and its members.
My suggested Code amendment shortens the consolidation process without
in any way diminishing members’ existing rights to receive notice of potential
consolidation, participate in the deliberation process, vote on consolidation,
and give or withhold consent with respect to consolidation.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the Code. Section 807.010 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§807.010. SPECIAL MEETINGS.
Except as provided in Section 807.020 of this Code, a Lodge may hold such
Special Meetings in addition to its Stated Meeting on such dates and at such
times as it determines or the Master shall direct. No Special Meeting shall
be held on the same day as a Stated Meeting. A postponed Stated Meeting
shall not be considered to be a Special Meeting.
Only the following business may be conducted at a Special Meeting:
A. Collections or appropriations for charity;
B. Examining a candidate in the Candidate’s Lecture of any degree;
C. Conferring of degrees;
D. Funeral service;
E. Installation;
F.

Electing a representative to the Annual or a Special Communication
of the Grand Lodge; or

G. The Master’s examination of the Lodge members’ consent forms on
the consolidation of the Lodge with another Lodge or other Lodges,
and his declaration of the Lodge’s approval to such consolidation, if
applicable, pursuant to Section 813.010 of this Code; or
GH. After dispensation from the Grand Master:
1.

Balloting for and conferring the degrees upon an applicant without
reference to a committee, or

208

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

2.

Receiving and acting upon the application of a rejected applicant
within less than 12 months after the date of his rejection.

If the Grand Master determines that assembling the required number of
persons for holding a Special Meeting is prohibited by competent local, state
or national authority, the Grand Master may authorize the Lodge to hold a
Special Meeting through the use of conference telephone, electronic video
screen communication or electronic transmission so long as each member
of the Lodge participating in the meeting can communicate with all of the
other members concurrently and each member participating is provided the
means of participating in all matters before the meeting, including, without
limitation, the capacity to propose, or to interpose an objection to, a specific action to be taken by the Lodge. Such meetings shall be held without
the Lodge opening and closing ceremonies in the Ritual and without any
other esoteric or secret portion of the Ritual. The following business may
not be conducted at any such meeting: balloting, examining a candidate in

of electronic access to the meeting, for tiling such a meeting and for any
other requirements which he may deem appropriate.

or not the consolidated Lodge will have a Life Membership Plan.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to give each Lodge the right to

WHEREAS, Lodges need active and involved members in order to be relevant;

Resolution No. 23-03
Allows Special Meetings to Be Held on the Same Day
as a Stated Meeting
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow Special Meetings to be
held on the same day as a Stated Meeting.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 807.010 of the California Masonic Code states that “No Special
Meeting shall be held on the same day as a Stated Meeting”; and
WHEREAS, certain business such as the conferring of the Fellow Craft or Master
Mason degrees, conducting a funeral service in a Lodge of Master Masons,
installing officers in a Lodge of Master Masons, and the consideration of relief
of a worthy Mason in a Lodge of Master Masons cannot be done during a Stated
Meeting, and

216

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

WHEREAS, Masons often travel long distances to attend Lodge meetings,
occasionally making it desirable (especially for seniors and plural members)
to consolidate business to Stated Meeting dates in order to reduce the cost,
burden, and additional travel risks of returning for extra meetings, and
WHEREAS, this resolution, if adopted, will permit but not require Lodges to
confer any degree and conduct other Fellow Craft and Master Mason business
on the same date as a Stated Meeting, and
WHEREAS, this resolution, if adopted, will not compel any Constituent Lodge
to change their current practice of holding Special Meetings on days other than
Stated Meeting days,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.010 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.010. SPECIAL MEETINGS.
Except as provided in Section 807.020 of this Code, a Lodge may hold such
Special Meetings in addition to its Stated Meeting on such dates and at such
times as it determines or the Master shall direct. No A Special Meeting
shall may be held on the same day but not at the same time as a Stated
Meeting or other Special Meeting. A postponed Stated Meeting shall not
be considered to be a Special Meeting.
Only the following business may be conducted at a Special Meeting:
A. Collections or appropriations for charity;
B. Examining a candidate in the Candidate’s Lecture of any degree;
C. Conferring of degrees;
D. Funeral service;
E. Installation;
F.

Electing a representative to the Annual or a Special Communication
of the Grand Lodge; or

G. After dispensation from the Grand Master:
1.

Balloting for and conferring the degrees upon an applicant without
reference to a committee, or

2.

Receiving and acting upon the application of a rejected applicant
within less than 12 months after the date of his rejection.

If the Grand Master determines that assembling the required number of
persons for holding a Special Meeting is prohibited by competent local, state
or national authority, the Grand Master may authorize the Lodge to hold a
Special Meeting through the use of conference telephone, electronic video

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

217

screen communication or electronic transmission so long as each member
of the Lodge participating in the meeting can communicate with all of the
other members concurrently and each member participating is provided the
means of participating in all matters before the meeting, including, without
limitation, the capacity to propose, or to interpose an objection to, a specific action to be taken by the Lodge. Such meetings shall be held without
the Lodge opening and closing ceremonies in the Ritual and without any
other esoteric or secret portion of the Ritual. The following business may
not be conducted at any such meeting: balloting, examining a candidate in
the Candidate’s Lecture of any degree or conferring of degrees. The Grand
Master may make provision for voting if a written ballot is requested on
any matter, for notice to the Lodge members of the date, time and means
of electronic access to the meeting, for tiling such a meeting and for any
other requirements which he may deem appropriate.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the cipher ritual and Monitor and Officers
Manual be amended as necessary by the Ritual Committee, with the consent
of the Grand Master, to implement the foregoing resolutions.

Resolution No. 23-05:
Permits a Lodge to Designate the Voting Past Master
at Annual Communication
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit Lodges to designate
the specific Past Master entitled to cast the vote for the Past Masters of such
Lodge at an Annual Communication and to collect the ballot for said vote.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 403.075 identifies that one vote
during Annual Communication shall be assigned to the “Past Masters collectively
of each chartered Lodge”;
WHEREAS, this ballot has historically been available to be collected by ANY
Past Master of each chartered Lodge who first claims it;
WHEREAS, a Lodge may choose to designate a specific Past Master to collect
the ballot internally to represent the collective Past Masters of the Lodge;
WHEREAS, the designated Past Master may find, when he arrives to register
at Annual Communication, that the Past Master ballot for his Lodge may have
already been collected by another Past Master not so designated by the Lodge;
WHEREAS, such a situation may disrupt harmony within the Lodge and
allow a ballot to be cast that conflicts with the collective perspective of the
Lodge’s Past Masters;
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code already provides for a Lodge to elect a
representative to collect the ballots of the Master and Wardens and cast their
votes if they are unable to attend Annual Communication;
WHEREAS, similarly providing for the Past Masters’ ballot to be assigned to
a designated Past Master within the Lodge would minimize disharmony and
ensure that the full voice of the collective Past Masters of each Lodge would
be properly accounted for in balloting;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 403.075 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§403.075. VOTES.
Except as provided in Sections 403.080 and 403.085 of this Code, the following shall each be entitled to one vote only:
A. Elective and appointive Grand Lodge Officers except the Grand Tiler
and the Assistant Grand Tiler;

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

219

B. Past Grand Officers;
C. Masters, Senior Wardens and Junior Wardens of chartered Lodges; and
D. Past Masters collectively of each chartered Lodge.
If neither the Master nor either of the Wardens of a Lodge has registered, the elected representative of the Lodge may cast the votes of Master
and Wardens of the Lodge.
A Designated Past Master may cast the vote of the Past Masters collectively of a charted Lodge at an Annual Communication if a specific Past
Master is chosen to do so by such Lodge as provided in this section. The
Designated Past Master may be chosen by either those members of the
Lodge or by those Past Masters of the Lodge, present and voting at a Stated
Meeting, as the Lodge may determine. The Lodge Master with the attest
of the Lodge Secretary shall certify to the Grand Secretary the Lodge’s
Designated Past Master, if any, for the applicable Annual Communication.
If a chartered Lodge has chosen a Designated Past Master and the Lodge
Master of such Lodge, with the attest of the Lodge Secretary, has certified
to the Grand Secretary the Lodge’s Designated Past Master, as provided in
this section, then such Designated Past Master shall have the sole right to
collect the Past Masters’ ballot for such Lodge for the applicable Annual
Communication.
Respectfully submitted,
s/ Adam J. Hanin, PM, No. 480
s/ Michael D. Tagulao, PM, No. 113
s/ G. Michael Wilson, PM, No. 144

RESOLUTIONS FOR 2024
Resolution No. 24-01
Makes Third Degree Proficiency a Prerequisite for
Nomination to the Office of Master, Senior Warden, or
Junior Warden
The proponents of this resolution seek to make the receipt of a Certificate
of Proficiency in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Master Mason Degree a prerequisite for nomination to the office of Master, Senior Warden, or Junior Warden
and remove the receipt of a Certificate of Proficiency as a condition to an officer-elect’s installation to those offices.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, The Grand Lodge of Free And Accepted Masons of California
upholds the values of knowledge, proficiency, and preparedness among its
members, especially those in leadership positions within the Lodges; and
WHEREAS, the esteemed positions of Master, Senior Warden, and Junior
Warden are critical to the effective governance and ceremonial duties of Masonic
Lodges, requiring not only dedication but also a deep understanding of Masonic
law, rituals, and traditions; and
WHEREAS, one of the current installation requirements for these principal
officers include the completion of the Third-Degree proficiency as stated in
Chapter V, Article V; [Installation of Lodge Officers], sections 805.520, 805.530,
and 805.540; and
WHEREAS, to further ensure that nominees for these offices are thoroughly
prepared and qualified, a proposal to amend the current California Masonic Code
/ Constitution and Ordinances is hereby submitted to require the completion
and certification of the Master Mason proficiency at the time of nomination,
which would serve to enhance the leadership quality within the Lodges and
to further ensure that nominees for these offices are thoroughly prepared and
qualified; and

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

221

WHEREAS, the requirement for proficiency at the nomination stage will ensure
candidates are well-prepared for their respective roles and duties, leading to
more effective leadership; and
WHEREAS, that the proposed amendment resolution will not incur additional
costs to the Lodges nor impact existing rituals; and
WHEREAS, that the proposed amendment consistently promotes a culture of
excellence and proficiency in Masonic ritual work, enhancing the quality and
solemnity of our ceremonies; and
WHEREAS, that this proposed requirement will also reduce the administrative burden on District Inspectors, as the process and requirement will ensure
candidates are fully prepared for their leadership roles and encourage brothers
to plan their Masonic progression; and
WHEREAS, that this proposed amendment resolution does not hinder the
progress of worthy brethren, but rather sets forth a clear path for those aspiring
to leadership roles within the Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the successful passage of this resolution would render moot the current stipulation in CMC / Chapter V, Article V Installation of Officers §805.520
(Conditions to Installation of Master-Elect), §805.530 (Conditions to Installation
of Senior Warden-Elect) and §805.540 (Conditions to Installation of Junior
Warden-Elect) which mandates the completion of Master Mason proficiency
as a condition for installation, given that this requirement would have been
fulfilled prior to election100..
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Sections 805.410 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.410. ELECTED OFFICERS.
The Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary of each Lodge shall be
elected annually at the Stated Meeting in November each year, except
as otherwise permitted in Section 807.000 of this Code. A Certificate of
Proficiency in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Master Mason Degree shall
be a prerequisite for nomination to the office of Master, Senior Warden,
or Junior Warden. The election shall be by ballot. A majority of all votes
cast shall be necessary for an election. A blank ballot shall not constitute a
vote cast. The Lodge, by unanimous consent, may permit any designated
officer to cast the ballot for the Lodge.
If an eligible candidate fails to receive a majority of the votes cast, and
the candidate receiving a majority is ineligible, there is no election. When
a candidate for office is ineligible because he is delinquent in his dues, but
his dues are paid before a second ballot, and he receives a majority of the
votes cast a second time, he is properly elected.

222

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

All members of the Lodge in good standing shall be entitled to vote
at an election of Lodge officers. An annual election held contrary to the
provision of this section shall be void.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 805.520 of the California Masonic
Code be amended as marked:
§805.520. CONDITIONS TO INSTALLATION OF THE MASTER-ELECT.
Before a Master-elect can be installed, there shall be presented to the
Installing Officer a Certificate of Qualification of the Grand Lecturer, the
Assistant Grand Lecturer of the division in which his Lodge is situated, or
the Inspector of the district in which his Lodge is situated, certifying that:
A. He has personally examined the Master-elect and that he is qualified to
give the Master’s work and lectures of the Entered Apprentice, Fellow
Craft and Master Mason Degrees; and
B. He has received a Certificate of Proficiency in the Candidate’s Lecture
of the Master Mason Degree; and
C.B. He is proficient in those portions of this Code that relate to the government of a Lodge.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 805.530 of the California Masonic
Code be amended as marked:
§805.530. CONDITIONS TO INSTALLATION OF THE SENIOR
WARDEN-ELECT.

the Installing Officer a Certificate of Qualification of the Grand Lecturer,

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Masonic Homes of California
In its 126th year of operation, the Masonic Homes of California served
more people than ever before, both within the fraternity and outside it, through
its residential and community-based services. In a year marked by change, the
Masonic Homes’ capacity and health services were expanded on the Covina
campus, and, system-wide, eligibility was opened to a wider pool of applicants.
Through Masonic Outreach Services, the organization was able to extend itself
beyond those campuses and deeper into our communities.
Expansion of Eligibility and Increased Census
In November 2023, as part of its promise to help more Masons and their families,
the Masonic Homes board approved a revision of the eligibility requirements to
access its services. Under the new guidelines, all California Masons, as well as
California Prince Hall Masons and Masons belonging to the California Grand
Lodge of Iran in Exile, as well as their parents and parents-in-law, have access
to the Masonic Homes’ residential campuses, Masonic Outreach Services, and
the Masonic Center for Youth and Families. This expansion provides real relief
for members as they grapple with the rising cost of senior care for themselves
or their family members and deepens our bond with other Masons in California.
As part of this development, the Masonic Homes has agreed to offer additional
apartments to independent seniors at its sister campus, Acacia Creek.
Since these changes were announced, the Masonic Homes received 92
calls and 20 applications from those who would not otherwise have had access
to these life-changing services. Additionally, applications to MHC retirement
homes from those choosing month-to-month contracts have risen as a result of
new pricing strategies that appeal to those who prefer a pay-as-you-go option.
As occupancy sits at 88 percent across the two senior campuses, the existing
310 residents continue to welcome new neighbors at every level of living on a
regular basis—a striking change from just a year ago, when the campuses were
still challenged by the protracted recovery from the pandemic.

228

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Citrus Heights Health Center Opens
On April 29, the newly built Citrus Heights Health Center in Covina welcomed
residents for the first time. As promised, this meant that eight former MHC
residents, who’d previously been forced to move elsewhere to receive skilled
nursing care, were able to return to the Covina campus and get the care they
need while surrounded by friends and family. As the center awaits official
Medicare certification, staff are working to increase occupancy at this beautiful
building. Once fully open, the Citrus Heights Health Center will offer accommodations to those in need of short- or long-term skilled nursing, including
dementia care. This addition to the Covina campus was made possible in part
by the landmark Let’s Write the Future fundraising campaign, through which
California Masons raised more than $7.5 million.
With the Citrus Heights Health Center complete, the Masonic Homes’
Covina campus now offers the same high-quality skilled nursing care that’s
available in Union City through the Lorber facility—the only such offering with
a five-star Medicare rating in the East Bay.
Community-Based Services and Partnerships
The Masonic Center for Youth and Families (MCYAF) and Masonic Outreach
Services (MOS) have grown rapidly to serve clients throughout the state both
in person and remotely. In 2024, MCYAF worked with 750 individual clients
and 60 Masonic Homes residents, while MOS fielded 2,710 calls to the Masonic
Assistance hotline from Masons needing advice, resources, and emergency funds
through the Distressed Worthy Brother Relief Fund. It ultimately supported 455
clients with case management or financial assistance. All told, MOS provided
more than $2.5 million in relief this year.
Lodge Outreach Services held meetings throughout the state to train 208
members of the fraternity to provide support to members in their community.
These important trainings help Masons understand how to reach out to members locally to provide information and aid to those who may not be in contact
with the lodge. By strengthening its partnership with the Grand Lodge Member
Services team, staff at MOS are able to help members return to lodge for the
first time in what for many has been several years.
The Masonic Center for Youth and Families continues to see high demand
for mental health services across the lifespan. This year, MCYAF relocated to
Union City from the Presidio in San Francisco. Moving forward, this change
will allow it to serve more residents of the Masonic Homes and the community
in Union City, which is in great need of services such as these. At its Covina
location, MCYAF retained full caseloads in 2024, including new group programs
for residents of the Masonic Homes there. Partnerships with nearby Pomona
Unified School District and the Children’s Advocacy Center continue to be
beneficial.
These kinds of community partnerships are central to the mission of the

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

229

Masonic Homes. In recent years, the Masonic Homes has worked closely with
Unitek College, a provider of high-quality nursing and technical education for
the senior care industry, to run the Masonic Homes Academy. Through this
program, students working toward licensed vocational nursing and certified
nursing-assistant degrees receive hands-on training. So far, 72 percent of the
students in this program who passed their state exams have gone on to accept
jobs with the Masonic Homes. Others have taken positions at senior communities in the area. This type of partnership not only enhances the reputation of
the Masonic Homes locally but provides desperately needed healthcare workers
for the entire community.
Facilities and Personnel Updates
Meanwhile, the physical footprint of the Masonic Homes’ locations continues to
change. As MCYAF takes up residence in what was formerly the administrator’s
house and plans progress for a new swimming pool and outdoor dining venue
in Covina, the Masonic Homes is evolving to meet the changing needs of the
fraternity and our communities.
This year also marks the first 12-month period under the leadership of
president and CEO Terry Quigley, who joined the organization in July 2023. Her
deep industry experience and compassionate leadership were important assets
over the past year. Consequently, after longtime Acacia Creek president and CEO
Chuck Major announced his retirement, the Acacia Creek and Masonic Homes
boards appointed Quigley as CEO of Acacia Creek upon Major’s departure.
The board made this decision with confidence that her leadership will build a
bright future for both organizations as they care for seniors and their families
throughout California.

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Acacia Creek Retirement Community
Since the pandemic, the board of Acacia Creek Retirement Community has
focused its attention squarely on increasing its census count. In 2024, those
efforts began paying off. Thanks to a revamped sales and marketing approach
that is better aligned with the Masonic Homes, the board is able to project close
to 90 percent occupancy at Acacia Creek by the end of this fiscal year—up from
a recent low of 69 percent. Victory is in our sights!
That figure is a testament to the hard work and creativity of the staff, board,
and residents of Acacia Creek, as well as several significant developments that
have helped us turn the corner over the past year.
Leadership Changes
Perhaps the most significant development at Acacia Creek is that president
and CEO Chuck Major will retire at the end of October 2024. That position
will be filled by Terry Quigley, the president and CEO of the Masonic Homes of
California, whose role will expand to include responsibility for the operational
leadership of both Acacia Creek and the Masonic Homes.
Chuck Major has led our community for the past 13 years. He helped get
Acacia Creek off the ground and ultimately reach 99 percent occupancy pre-pandemic. He also safely guided our community through the Covid crisis and has
laid the foundation for a very bright future here. He has consistently made
resident satisfaction his top priority and has earned the respect and admiration
of his staff and our board. He is a true professional and will be sorely missed.
On behalf of the board, staff, and Grand Lodge, we wish Chuck a wonderful
and joyous retirement. He has earned it.
Looking forward, we are excited to welcome Terry Quigley, who was unanimously approved by the board. Quigley is a proven and experienced leader in
the retirement-care industry and has earned our absolute faith and confidence
in her ability to manage Acacia Creek. This change in leadership will help us
deepen our partnership with the Masonic Homes on our shared campus. The
residents, board, and staff have been meeting with Quigley to start this transition and ensure that our excellent service levels are maintained throughout
the change in leadership.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

255

Working with The Masonic Homes of California
Quigley’s appointment reflects Acacia Creek’s close partnership with the
Masonic Homes of California, and indeed the two organizations have cooperated closely over the past year on efforts to increase census on both campuses.
Beginning in 2023, the board, together with that of the Masonic Homes of
California, engaged an outside sales and marketing consultant to train a larger
sales team. This team provides sales services for all levels of care on the Union
City campus, at both Acacia Creek and the Masonic Homes, while developing
new-prospect events and marketing materials in collaboration with the Grand
Lodge’s communications department.
In addition, that year the Masonic Homes of California bought 12 more
apartments at Acacia Creek with a view toward offering an additional independent-living option to Masons on an “assignment of assets” contract. With this
addition, our organizations are able to welcome more members of our fraternal
family to the Union City campus with more financing options.
With Quigley now heading both organizations, we expect to see more
cooperation of this sort between the communities, which brings more Masons
and their families into Acacia Creek and more of Acacia Creek’s best-in-class
services to the broader fraternity.
New Sales and Marketing Strategies
As mentioned, the board has engaged a marketing and sales consultant, Amy
LaGrant, to help augment this department during a time of change. In that time
(and since in-person tours resumed mid-2022), we have seen month-over-month
increases in tour activity and a significant increase in sales leads. In fiscal year
2024, the sales team held monthly open houses and a frequent lineup of public
events including seminars on downsizing, successful aging, nutrition, and the
basics of continuing-care retirement communities. Along with these events,
we developed new marketing materials and direct-mail advertisements to help
promote sales. In all, these events brought hundreds of prospective buyers onto
campus to get a look at our wonderful community.
Strategic Plan
The board and staff of Acacia Creek have remained steadfast in their commitment to providing residents with an active and meaningful life. That promise is
supported by a strategic plan adopted in 2022 centered on four key themes: quality of life, operational integrity, board engagement, and Masonic connections.
The first theme, quality of life, represents the well-being, safety, and happiness of our residents—which have always been the most important goals at
Acacia Creek. The second theme is operational integrity, or the management of
fiscal responsibilities. The third theme is board engagement, aimed at developing a culture in which members of the board participate actively in the Acacia
Creek community. The final theme, Masonic connections, aligns Acacia Creek’s

256

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

strategic plan with other Grand Lodge entities.
Industry Recognition
Acacia Creek remains a singularly special place to age and grow. It is one of just 15
senior communities nationwide to be certified as a Center for Successful Aging,
and its residents demonstrate through annual reviews that they enjoy better
health, nutrition, and rates of physical activity than do seniors at comparable
communities, or even in their own homes.
Acacia Creek’s partnership with Masterpiece, a national organization that
provides education and programs on physical and mental wellness, remains a key
part of that success. Through Masterpiece programs, Acacia Creek residents and
staff are empowered to pursue new skills, physical activities, and opportunities
for personal fulfillment, and to contribute to the wider community.
Giving Thanks
As this will be my last report as a member of the Acacia Creek board of directors, I would like to thank my fellow members of the board, the Grand Lodge
Executive Committee, the Grand Lodge staff, and the Masonic Homes board of
trustees. In particular, I would like to thank Allan Casalou and Andy Cameron
for their counsel, as well as past chairmen Larry Adamson, Ara Maloyan, Ken
Nagel, and Michael Neben for showing me the way. Thank you all for your
continued investment in our shared success and for the trust you have placed
in me. Nine years have gone by very quickly, and it has been a distinct honor
and pleasure to be a part of our wonderful Acacia Creek community.
Acacia Creek has a bright future, and I look forward to watching from the
sideline as our community continues to succeed and thrive.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
California Masonic Foundation
Masons have an obligation to support one another and improve the
world around them. The California Masonic Foundation is one of the most
important ways we act on that obligation. By supporting and partnering with
outside community organizations, the Foundation extends the reach of our
members and lodges, amplifying the good work each is engaged in, while also
launching its own efforts aimed at bridging gaps for those in need.
The Foundation’s work over the past year has been a testament to that
approach. By collaborating with trusted partners and proactively seeking out
opportunities for new cooperative efforts, the Foundation is bringing Masonic
philanthropic dollars, muscle, and know-how into more communities than ever
before—and helping fulfill our organization’s need for positive public awareness.
Once again, this work has involved several new and ongoing programs,
largely centered on supporting young people and youth and family literacy. And
with record-high giving by the Foundation to many of these initiatives, we can
see that we’re making a significant mark.
Place-Based Philanthropy: Sacramento
Over the past two years, the Foundation has pursued a new philanthropic
strategy by focusing its energy on a single region, beginning with San Diego. By
bringing Foundation staff and Masonic representatives together with community partners there, we were able to initiate several new and exciting programs,
including launching the Johnny Ritchey Scholarship, a new award presented
alongside the San Diego Padres Community Foundation and the college-readiness nonprofit Reality Changers of San Diego. In addition, the California
Masonic Foundation and Padres Foundation began work on an ambitious plan
to revitalize several spaces at a single local school, Perkins Elementary. That
work culminated with the announcement of a three-year gift to the San Diego
Unified School District worth $390,000 to expand the district’s college, career,
and technical education programs.
This year, Foundation staff worked in earnest to bring the same strategies
to bear on a new community: Sacramento. Working with local school districts,
community colleges, nonprofits, and other partners, the Foundation identified

258

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

several opportunities to make an impact through its family literacy and Working
Tools technical education programs.
Already, the Foundation has begun working with the Washington and
Sacramento City Unified School Districts, including Westfield Village, Riverbank,
and Elkhorn Village elementary schools, as well as Sacramento Community
College and other technical schools. Additionally, the Foundation has met with
the California Mobility Center and Sacramento Municipal Utility District to
pursue college and career opportunities for young people.
Much of this work will bear fruit over the coming year, but already several
exciting opportunities have been presented. These include working with Raising
a Reader, one of our closest partners, to introduce a Farsi-language component
to its family reading-engagement materials particularly for the many Afghan
families in West Sacramento. Additionally, the Foundation is excited to launch
its Working Tools career and technical education program in the area to train a
new generation of Sacramento high school graduates on careers in green energy
and zero-emissions automotive engineering.
Family Literacy
Sacramento isn’t the only area in which the Foundation continued to work
closely with Raising a Reader. In addition to Sacramento, the Foundation identified Orange County and Long Beach as priority regions for investment, as well
as the Oakland, West Contra Costa, and Hayward school districts. Additionally,
the Foundation has worked closely with Fontana Unified School District on
plans to introduce Raising a Reader to 15 more classrooms there over the
next year, with Fontana Unified set to match a $30,000 investment from the
Foundation. Since launching our partnership with Raising a Reader more than
12 years ago, the Foundation has helped bring its signature book-bag program
into 873 elementary-school classrooms around the state, nearly all in the lowest-performing quartile. That included 44 more first-grade, kindergarten, and
transitional kindergarten classrooms in 2023–24. The Foundation expects to
reach its goal of 1,000 classrooms by the 2025–26 school year.
College Readiness
Despite several significant challenges in identifying scholarship nominees
since the pandemic and administrative delays related to the Department of
Education’s FAFSA rollout, the Foundation is pleased to report that 2023–24 was
one of its most successful years for college scholarships. All told, the Foundation
has issued more than $8.7 million to 1,200 students since 2011.
Investment in Success: The Foundation granted 93 awards for this signature
scholarship program this year, the most since 2017. That included issuance to
a record number of students in San Francisco (47), Los Angeles, the East Bay,
and Sacramento. Much of the credit for this rise can be attributed to a new
partnership with the college-readiness program 10,000 Degrees, which helped

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

259

identify worthy and deserving high school seniors all over the Bay Area. Since
2011, Investment in Success has helped 968 students realize their higher-education potential through more than $6.7 million in gifts.
C.E. Towne Scholarship: Working with our partners at the Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of California, the Foundation was able to administer a record high of
25 awards through the C.E. Towne Fund to the children and grandchildren of
Prince Hall Masons this year, ranging from $5,000 to $10,000. In all, that totaled
$200,000 in 2023–24. Since its launch in 2019, it has now allocated $910,000
to 127 students.
Masonic Youth Leadership Award: One of the highlights of the past year was
crossing the $1 million threshold for this scholarship fund benefitting members
of Job’s Daughters, the International Order of Rainbow for Girls, and DeMolay.
This year, the fund issued 13 awards totaling $120,000. Since 2016, it has been
issued to 216 students, totaling $1,070,110.
Masons4Mitts
One of the longest-running and most cherished Foundation programs,
Masons4Mitts has had another banner season—and one that was highlighted
on July 10, when representatives from the Foundation, the Grand Lodge, and the
Masonic Homes of California were on hand at Oracle Park in San Francisco to formally announce a new three-year gift totaling $650,000 to the Giants Community
Fund to support its Junior Giants and other youth sports and education programs.
Building on more than 15 years of collaboration between the Foundation
and the Giants, this gift will help expand the free, co-ed, and non-competitive
Junior Giants baseball and softball leagues throughout Northern California, as
well as Junior Giants Schools (an afterschool PE program in San Francisco public
schools) and the Giants Community Fund Academy, which will add a career
and technical education component to its middle and high school programs.
The gift also cements the Masons as the “Official Mitt Champion” of the San
Francisco Giants Community Fund.
Cornerstone Society
When the three-year Let’s Write the Future campaign ended in 2022,
Foundation staff shifted their energy toward cultivating planned gifts through
the Cornerstone Society, a group of Masonic donors who have pledged to leave
a gift for the Foundation or the Masonic Homes in their will or trust. In 2024,
61 new Masons joined that group—a nearly 30 percent increase in overall
membership. In all, the Cornerstone Society now counts 260 living members,
representing millions of dollars in planned gift expectations.
Further, 2024 saw a sharp spike in realized planned gifts, with nearly $2.4
million coming in to the Masonic Homes and California Masonic Foundation
funds. This number can vary widely from year to year, and indeed 2024 is more
than $1.5 million ahead of 2023 figures.

260

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Annual Fund
Overall giving to the Foundation’s annual fund was generally in line with
pre-pandemic, non-campaign years. Overall, Masons raised $777,086 (as of
August 1) through the annual fund, down approximately 26 percent compared
with 2023. Much of this was a result of Let’s Write the Future pledges being
fulfilled. Average member gift, total number of member gifts, Grand Master
Circle–level donors, and Anniversary-level donors were all down slightly as well,
while lodge-officer gifts and recurring online gifts both trended up. Looking
back, the average member gift is 28 percent higher than it was in 2016, while
the average size of lodge gifts has risen dramatically. The past year was also the
final year for many five-year gifts given during the 2018 Let’s Write the Future
campaign, and to date 91 percent of individual and 94 percent of lodge pledges
to that campaign have been fulfilled.
Thanks as always always are due to members of the California Masonic
Foundation’s board of trustees and professional staff, including president Doug
Ismail and his staff, Emily LimÓn and her staff, and Most Worshipful G. Sean
Metroka for their vision, dedication, and continued support. It is through the
generosity of California Masons that we are able to undertake these programs
and reach into communities to make a positive difference. To everyone who
has given to the Foundation, your gift is bringing tangible benefits to the lives
of people in need. On behalf of those thousands of Californians, we thank you.

California Masonic Memorial Temple
Masonic Memorial Temple continues to thrive as both a business unit
supporting the charitable programs of the California Masonic Foundation and
as the entity responsible for ensuring that our headquarters remains a physical
testament to Freemasonry in California.
Overall, financial performance has been strong over the past year, with an
increased event calendar at the Masonic Auditorium put on by Live Nation and
continuing strong community relations. Meanwhile, the 2030 capital improvement plan is progressing on track. At the same time, the board has explored
several exciting new ideas to increase public exposure and visitation to the
CMMT and to highlight the building and the fraternity’s importance locally.
Increased Events And Revenue
Last year, the San Francisco Planning Commission approved an amendment to
the CMMT conditional-use permit, increasing the maximum number of annual
live entertainment events from 79 to 91. This pivotal change has resulted in a
substantial rise in visitor numbers, with 2024 expected to see more than 250,000
guests enter the building. December 2023 alone set a new monthly record with
40,000 attendees.
The expanded range of concerts and comedy shows has been transformative
for our community. Beyond the thrilling performances and heightened excitement, these events have had a significant economic impact. Visitors are spending
more than twice the price of their tickets at nearby businesses, fueling growth
across hotels, restaurants, shops, and transportation services. This influx of
tourism not only revitalizes our economy and supports local businesses but also
stimulates community development. The increased activity is a powerful driver
of positive change, enhancing economic vitality and community engagement.
Freemasons’ Hall
This year marks the fifth anniversary of Freemasons’ Hall. Over that time, it
has established itself as one of the most modern and engaging lodge facilities
in the state. Currently, 10 Masonic lodges regularly use the space, making it a

262

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

vibrant and active hub of Masonry in California.
In 2024, we returned to our pre-pandemic slate of programming at
Freemasons’ Hall, offering a variety of events and activities alongside regular
lodge meetings. Highlights include the grooming and tailoring event held in
May; the Saint John’s Day Banquet, co-sponsored by La Parfaite Union No. 17,
in June; and several other workshops on Masonic ritual, speaker sessions, and
social gatherings. Additionally, we have introduced a private barbershop and
enhanced catering services for lodges and other Masonic organizations.
Freemasons’ Hall aims to deliver an exceptional experience for our lodges
while also welcoming all Masons. We hope that these efforts can serve as
a model for activating Masonic halls across the state and beyond. A special
thank-you goes to Jose Camello for his unwavering dedication as the manager
of Freemasons’ Hall.
Building Improvements
The California Masonic Memorial Temple is approaching the midpoint of its
2030 capital plan, with significant projects slated for completion in the next
two years that will mark a period of substantial transformation for the facility.
Key projects include:
HVAC Improvements and Building Management System: These upgrades
aim to enhance control over heating and air-conditioning, optimize
efficiency for the auditorium and exhibition hall, and reduce energy and
operating costs. The projected completion is Fall 2024.
Building Envelope and Facade Rehabilitation: This project will address
water intrusion and repair the deteriorating marble cladding on the
south wall and fire-escape staircase, as well as undertake essential
generational restoration work. The timeline for this project is from
November 2024 to February 2026.
Elevator Modernization: The modernization of all four building elevators is designed to improve reliability, aesthetics, and energy efficiency
while lowering maintenance costs. This project is scheduled to run
from December 2024 to April 2025.
Given the shortage of building engineers and managers in the Bay Area,
CMMT has enlisted the Montgomery Corporation to manage these capital projects and provide operating plans and strategies for daily facility
services. Their expertise is crucial for navigating a currently tight and
costly labor market, ensuring our projects are executed effectively and
efficiently.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

263

Emile Norman Arts Foundation Partnership
In alignment with our strategic goals, the board of the CMMT is leveraging its
stunning artwork to forge new partnerships and attract more visitors. As the
custodian of Emile Norman’s most significant works—including the striking
endomosaic mural, the dramatic exterior relief of a tug of war, and the two
exterior pillars—it is a natural fit for us to collaborate with the newly established
Emile Norman Arts Foundation.
Over the past year, we have cultivated a strong relationship with the foundation and are actively exploring the creation of an Emile Norman Gallery at
CMMT. Additionally, we are discussing the possibility of using our facility to
archive Emile Norman’s extensive collection of works. In June, senior board
members and Masons from Carmel and Monterey attended the Emile Norman
birthday celebration at his Big Sur home, now preserved by the foundation. In
September, we welcomed their leadership to CMMT to view Norman’s works,
tour our facility, and evaluate the proposed gallery space. We anticipate that
this collaboration will attract a new audience to CMMT, enhancing our profile
and significance in the art world and beyond.
Neighborhood Relations
As a major landowner on Nob Hill, the CMMT board recognizes the vital importance of maintaining strong relationships with the local community. Executive
vice president Allan Casalou has spearheaded several initiatives to reinforce
our role as a respected and engaged community partner.
Casalou’s two-year term as president of the Nob Hill Association, San
Francisco’s oldest neighborhood association, will conclude on October 30,
though he will continue to contribute as a board director as he has for 12 years.
Khalil Sweidy will remain on as treasurer of the association.
Our efforts to collaborate with neighborhood representatives through
the Nob Hill Liaison Group have been well received, with no issues reported
regarding the operation of our building. We’ve been commended for our proactive work with city agencies to address unpermitted food vendors, demonstrating our commitment to maintaining a vibrant and orderly neighborhood.
Furthermore, Khalil Sweidy, Jose Camello, and Allan Casalou actively support
several key neighborhood events, including Rośe in the Park, a fall movie night,
and the annual holiday lighting celebration. These events not only foster community spirit but also highlight our dedication to enhancing the quality of life
of residents and strengthening our ties with the local area.
The board wishes to extend its appreciation to executive vice president and
Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, chief financial officer Carol Hunter, director of
financial planning and real estate Khalil Sweidy, general counsel Andy Cameron,
and Grand Treasurer Charles Cross. Thanks also go to Jake Winn for his work
in preparing and managing board meetings and materials, and to Joe Evans for
his excellent curation and management of the Henry Wilson Coil Library and

264

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Museum of Freemasonry collections and his significant assistance in engaging
with the Emile Norman Arts Foundation. Sincere thanks and appreciation also
go out to the staff who work so diligently in representing the board’s interests
and maintaining and managing the building.
Finally, thanks to our grand master, Most Worshipful Sean Metroka, for
the opportunity to serve, and for his support of our efforts.

REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Nob Hill Masonic Center
As one of the five business entities of the Grand Lodge of California and
the only for-profit corporation, the Nob Hill Masonic Center plays a vital, yet
often understated, role within the fraternity. The NHMC manages a 565-stall
parking garage under the California Masonic Memorial Temple in San Francisco,
along with a smaller facility situated across California Street at Grace Cathedral.
Profits generated from these assets are distributed as an annual dividend to the
Grand Lodge, supporting its operations and charitable initiatives. Additionally,
rental fees from the NHMC are paid to the California Masonic Memorial Temple,
indirectly benefiting the California Masonic Foundation.
2024 Performance Summary
In 2024, the NHMC demonstrated a significant recovery from the pandemic,
attributed to an adaptive business strategy that is shifting to meet to the current economic landscape. There has been a noticeable surge in event parking,
thanks to an increase in scheduled performances at the California Masonic
Memorial Temple through Live Nation, which has helped balance declines in
daily and monthly parking revenues. We anticipate total revenue for the fiscal
year to reach $4 million, helping to confront the headwinds of slower business
activity and inflation. While profits remain below pre-pandemic benchmarks,
the NHMC is positioned to meet the projected dividend in the Grand Lodge
budget.
Event Parking
Event parking has emerged as the strongest component of NHMC operations in
2024. With an expanded concert and comedy lineup from Live Nation—growing from 79 events in 2023 to 91 in 2024—revenues have thrived. The total is
expected to reach nearly $1.4 million by October 31, a remarkable 66 percent
increase compared with fiscal year 2023.

266

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Monthly Parking
Monthly parking sustained the NHMC through the pandemic. Although
event-parking demand has reduced monthly availability, revenues from this
segment remain robust.
Daily Parking
Conversely, daily parking has experienced a marked decline, with revenues dropping by 20 percent in 2024. This trend reflects the broader economic challenges
facing downtown San Francisco generally and Nob Hill in particular. The board
is actively exploring strategies to enhance daily and monthly parking revenues
while capitalizing on strong event-parking performance.
Grace Cathedral Parking
Since assuming management of the parking facility at Grace Cathedral (1051
Taylor St.) in January 2022, this asset has consistently reported quarterly profits
and contributed to record revenues for the NHMC.
Garage Enhancements
Ongoing improvements to the garage include a revamp of exterior signage
aimed at optimizing traffic flow and enhancing driver awareness. In 2024, we
prepared and distributed a request for proposals from external vendors, ultimately contracting with Flouresco, which initiated the project and is currently
obtaining the necessary permits. In recent years, the board has also overseen
the installation of new license-plate recognition software, upgrades to the
parking-access and revenue-control systems, leasing of several parking spaces
to the EV-charging company Volta, and continued collaboration with Tesla to
promote electric-vehicle use.
Neighborhood Relations
Under the leadership of board president Allan Casalou, the NHMC maintains a
strong presence on the Nob Hill Association and with the Nob Hill Community
Liaison Group. These associations foster solidarity with neighboring businesses
and residents, and reflect our commitment to community engagement. In 2024,
Casalou will conclude a two-year term as president of the Nob Hill Association.
As we look to the future, the NHMC remains optimistic as San Francisco’s
business environment continues its gradual recovery from the pandemic. We

REPORT OF THE GRAND LODGE
COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE
The Masons of California corporate insurance program provides
coverage for lodges including historic lodges, hall associations, the Masonic
Homes, Acacia Creek, and the California Masonic Memorial Temple (CMMT)
and Nob Hill Masonic Center. The program includes property, general liability,
umbrella liability, earthquake, D&O, employment practices liability, and crime
insurance policies, all renewed April 1, 2024. We added travel accident, special
contingency, and foreign liability/executive assistance coverage to the program
this year.
I would like to acknowledge the positive work on this committee by Wor.
David Anderson, who sadly passed away a few weeks ago. During his time as
committee chair, he led the insurance broker transition and helped guide us
thorough a very tough insurance marketplace. He will be missed.
We continue as we ended last year’s insurance program, with another
difficult renewal. The insurance marketplace has not changed much from the
same highs and lows we encountered in 2023 and so we continue to face the
challenge of capturing an ever-evolving marketplace. The committee is exploring
alternative risk transfer models for the property coverage and will report back
as soon as possible. We note that property underwriters continue to be wary
of certain classes of business and geographic areas that may face higher rates
as well as more restrictive terms.
Grand Lodge staff and the Insurance Committee worked diligently to look
at cost-saving areas as well as ideas beyond the traditional insurance transactions mentioned. These included self-insurance, insurance captives, and
other risk-transfer methods. The committee will continue to review alternative
risk-transfer methods and hope to produce an update by the end of this year
or early 2025.
