REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON INVESTMENTS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California,
The investment committee is charged with the prudent management
of the Grand Lodge Investment Fund (GLIF), with priority given to income
generation, capital preservation, and asset growth. The committee has adopted
a long-term target return of 6.75 percent annualized.
As of the fiscal year ending October 31, 2024, the GLIF stands at approximately $1.059 billion, and withdrawals by the Masonic entities during the
trailing 12 months were in the amount of $72.8 million.
As of October 31, 2024, the GLIF delivered a trailing 12-month annualized
return of 20 perent compared to the allocation index’s return of 20.4 percent
over the same period and meaningfully above the 6.75 percent long-term target
return. The double-digit return was driven by the relatively high returns of public
equity and debt. The private allocation within the portfolio continues to be
built out and the committee anticipates a substantial contribution to the overall
performance in the upcoming years. Absent any major shifts, the committee
continues to believe that the current long-term investment strategy has served
the portfolio well in the past and should continue to do so. In that effort, the
committee and NEPC actively modified the lineup of investment managers in
the past 12 months.
Purpose
The investment committee is charged with the prudent management of GLIF.
The pool of assets invested is composed of the general and endowment funds
for the Masonic Home of California, investment funds of the California Masonic
Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, and Grand Lodge. The
investment committee’s responsibilities and activities are governed by the
CMC sections 406.045, 407.040 B and D, and the approved Investment Policy
Statement (IPS).

280

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Investment Objectives
The primary objectives of the investment committee are inculcated in the language of the IPS:
“The primary objective of the funds is to provide a regular and reliable source
of financial support to the Masonic entities or its beneficiaries, while preserving
the purchasing power of the funds after reasonable withdrawals are taken.”
Simply put, the investment objectives that the committee is engaged in are
income generation, capital preservation, and asset growth. With that in mind,
the committee has adopted a long-term target return of 6.75 percent annualized.
Investment Selection And Monitoring
The committee is comprised of diligent financial professionals who are astute in
portfolio construction and global economics. NEPC, LLC serves as the committee’s investment consultant, which provides services in the areas of identifying
investment managers, due diligence, and modeling/evaluations.
The Investment Committee, with the assistance of NEPC, regularly identifies and selects investment managers that have a higher probability of providing
incremental benefit to the overall fund’s performance. This is accomplished
through global economic and markets analysis to identify appropriate asset
classes and allocation. Once the allocation is determined, individual managers
are selected utilizing data, research, and due diligence services provided by NEPC.
Once managers have been thoroughly vetted and consistently monitored, as long
as the manager’s investment style is still part of the committee’s investment
thesis, it is relatively rare that a manager be terminated, unless the committee
have adjusted the positioning of the portfolio. This philosophy is founded in
the committee’s adopted IPS which states:
“We believe that manager turnover is very expensive and extremely disruptive
to the efficiency and productive operation of an investment program. Mangers
should be hired with a long-run view… We also believe that constant and/
or rapid turnover of mangers, justified solely on the basis of relative underperformance, is usually an indication of a lack of adherence to the selection
and retention process. In particular, short-term (generally less than one
year) underperformance should not be a reason for termination, unless it
is accompanied by other adverse key retention characteristics.”
In monitoring the portfolio, the committee receives monthly performance
reports and meets quarterly. Quarterly meetings, aside from discussing outstanding business or tactical decisions, regularly involve meeting with one or
two individual investment managers to review quarterly due diligence and performance reports from NEPC. This allows the committee to monitor the respective
performance of the managers compared to various indices representing their

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

281

objective. This process provides the committee with the necessary data to
evaluate each investment manager on a timely basis, and to observe whether
they continue to achieve the objectives of their mandate.
During the fiscal year ending October 31, 2024, the following changes were
made to the portfolio:
In Cash Management: Investment in a U.S. treasury note maturing in
2026 in the amount of approximately $41 million to immunize a debt obligation
of the Masonic Homes coming due around the approximate time the treasury
note matures.
In U.S. Equity: Eagle Capital was substituted in for Epoch U.S. All Cap
Value Fund.
In Global Equity: The entirety of the allocation to Global Equity was
reengineered, which resulted in the addition of Independent Franchise Partners
Global Equity and Jennison Global Opportunities and the removal of Artisan
Global Opportunities and Lindsell Train Global Equity.
In Fixed Income: The allocation to fixed income was expanded to include
two managers: Artisan High Income and Barings U.S. High Yield Fund.
Private Investments
NEPC continues to build the private allocation portion of the portfolio. In that
effort they have added:
• Private Real Estate/Real Assets: Ares U.S. Real Estate Opportunity IV
• Private Equity: EMK Capital Partners III, Spark Capital VIII, and
Spark Capital Growth Fund V
• Private Debt: Blue Torch Credit Opportunities Fund III, LP Dawson
IV, and Dawson VI
Performance
As of October 31, 2024, the GLIF delivered a trailing 12-month annualized return
of 20.0 percent compared to the Allocation Index’s 20.4 percent over the same
period. For the five-year period ending October 31, 2024, the GLIF returned
an average of 7.6 percent compared to the Allocation Index’s 8.00 percet. The
one- and five-year return numbers encompass a period of meaningful volatility stemming from the COVID pandemic, global hyperinflation, tightening
monetary policy (central banks increasing interest rates and aggressive fiscal
policy) and a significant increase in federal government spending and deficit ($2
trillion in 2023 and 2024 estimated federal government deficit). With inflation
retreating and the Federal Reserve initiating a more relaxed monetary policy, it
is appropriate that these factors should be viewed favorably by the investment
community. What has yet to be more defined, as it relates to investments globally
and global economic performance, is the impact, domestically and globally, of
the United States’ election results.

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California,
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the grand
master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the
next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the grand master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Metroka’s decisions and
dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion. In
the committee’s view, the legislation posted by the grand secretary to the Grand
Lodge website on August 26 of this year is sufficient to carry out the intent
of the proponents and the legislation contained in Grand Master Metroka’s
recommendations which he will present in his message are sufficient to carry
out his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect
set forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no recommendations as to the action to be taken with it. While the committee has written the
title and introductory explanation for each resolution before you and assisted
the proponents in drafting the code changes required to effect their intent, the
proponents’ arguments in their whereas clauses are their own. The committee
does not assist in drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the grand secretary to the Grand Lodge website on August 26 of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master
Metroka’s recommendations require no separate motion because they are
automatically before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will
announce the vote required for the passage of each item before discussion
begins. Any legislation which does not amend the California Masonic Code or
the ritual requires a simple majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the
California Masonic Code or the ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative

284

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

vote. If the amendment receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths
affirmative vote, it carries over to the next Annual Communication when only
a two-thirds affirmative vote is required for adoption.
In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee reviews all
charges and specifications of unmasonic conduct, strikes out those portions
which are not supported by a clear and precise specification of unmasonic conduct, and revises those portions which are incorrect, ambiguous, or insufficient.
The committee may dismiss charges if all the facts set forth in the specifications,
even if true, would not warrant a verdict of unmasonic conduct. As part of its
review, the committee provides the parties with every essential factual element
which must be proven at trial for the accused to be found guilty of each charge.
Since the last Annual Communication, the committee commented on 33 sets
of charges and specifications.
If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of this grand lodge has pleaded
guilty or nolo contendere (or no contest) to, or has been convicted of, a crime of
moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he shall be deemed automatically
expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry without any further
action of his lodge or grand lodge. The committee reviews a certified copy of
the record of conviction to determine whether there has been an automatic
expulsion. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee has reviewed
four federal or state court records to evaluate whether there has been an automatic expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding. These matters are
summarized in the attached exhibit.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any constituent lodge
who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted of, a crime
involving a violation of the moral law unless, for the reason that he did not
commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of conviction vacated or reversed. All applicants are subject to background checks to
determine compliance with this rule. The grand secretary reviews all background
checks received and evaluates whether an applicant is ineligibility for the degrees
because of a federal or state court record disclosed in his background check.
The committee assists in this process as requested. The committee provides
the grand secretary assistance in reviewing any federal or state court records
to evaluate whether an applicant is eligible for the degrees.
We thank the grand master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.
Respectfully submitted,
Standing Committee
David M. Ferreria, Chair

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON LEGISLATIVE ANALYSIS
Grand Master’s Recommendations
Recommendation No. 1
This recommendation seeks to modernize and streamline the procedure by which notice and service of process are given to brothers who have
become subject to charges of unmasonic conduct at both the beginning of
Masonic trial proceedings as well as during those proceedings.
Part 14 of the California Masonic Code governs Masonic trial proceedings
and provides detailed protections for accused brothers to ensure that they are
sufficiently made aware of the proceedings, that they have reasonable opportunity to respond and participate in the process, and that they receive adequate
notice before any consequences of the proceedings are imposed on them.
Many of these protections are similar to protections that have existed in the
common law and civil courts for hundreds of years. For example, the current
requirement that initial notice of pending trial proceedings must be personally
served upon the accused at his home by a disinterested Mason is consistent with
how service of process has historically been done in civil court proceedings.
At the same time, the practice of how service is accomplished in civil courts
is evolving. In some states, civil proceedings may now be initiated simply by
mailing initial pleadings by regular mail. In other states, including California
in some types of cases, civil court proceedings may be initiated by registered
mail or by certified mail with return receipt requested. In California civil court
proceedings, service of all papers on a party who resides out of state may be by
registered or certified mail with return receipt requested. When it is evident
that a party in a California civil court proceeding is evading service, judges will
often grant a request by the opposing party that service of legal documents for
which personal service is required be instead accomplished by regular mail.
And in more recent developments, there are now many cases when electronic
service of papers is perfectly acceptable.
The Grand Master contends that the current requirements under the CMC
which require personal service of certain notices at the commencement of and
during Masonic trial proceedings impose significant burdens on the efficiency
and cost of those proceedings, without necessarily providing the enhanced

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

289

protections envisioned. These requirements can be cumbersome, cause delay
and stalling in the proceedings, and rely on volunteer efforts which are increasingly becoming more difficult to obtain. In fact, some of our lodges are located in
very remote areas which are significantly distant from other lodges, and brothers
live increasingly far from each other, which creates even more of a burden in
finding disinterested Masons who are willing to serve papers.
To address these issues, the grand master recommends that the relevant
sections of the CMC be amended to provide that service upon the accused of
the initial charges and notice at the commencement of Masonic trial proceeds
would no longer be completed by personal service but would instead be completed electronically by email with read receipt requested and supplemented by
United States Postal Service regular mail. After service of the initial charges and
notice, subsequent service of notices to the accused may be sent electronically
by email with read receipt requested to his last known email address as shown
in the Grand Lodge records without the need to be supplemented by regular
mail, except that the trial summons must be sent via e-mail and regular mail.
The grand master submits that this will streamline the service process and
provide quicker, more private, and less embarrassing notification to brothers
that charges have been filed against them.
If this recommendation is adopted, the date of service would be established
as the mailing date, which is consistent with the practice in California civil court
proceedings. Accordingly, the period of time for a brother to respond to charges
or other notices would begin to run on the date of mailing, and he might find
that he has slightly less time to respond than if he had been personally served
in the first place due to potential delays with the U.S. mail.
Permitting service of important documents electronically by email may
also raise concerns about the efficacy of service and whether or not a brother
actually receives the documents, whereas those same concerns would not arise
if he were instead personally served.
However, supplementing the initial electronic service of Masonic charges
and notice with the requirement that charges and notice also be sent by U.S.
regular provides assurances that a brother has been properly notified of the
proceedings. The trial master, accused, and accuser are all aware of the parties’
contact information, and members of the fraternity have a personal responsibility to ensure that they update their contact information with their respective
lodges, which also updates Grand Lodge records. This recommendation would
permit electronic and mail service on a party’s last known electronic and mailing
addresses as shown in the Grand Lodge’s records, which is also consistent with
California civil procedure.
The grand master contends that these recommended amendments to
the code will not prejudice brothers, because they will continue to receive
the same documents and notifications as they do presently, just by different
methods, and they would continue to have the same opportunities to explain
circumstances when they contend that they did not receive required notices.

290

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

He further contends that the Masonic trial system will operate more quickly
and efficiently with these new procedures.
It is for this Grand Lodge to decide whether the benefits afforded by the
recommended amendments to the code to streamline and simplify process
service requirements, and to make that process more efficient, sufficiently
outweigh any concerns about whether a party to Masonic trial proceeding has,
in fact, received notice.
Recommendation No. 2
Under our current procedure, copies of documents from courts must be verified
as accurate by the court clerk. Obtaining certification can delay Masonic trials,
to the detriment of all involved.
This recommendation would, if adopted, allow documents publicly available
from the court to be obtained and presented without the burden of certification.
The accused would still be able to challenge or explain them, the trial master
would still rule on their admissibility, and in all ways the principles of due
process, justice and fairness that are the hallmarks of Masonic trials would be
preserved, while addressing an unnecessary cause of delay.
It is up to the voting members of this Grand Lodge to decide whether this
procedural adjustment should be adopted.
Recommendation No. 3
This recommendation seeks to modify California Masonic Code Section 1404.410
wherein if an accused fails within 30 days, as required, to file a statement in
writing containing a plea of guilty, not guilty, or no contest, the trial master
must nevertheless personally investigate the matter to make a determination
of guilt or innocence, reduce his findings to a writing and if guilty fix a penalty.
From the time the accusation is made until the time of the trial master’s findings, the accused retains the rights and privileges of Masonry without engaging
in the trial process.
The proposed change would modify the code in that if an accused failed to
file a written statement within the 30-day time period, as required, the grand
master would be authorized, if he chose to do so, to suspend the accused from
all the rights and benefits of Masonry. This right is already provided to the grand
master pursuant to CMC Section 1404.340.
The modification would require the grand secretary to notify the accused,
the master, and secretary of each of the accused member’s lodge or lodges via
electronic mail and US Mail of the suspension.
The existing code sections regarding notification of a suspended member
would still apply.
This modification would relieve the trial master from performing any

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

291

further duties in connection with the applicable charge or charges.
If the accused submits a plea with an explanation of the circumstances that
prevented him from filing the required statement within the 30 days as required,
his suspension is lifted, and the trial process would then resume
Recommendation No. 4
This recommendation would modify the California Masonic Code (CMC) to
allow for budget-based modifications to the fees constituent lodges pay per
application, the amounts each candidate must donate to Masonic causes and
charities, and adds the California Masonic Foundation as one of the charities.
Since the formation of the Grand Lodge of California, every lodge has paid
a fee to Grand Lodge for each member. The method of determining the fee and
the amount has changed over the years. Currently, CMC Section 407.030 sets
the fee at $30 per new candidate. Since the amount is specified in the CMC, it
can only be changed by modifying the code, which requires a 5/6 vote.
Since the inception of the Masonic Homes, we have collected donations
from each applicant. The amount has been set at $25 for more than 100 years
without change. In today’s dollars, that would be approximately $460. When
the membership decided to build this beautiful building as a memorial to our
brothers who served and lost their lives in the defense of our nation, donations
were collected from every member and from each applicant. The fee for applicants is set at $9 and has not changed in more than 70 years. In today’s dollars,
that would be approximately $98. When the George Washington Memorial was
proposed, our Grand Lodge voted to support it and a donation to it by each
candidate was added to the CMC, which is currently set at $15. All three of these
amounts are specified in the CMC, therefore each of them can only be changed
by modifying the code, which requires a 5/6 vote.
When the California Masonic Foundation was formed in 1969, it was funded
by the sale of the Masonic clubhouses on two University of California campuses.
There was no assessment of members, nor was the code modified to add a donation from each new candidate. The grand master asserts that the outstanding
work of the Foundation in our various communities should be included in the
charitable contributions of our applicants. Therefore, he proposes to amend
the code to include a contribution from each applicant for the Foundation, the
amount to be determined during the preparation of the Grand Lodge budget.
The grand master’s recommendation will remove the specific dollar amount
of the application fee and donations to the Masonic causes and charities, and
replace it with the following language: “The contribution amount shall be
established from time to time with the adoption of the Grand Lodge budget.”
This is the same process used to establish the fee for background checks on
applicants (CMC Section §804.210) and has been in place since 2010. This
change will allow for modifications of the contributions as part of the annual
budget process and will still be subject to the approval of a majority of delegates

292

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

voting on the budget at each Annual Communication.
The current contributions to the Masonic Homes, California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the George Washington Memorial, and the application fee
total $79. If this recommendation is adopted, the California Masonic Foundation
will be added as a mandatory donation. All of these contributions are paid by
the applicant and not the lodge.
If this recommendation is adopted this year, the increase in contributions
would not take effect until after the next Annual Communication and your
approval of the 2025-26 Grand Lodge budget containing the amounts for each
of these contributions.
Recommendation No. 5
This recommendation would amend the California Masonic Code (“CMC”)
sections 809.370 and 809.380 to do two things: (1) Extend the automatic restoration period for a suspended brother from two years to three years; and (2)
extend the period that a lodge is prohibited from suspending a brother on active
military combat duty from two years to three years.
Under our current law, if a Mason who was appropriately suspended for
non-payment of dues, military or otherwise, makes payment of the outstanding portion of his dues within two years, he is automatically restored to good
standing. After the two-year mark, a vote of the lodge is required to readmit
him to good standing. If this resolution is adopted, the length of time in which
a Mason may be automatically restored to good standing by paying such dues
as are required, or receiving remission of dues, would be extended to three
years. The positive effect of this could be to possibly spare a lodge the burden
of a vote by allowing a brother experiencing hardship the ability to recover and
make payment prior to suspension.
With regard to military Masons, if it is known that a Mason has served
on active military combat duty and has failed to pay his dues or arrange for a
remission of those dues for 24 months, a lodge may suspend him. If the lodge
learns that he has been on active military combat duty within 24 months prior
to that suspension, the lodge must automatically restore him, without a vote,
and remove any evidence of that suspension from his Masonic record. A remedy
that currently exists would be for the lodge to remit the dues of a worthy brother
who is serving on active military combat duty.
This resolution would extend the 24-month rule to 36 months. Thus, if a
brother has been on active military combat duty 36 months prior to being eligible for suspension, he will have had a whole extra year to become current in
his dues before the lodge may suspend him. If this recommendation is adopted,
a lodge may find itself liable for three years’ worth of per capita being paid to
the Grand Lodge, rather than two, that can only be recovered if the brother
eventually makes full payment and restores himself. If he does not, then the
lodge has incurred an additional expense in per capita in the third year prior

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

293

to suspension. It is pointed out that many servicemen returning from active
military combat duty are met with particular obstacles that present themselves
after serving in combat, and a Mason may require additional time to sort out
finances, physical and mental health challenges, and readjust to civilian or
peacetime military life. Again, a lodge could avoid paying per capita on such a
member by remitting his dues.
It is up to the voting members of this Grand Lodge to determine if they
wish to maintain our present suspension and restoration policies or if they
wish to provide an added grace period to Masonic brothers who may need it.
Recommendation No. 6
This recommendation would allow a Mason who is not eligible for automatic
restoration for non-payment of dues to seek restoration to his lodge, subject
to a majority vote of its members, as opposed to the current requirement of
two-thirds vote.
It is up this Grand Lodge to decide whether reducing this voting threshold
for restoration from a two-thirds supermajority vote to a simple majority would
benefit our lodges and their members.
Recommendation No. 7
This recommendation seeks to allow a plain text ritual to be used in our constituent lodges. In essence, to decipher our cipher. As written, the recommendation
would define the secret or esoteric work we are charged to protect as the signs,
words, and modes of recognition only.
If this recommendation is adopted, the disclosure of any portion of our
ritual other than signs, words, and modes of recognition would not be a Masonic
offense.
A plain text ritual would be published for the fraternity only, not to those
outside of our craft, just as we now do in plain-text French, Spanish, and
Armenian. The Grand Lodge’s authority to publish a cipher would continue,
with the plain and cipher texts coexisting, subject to the same limitations on
use as now exist.
You will hear the pros and cons in debate today, and it is up to the voting
members of this body to decide what is in the best interest of our lodges.
Recommendation No. 8
This recommendation would provide guidelines for the grand master and grand
lecturer to use in the exercise of their discretion in authorizing constituent
lodges to use alternative ritual.
Presently, the grand master and grand lecturer may use their discretion to

294

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

authorize any constituent lodge to utilize an alternative ritual rather than the
American Rite (as modified by our Grand Lodge) which is required under the
California Masonic Code. For example, La Parfaite Union No. 17 has practiced a
version of the Scottish Rite since the 1850s, and La France No. 885 was granted
authority to perform a version of the Scottish Rite in 2023.
Although CMC Section 402.010 permits the use of alternative ritual and
permits lodges which presently use an alternative ritual to continue using that
ritual for so long as it has not been disapproved by the grand master and grand
lecturer, it does not actually give any guidance on what standards or principles should govern when the grand master and grand lecturer are considering
whether to authorize a lodge to use an alternative ritual.
The grand master asserts that interest in the use of alternative rituals is
growing, and this may arise as an issue more frequently in the future as California
becomes a more diverse state. He contends that there are a number of lodges,
both old and young, physically located within California but outside of our
jurisdiction who use alternative ritual, and that their practice of Freemasonry is
“no more or less pure, correct, or wise” than our own practice of Freemasonry.
The grand master proposes that in the future, the grand master and grand
lecturer should continue to have the authority to use their discretion to consider
and authorize lodges to use alternative ritual, but that the code be modified to
make it less ambiguous and to establish those missing standards and principles
by which future decisions should be governed.
Specifically, the Grand Master proposes that CMC Section 402.010 be
modified so that the use of alternative ritual may be authorized as determined
by the grand master and grand lecturer provided that: (1) the alternative ritual
includes the same obligations contained in the ritual adopted by the Grand
Lodge; (2) that the alternative ritual includes the same signs, words, and modes
of recognition contained in our ritual; and (3) that the alternative ritual is “consistent with the culture, integrity, and ideals of our fraternity.” The proposed
modification does not require that the language used for the obligations in
alternative ritual be “exactly identical” to the language used in our ritual. And
the proposed modification permits lodges who have used an alternative ritual
since at least January 1, 2024, which has not been disapproved by the grand
master and grand lecturer, to continue using that ritual into the future without
requiring the affirmative consent of the grand master and grand lecturer.
This recommendation would not enhance or increase the ability of the
grand master and grand lecturer to approve the use of alternative ritual beyond
the authority already granted to them in our code. Rather, if anything, the
recommendation proposes that this authority be tempered and shaped somewhat, such that the exercise of their discretion in the future is guided by these
newly established standards and principles which would be set forth in CMC
Section 402.010 instead of relying on ambiguous language which gives little to
no guidance for how to any such decisions should be reached.
This recommendation preserves the ability of the grand master and grand

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

295

lecturer to continue exercising their discretion in making decisions about the
use of alternative ritual. It does not require them to approve a lodge’s request
to use alternative ritual simply because the alternative ritual contains the same
obligations, signs, words, and modes of recognition in our ritual. In fact, it is
evident that it requires discretion to determine whether an alternative ritual is
consistent with the “culture, integrity, and ideals of our fraternity.”
The grand lecturer is the custodian of our ritual. The grand master is not
only the presiding officer of the Grand Lodge, but he is also the guardian of our
Masonic tradition, culture, and ritual, and he is charged with the interpretation
of our Masonic law. In exercising their respective authority under the CMC and
in fulfilling the duties of their respective offices, this recommendation seeks
to provide some clarification and guidance to assist future grand masters and
grand lecturers in fulfilling their obligations when they consider requests by
lodges for the use of alternative ritual as they arise in the future.
It is for this Grand Lodge to decide whether the recommendation to establish the aforementioned standards and principles would be a benefit to our
fraternity by giving the grand master and grand lecturer guidelines by which
to make those decisions.
Recommendation No. 9
This recommendation would modify provisions applicable to the nomination
of elected Grand Lodge officers.
The most significant changes pertain to the submission of biographical
sketches and written statements to the grand secretary in accordance with proscribed timelines and the affect upon potential nominees for failures to do so.
Currently, under Section 404.410 of the California Masonic Code (CMC), recommendees for elected Grand Lodge offices (i.e., the junior grand warden, grand treasurer, grand secretary and grand lecturer) are required to submit their biographical
sketches to the grand secretary within two weeks prior to the start of the Annual
Communication while all other potential nominees may (but are not required) to
do so. This recommendation would require recommendees and all other nominees
to submit their biographical sketches to the grand secretary at least 60 days prior
to the start of the Annual Communication. All potential nominees other than recommendees would also be required to submit a written statement of his nomination
signed by another voting member of Grand Lodge to the grand secretary at least
60 days prior to the start of the Annual Communication. Under this recommendation, nominations of members who have not provided their biographical sketches
and written statements by the required date would be rejected; and accordingly,
such nominees who failed to meet the new requirements would not be eligible
for election. Under current CMC provisions, a nominee whose nomination was
made and seconded “on the floor” during the Annual Communication is eligible for
election irrespective of whether the nominee previously submitted a biographical
sketch to the grand secretary.

296

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Other changes to Section 404.410 of the CMC would be made if this recommendation is adopted. The grand secretary would be required to provide
the names, current title, and facts contained in the biographical sketches of the
recommendees and those other nominees that met the submission deadlines
to all lodges and to such other members of Grand Lodge as he determines, at
least 21 days prior the start of the Annual Communication. With all recommendees and other nominees being required to submit biographical sketches
under this recommendation, the grand orator would be required to read the
facts contained in biographical sketches of all nominees immediately prior
to the election (whereas currently, the grand orator is only required to do so
when there are multiple nominations for an office and for all recommendees
regardless of whether there are multiple nominations for the applicable office).
This recommendation is intended to give the voting members of Grand
Lodge the opportunity to evaluate all nominees for an elected Grand Lodge
office. By requiring timely submissions of biographical sketches and the subsequent distribution of those sketches weeks before the Annual Communication,
this recommendation would give Grand Lodge voting members ample time to
review the qualifications of all eligible nominees. The recommendation is also
intended to prohibit snap or floor nominations for elected Grand Lodge offices
and avoid procedural problems that may arise from those types of nominations.
The use of scannable ballots with unspecified fields for purposes of voting on
emergent matters or for nominees not previously identified has diminished
procedural problems with floor nominations in recent years. But, if this recommendation is adopted, all floor nominations would effectively be prohibited.
However, if, due to unforeseen circumstances, there are no eligible nominees
for an office, then Grand Lodge would vote on an emergent matter resolution to
permit floor nominations for the affected office and elect a member to that office.
This Grand Lodge should also consider how the ability to make floor nominations for elected officer positions is similar to the practice of having write-in
candidates in U.S. elections. As with that practice, the ability to make floor nominations gives Grand Lodge members greater flexibility to consider a broader
range of nominees for an elected office. If this recommendation is adopted, that
flexibility would be diminished as a result of floor nominations being prohibited.
It is up to this Grand Lodge to decide whether the certainty in the nomination process, and the ability to have ample time to review nominees for elected
offices, that this recommendation would afford outweighs the concerns raised
by prohibiting floor nominations.
Recommendation No. 10
This recommendation would amend California Masonic Code Section 404.315 to
remove the requirement that an assistant grand lecturer (AGL) be a past master
of a lodge in the division he serves. Currently, an AGL must be a past master
and member of a lodge in the particular division where he serves.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

297

Adoption of this recommendation will grant the grand master authority to
appoint a past master as an AGL who he determines to be the best fit for the
office, rather than one who best fits geographically. Since the boundaries and
number of Masonic divisions change every few years, a lodge in one division
may shift into a different division. A strict application of the code as currently
written could see an effective AGL’s appointment end strictly due to his lodge’s
location. Recent practice has seen divisions staffed with qualified AGLs whose
own lodges were located outside the boundary of their assigned divisions. This
resolution would bring that practice into conformity with the code.
This resolution does not remove the requirement that the AGL be a member
of a lodge in the division to which he is appointment. That impediment is usually
solved by the AGL affiliating into a lodge in his appointed division. This resolution would remove any possible confusion over whether the AGL appointee
is merely a past master by affiliation of that lodge with the proposed language
change of “a past master of any constituent lodge.”
This resolution recognizes the arbitrary and changing lines drawn among
divisions for the sake of administrative necessity, and it recognizes the fluidity
of population shifts that cause exceptional past masters and possible AGL
candidates to become far removed from their home lodges.
It is up to the members of this voting body to decide if grand masters
should have the ability to select AGLs who are the most qualified past masters
regardless of where they served as master.
Recommendation No. 11
This recommendation will modify the California Masonic Code (CMC) to allow a
brother to be secretary in more than one of the lodges of which he is a member.
Currently, CMC Section 805.010 only allows a master, a senior warden, a junior
warden, and a secretary to hold one of those offices in only one lodge.
It has a been a long-standing practice of the Grand Lodge of California to
prohibit a member from being a master, warden, or secretary in more than one
lodge to prevent a potential conflict of interest and to maintain the autonomy
of each individual lodge. In 2009, Resolution 09-07 proposed to make the same
change and was not adopted.
The CMC provides for an assistant secretary to assist the secretary and/
or to teach a brother how to do perform the duties of a secretary. The code
does allow a secretary to be an assistant secretary in another lodge if they are
a member of it. This allows a brother to be trained by an experienced secretary
when one is not available to serve in that lodge.
If this recommendation is adopted, then a member could be a secretary in
every lodge they are a member. A master or warden of one lodge could be the
secretary in another lodge at the same time. The grand master asserts that some
small lodges need this change. It is up to you, the voting members of Grand
Lodge, to decide if this change could create a conflict of interest and threaten

298

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

the autonomy of a lodge or the change is in the best interest of our lodges.
Recommendation No. 12
This recommendation would amend the California Masonic Code (CMC) sections 807.010 and 813.010 to reduce the number of meetings required to effect
a consolidation of lodges by one meeting, and to add a final consolidation vote
as an acceptable item of business at a special meeting.
Since at least 1991, the CMC has required no fewer than four stated meetings for a consolidation to go into effect. This recommendation would reduce
that number to three meetings.
The current process exists to provide members of lodges seeking consolidation ample time to be given notice and for the members to be able to respond to
the notice of consolidation. This feature of the code was helpful when all lodges
met monthly; in the present time it has become a burden for lodges that meet
quarterly. The addition of the option of a special meeting to examine consents
and approve the consolidation could speed up processes for lodges that do not
meet on a monthly basis. Lodges that meet on a quarterly basis would see the
process spread out over a year under the current code.
It is up to the voting members of this Grand Lodge to determine if they
wish to maintain our present consolidation system, or if they wish to provide
a more streamlined process to help our lodges in distress wrap up their affairs.

CARRY-OVER LEGISLATION

Carry-over Resolution No. 23-01
This resolution seeks to allow lodges to send minutes to members by electronic
mail.
This resolution would amend California Masonic Code (CMC) sections
805.230 and 807.030 to permit electronic distribution of lodge minutes to lodge
members prior to the stated meeting at which those minutes would be required
to be read. Upon successful appropriate motion, the reading of the minutes that
have been so distributed could be waived and the minutes adopted. The monitor would also require a revision as the new language would be included in it.
Prior distribution of the minutes may give lodge members more time to
review and potentially correct them, resulting in more accurate record keeping for lodges. The draft minutes must be provided 72 hours prior to the next
stated meeting. Waiving the reading of minutes may shorten the length of stated
meetings. Recently our jurisdiction has amended sections of our CMC to allow
for the use of new technology, such as Zoom or Google Meet, if all security and
privacy policies are met to conduct limited lodge business. Conversely, distributing lodge communications to members via e-mail might see those minutes
inadvertently distributed to unintended parties or appropriated by third-party
bad actors. Not being able to review the waived minutes prior to signature could
lead to an inadvertent or willful substitution of the distributed minutes with
a different draft. It is noted that the legislation does not contain any verbiage
relative to maintaining lodge confidentiality.
This resolution creates a choice rather than a mandate for the lodges. If
authorized by a standing resolution of the lodge, the secretary shall provide
electronically all minutes of meetings of the lodge to the electronic mail address
of record for each Mason of the lodge. Any objection to the motion or vote
that is not unanimous to waive reading automatically causes the minutes to be
required reading at the stated meeting. It is up to the members of this Grand
Lodge to decide if they trust the secretaries and brethren with the veracity of
the minutes, their diligence in secure distribution, and all brothers’ sworn duty
to maintain confidentiality.

300

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Carry-over Resolution No. 23-03
Section 807.010 of the California Masonic Code expressly prohibits lodges from
holding a special meeting on the same day as a stated meeting. The proponents
of this resolution seek to amend this section to give lodges the right to hold one
or more special meetings on the same day as a stated meeting.
Under this resolution, while a lodge would be able to hold a special meeting
on the same day as a stated meeting, a lodge would not be allowed to hold a
special meeting at the same time as the stated meeting. Similarly, a lodge would
not be allowed to hold two or more special meetings at the same time. This
resolution is permissive only and does not require lodges to hold other meetings
on the day of the stated meeting. This resolution does not change any of the
other requirements applicable to special meetings or stated meetings under
the CMC. For example, a lodge meeting must still conclude and close prior to
midnight on a given day.
If this resolution is adopted, lodges could benefit from having more flexibility in the scheduling of their meetings. As the proponents noted, lodges in
remote areas often have members traveling long distances to attend meetings,
and the ability to have one or more special meetings on the same day as the
stated meeting would decrease the number of times those members would
have to make such long journeys. It is also possible that smaller lodges, and
even lodges whose members have busy work or family schedules, could likewise
benefit from consolidating their meeting dates.
This resolution could also benefit those lodges who only meet quarterly,
perhaps because of extreme weather or remoteness of their location, by enabling
them to open and close a stated meeting, and then open a special meeting on
the second or third degree to confer those degrees upon their candidates on
the same day members of the lodge regularly travel there. It would also enable
those quarterly lodges to advance their candidates through the degrees in a
more timely manner and minimize delays caused by their quarterly stated
meeting schedule.
Enabling a lodge to hold one or more special meetings on the same day as
the stated meeting could increase the number of degrees or other activities that
a lodge could accomplish in any given month. However, it would also mean that
members could possibly be at lodge for longer hours on the stated meeting day,
which might lead to member fatigue because some lodges have a limited number
of members available who have the ability or necessary qualifications to fulfill
certain roles. If this resolution is adopted, lodges should exercise their ability
to hold multiple meetings on a stated meeting day judiciously and consider a
variety of factors including the impact on their members and officers which
might result from such multiple meetings.
It is for this Grand Lodge to decide whether the various benefits afforded
by giving lodges the option to hold one or more special meetings on the same
day as a stated meeting would be of sufficient benefit to our lodges and to the
fraternity to warrant this proposed change to the code.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Carry-over Resolution No. 23-05
Currently, California Masonic Code (CMC) section 403.075 allows past masters
collectively of each chartered lodge to one vote only. The proponents of this
resolution seek to modify CMC section 403.075(d).
The proponents of this resolution seek to address a problem some lodges are
facing with a past master collecting the ballot and not exercising the collective
vote of the past masters present. If this resolution were passed, it would not
be mandatory for lodges to do this. Lodges would have to vote first on whether
or not to designate a past master. If they choose to designate a past master,
they will have to determine whether to vote by all members or by a vote of past
masters. They would have to use that method to designate a past master. They
would have to get the master’s signature and attest of the lodge secretary in
time to get that designation to the grand secretary in sufficient time to restrict
the ballot to that past master. As proposed, this would have to be done on an
annual basis.
There are some problems with the language of this resolution. The resolution does not state the manner in which notice would be provided to its members
to ensure all those desiring to participate in the balloting can be present. The
resolution does not address the issue of what would happen if the designated
past master failed to attend Annual Communication as the resolution restricts
the voting right to that one designated past master. The language in the resolution that the “designated past master may be chosen by either those members
of the lodge or by those past masters of the lodge as the lodge may determine”
may lead to disharmony between past masters and members.
The lodge would have sole authority for which group would be entitled to
make this election, thereby potentially turning this decision-making process
into an issue of personalities (members verses past masters) and could open
the door for politicking and could lead to lodge unrest.
It is up to this voting body to decide whether or not this issue and this
resolution requires an amendment to the CMC.
Resolution No. 24-01
This resolution would amend the California Masonic Code sections 805.520,
805.530, and 805.540 to make the receipt of a certificate of proficiency in the
candidate’s lecture of the Master Mason degree a prerequisite to nomination
for the offices of master, senior warden, and junior warden, and remove the
receipt of the certificate of proficiency as a condition to a pillar officer-elect’s
installation.
Adoption of this resolution would mandate that every Master Mason who
seeks a pillar office is proficient in the third degree candidates lecture prior to
nomination. It would not mandate that the brother be proficient in the work of
those three offices prior to nomination. Proficiency in the candidate’s lecture

302

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

and proficiency in the working of the three degrees of Masonry are two separate
things. Proficiency in the candidate’s lecture does not require any skill with
floorwork, whereas proficiency in the work of the three degrees does.
Lodges with large pools of talent may not have difficulty meeting the proposed requirement. Lodges with smaller memberships, particularly in rural
areas, may meet difficulty meeting the proposed requirements.
The proponents also point to this resolution raising the bar of leadership
in a lodge by requiring Master Masons in possession a certificate of proficiency
in the candidate’s lecture of the Master Mason degree be the only candidates
for election. However, no research points to ritual ability and leadership ability being the same thing. Strong leaders with middling ritual ability might be
precluded in the short-term from advancement to pillar offices.
Adoption of this resolution may create a quandary for constituent lodges
in the present short term. If a lodge has identified a brother for advancement
in any of the three offices heretofore listed who is not in possession of the certificate of proficiency in the candidate’s lecture of the Master Mason degree,
and was planning on having that requirement completed after election but prior
to installation, that brother would become ineligible for election at the CMC
required November election immediately following the Annual Communication
at which this resolution may be adopted, and could create a condition where a
lodge would then need to postpone election for that office or maintain a vacancy
in a pillar office until a qualified candidate presents himself.
It is up to the voting members of this Grand Lodge to determine whether
this change in our system of qualification is a benefit or creates a burden to
our constituent lodges.
Respectfully submitted,
Standing Committee
Justin J. Daza-Ritchie, Chairman
David R. Doan, PGM
David M. Ferreria
Ralph C. Shelton II
Gary D. Sparks

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON TRIAL REVIEW

Most Worshipful and brethren,
I am honored to be your chairman of the Committee on Trial Review,
and I am proud of the work the committee accomplished this year. I want to
thank our vice chair Rob Scott and committee members Jeff Bear, Freddie
Davis, George Turegano, Geoff Holbrook, and Gary Sparks for their dedication
to the Committee on Trial Review, which conducted a thorough examination of
records for all cases completed during this Masonic year. We confirmed that each
case adhered to the procedural requirements defined in the California Masonic
Code, and all decisions outlined in this report were reached by a majority of
our committee members.
While these matters must be addressed as part of our commitment to maintaining the high standards and principled values we uphold, we recognize they
are not the central focus of our fraternity. This year, the committee reviewed
and analyzed 19 cases, a significant number that included many outstanding
cases that were pending completion from prior years. We are pleased to report
that many of these delayed matters have now been resolved. As chairman, I will
strive to present our report with both brevity and integrity in the following
three resolutions:
As to the first resolution, we present the following cases that were resolved
through mediation or dismissed by the appointed trial master:
• In Case No. 2993, the accused was charged with embezzlement, defamation, and falsehoods related to a family estate administration issue
and asset division. The accused pled not guilty. After reviewing evidence and considering the concurrent civil litigation, the trial master
found no factual support for the allegations and dismissed the case.
• In Case No. 3054, the accused was charged with engaging in a pattern
of intimidating behavior and breaches of fiduciary duties. During a
pre-trial conference, the trial master facilitated an amicable resolution wherein the accused agreed to demit from the lodge and the
accuser requested to dismiss the charges. The motion to dismiss was
granted by the trial master.

304

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

• In Case No. 3072, the accused was charged with physical battery at a
lodge function. At the pre-trial conference, the trial master discussed
with both parties the lack of evidence in support of the allegations
and entertained their desire to resolve the dispute without formal
adjudication. Through mediation with the trial master, both parties
reached an amicable resolution, and the accuser requested to dismiss
the charges. The motion to dismiss was granted by the trial master.
• In Cases Nos. 2990 and 2991, both parties were charged with fraud
in a real estate property transaction. The cases were stayed due to
ongoing civil litigation concerning the same allegations of a fraudulent transaction. As the matter could not proceed without sufficient
evidence, the trial master ordered the cases dismissed without prejudice and the parties are free to proceed when sufficiently prepared.
Having completed our review of these matters, the Committee on Trial
Review therefore submits and moves for the adoption of the following resolution:
“THAT, IN THE MATTERS OF CASE NUMBERS 2993, 3054, 3072, 2990,
AND 2991 THE TRIAL MASTER’S PROCEDURES AND FINDINGS BE
HEREBY AFFIRMED AS PRESENTED.”
As to the second resolution, we present the following cases that were heard
before a trial master, finding the accused guilty, and setting a penalty accordingly:
• In Case No. 3014, the accused was charged with using and possessing a translated cipher during a third degree ritual. The accused pled
guilty. Considering mitigating factors such as the accused’s immediate admission, remorse, and cooperation, including identifying
others who were in possession of prohibited material, the trial master
imposed a penalty of reprimand in open lodge.
• In Case No. 2793, the accused was charged with breach of fiduciary
duty, theft of approximately $21,000, embezzlement of an additional
$83,000, and fraud related to his role as a hall association building
manager. The accused failed to respond to the charges. After an investigation, the trial master found him guilty and imposed the penalty at
expulsion.
• In Case No. 3063, the accused was charged with larceny, embezzlement, and breach of fiduciary duty for misappropriating over $26,000
of lodge funds. The accused pled guilty and expressed extreme
remorse for his actions, citing financial and personal hardships. The
trial master found the accused guilty and imposed the penalty of
expulsion due to the serious breach of trust. Remorse and personal
hardships were noted but did not alter the penalty.

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

305

• In Case No. 3069, the accused was charged with embezzling $2,350
of lodge funds. The accused pled guilty and cited financial and mental
hardships. Despite the accused returning the funds and expressing
remorse, the trial master imposed expulsion as a penalty, noting the
seriousness of the embezzlement. The accused and others submitted
additional information and statements suggesting the accused’s conduct should be excused, or the penalty should be modified, due to the
personal hardships the accused was experiencing at the time of the
embezzlement of fraternal funds. The additional information, along
with the accused’s expression of remorse, have been considered by
the Trial Review Committee, which voted to uphold the trial master’s
decision but will consider timely filed requests for reinstatement in
future years
• In Cases Nos. 3010 and 3011, the charges stemmed from a physical altercation between the two parties, which involved one party’s
unmarried romantic partner. The accused in Case No. 3010 was found
to have initiated the altercation, was found guilty, and the trial master
issued a penalty of suspension for 12 months. The ain Case No. 3011
was determined to have acted in self-defense and was found not guilty.
• In Case No. 3025, the accused was charged with theft by false pretenses involving a fraudulent investment scheme of several thousands
of dollars. The accused did not respond to the trial master’s multiple
service attempts. The trial master found him guilty based on substantial evidence that he had utilized his fraternal membership to obtain
substantial amounts of money from fellow brethren in an illegitimate
business and the trial master imposed the penalty at expulsion.
Having completed our review of these matters, the Committee on Trial
Review therefore submits and moves for the adoption of the following resolution:
“THAT, IN THE MATTERS OF CASE NUMBERS 3014, 2793, 3063, 3069,
3010, 3011, AND 3025, THE TRIAL MASTER’S PROCEDURES, FINDINGS
AND APPLICABLE PENALTY AFFIXIED, BE HEREBY AFFIRMED AS
PRESENTED.”
As to the third and final resolution, we present the following factually
related case Nos. 3029, 3027, 3028, 3030, 3031, 3032, and 3023. These cases all
involve charges of affiliation with an unrecognized organization, known as the
Travelers Tamblayan, and failing to comply with the proper edicts of the grand
master issued in 2019 and 2020, which remain in effect. These edicts mandate
that members cease any activity related to the unrecognized Masonic organization and that failing to do so would result in charges of unmasonic conduct.
The outcomes varied based on the accused’s responses, participation, remorse,
and cooperation, and the trial results were accordingly determined as follows:

306

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

• In Case No. 3029, the accused pled guilty and was suspended for
12 months. The mitigating factors considered by the trial master
included the accused’s admission, remorse, and willingness to testify
against others.
• In Cases Nos. 3027, 3028, and 3030, each of the accused pled not
guilty. After a consolidated trial, the accused were found guilty based
on witness statements, testimony, and evidence. The trial master set
the penalties at expulsion.
• In Case No. 3023, the accused pled not guilty. The trial, conducted
before a trial master and commissioners, revealed that the accused
had renounced the prohibited affiliation. There was conflicting
evidence presented at trial which determined the accused had not
committed the alleged unmasonic conduct, and the trial master found
the accused not guilty.
• In Case No. 3031, the accused pled not guilty. The accusers withdrew
the charges due to insufficient evidence available at the time the charges
were filed, and the trial master dismissed the case without prejudice.
• In Case No. 3023, the accused pled not guilty. The trial, conducted
before a trial master and commissioners, found the accused guilty of
maintaining his membership in the unrecognized organization and
failing to comply with the grand masters’ edicts. Accordingly, the trial
master set the penalty at expulsion.
Having completed our review of these matters, the Committee on Trial
Review therefore submits and moves for the adoption of the following resolution:
“THAT, IN THE MATTERS OF CASE NUMBERS 3029, 3027, 3028, 3030,
3031, 3032, AND 3023, THE TRIAL MASTER’S PROCEDURES, FINDINGS
AND APPLICABLE PENALTY AFFIXIED, IF ANY, BE HEREBY AFFIRMED
AS PRESENTED.”
Respectfully submitted,
Standing Committee
Ronald A. Lawrence, Chairman
Robert E. Scott, Vice Chairman
Freddie Davis
Jeffrey L. Bear

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON YOUTH ORDERS

To Most Worshipful Grand Master G. Sean Metroka and the members of the Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California,
This committee is charged with fostering positive fraternal relations
between the youth orders we support and the grand and constituent lodges
of California.
The committee has continued a program of open communication between
the youth orders and our constituent lodges through the district inspector corps
and established a communication channel for our youth orders through the
Grand Lodge communication staff to all Masons in California. The committee
has worked closely with and wishes to thank our grand lecturer and assistant
grand lecturers for their support in our efforts, as well as the grand secretary
and his exceptional staff who have provided support and guidance.
We have met several times with the youth order leaders, including the grand
worth advisor, grand bethel honored queen, and jurisdiction master councilors
of Northern and Southern California DeMolay. We have facilitated meetings
that included Most Worshipful Metroka and other grand officers to ensure that
our youth order members are clear that they have a voice in our work. We have
also met with the adult supporters of our youth orders and have continued to
have a clear view of their needs from their perspective. In short, we have asked
the youth order leaders what our Grand Lodge can best do to assist them in
their development. Their response has been very clear and unified that the
most important thing we can do is encourage our members to be present at
their meetings and activities.
We have also discussed supplemental leader training as a tool to assist in
their development and secured approval and funding for such an effort with a
major corporate entity that has a well-established leadership program and will
happily offer that training to our youth. While this relationship has not yet been
formalized by contract, we feel that we are poised to provide our youth leaders
with exciting resources in the area of leadership development.
We were also made aware of several situations through the year in which
there had been challenges between the youth orders and sponsoring or hosting lodges, and were able, in each such instance, to facilitate productive

308

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

communication that resolved those budding difficulties before they became
unduly problematic, which we feel is an appropriate and, at times, necessary,
function of the committee.
The committee was pleased to recommend the names of the following
brothers to receive the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award:
• Worshipful Brother Robert L. Pawneshing, a past master of Lakewood
No. 728, for his service to Job’s Daughters International, California.
• Brother Robert L. Meyer, a member of Drytown No. 174, for his service
to the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls, California.
• Brother Ever E. Mendoza, a member of Hollywood No. 355, for his
service to DeMolay International, Southern California Jurisdiction.
• Brother Steven Kolden, a member of Crow Canyon No. 551, for his
service to DeMolay International, Northern California Jurisdiction.
Each of these recipients had demonstrated outstanding commitment and
service to our youth orders and was honored during the public ceremonies at
our 2024 Annual Communication.
The members of the committee are most appreciative of the confidence of
Most Worshipful Metroka and the entire executive committee and look forward
to working closely with Most Worshipful Salazar and the entire Grand Lodge
Executive Committee in the coming Masonic year.
Respectfully submitted,
Standing Committee

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON CALIFORNIA FREEMASON MAGAZINE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California,
It is with immense pride that this committee presents the report for the
California Freemason magazine, our grand lodge’s flagship publication, for the
2024 Masonic year. This year has been one of bold creativity and meaningful
milestones for the magazine. It has continued to exemplify the values of our fraternity, uniting tradition with innovation to engage, inspire, and connect Masons
across California and beyond. Under the guidance of Chief Communications
Officer Emily Limón, whose leadership has shaped the committee’s vision
over the past decade, we have achieved new heights in storytelling, design,
and outreach. Her strategic insight and unwavering commitment have been
the cornerstone of our success, ensuring the magazine remains a beacon of
Masonic excellence.
The addition of Isabelle Guerin as the magazine and communications
team’s creative services manager has been a transformative step forward for our
operations. Isabelle has not only helped rebuild the magazine’s website with a
more modern, intuitive, and updated design but has also expanded our digital
footprint in meaningful ways. Her organizational skills have kept our timelines
precise, allowing us to meet the demands of producing four high-quality magazines each year while managing the robust workload of the communications
team. Isabelle’s presence has ensured a seamless workflow and provided the
structure and support necessary for creative innovation to thrive.
One of the defining moments of this year was our spring 2024 issue, which
featured a commissioned stained-glass window of Prince Hall on its cover. This
remarkable piece was presented to the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons in California at their Annual Communication,
symbolizing the strengthened relationship between our grand lodges. Later, it
was again presented to the current grand master of Prince Hall Masons, the
Most Worshipful Robert J. Eagle Spirit, Sr. at our own Annual Communication.
Accompanied by the captivating and inspiring interviews between the two
grand masters, Most Worshipful G. Sean Metroka and Most Worshipful David
San Juan, and extensive social media engagement, this effort marked a historic
milestone in our shared commitment to unity and collaboration.

310

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Throughout the year, the magazine continued to innovate, as exemplified by
the summer 2024 Heroes Issue. Under the creative direction of Pete Ivey, this
edition reimagined Masonic heroes as comic book action figures, celebrating
their dedication and generosity in a visually compelling and unique way. The
cover, styled as a vintage comic book, was among the most positively received in
the magazine’s history, resonating deeply with readers and further showcasing
the boundless creativity of our editorial team.
This year also saw the winter 2024 issue solidifying its place as a flagship
publication, with thought-provoking features and engaging visuals that explored
the fraternity’s enduring relevance in today’s world. Editorial director Ian A.
Stewart’s ability to curate fresh, meaningful content year after year ensured that
each issue reflected the diversity, values, and aspirations of our jurisdiction. His
work, alongside the remarkable efforts of our entire team, has been pivotal in
maintaining the magazine’s role as a leading voice in Freemasonry.
While we chose not to submit for awards this year due to changes in the
availability of previous peer review opportunities, we remain committed to finding
new avenues for recognition. The magazine’s success has always been rooted in its
ability to inspire, inform, and connect, and we are actively exploring peer review
options to ensure that we continue to hold ourselves to the highest standards.
Our digital storytelling also reached new dimensions this year, thanks to
the remarkable efforts of J.R. Sheetz. Through his multimedia expertise, we
brought the stories of Freemasonry to life in videos that resonated deeply with
both members and the wider public. These projects, combined with targeted
social media strategies, extended the reach of our magazine and reinforced its
relevance in a digital age.
As we look to the future, our sights are set on further expanding the magazine’s digital footprint, introducing more interactive features, and exploring new
ways to celebrate the values and contributions of our Masonic family. With the
steadfast support of our committee and readers, we are confident that California
Freemason magazine will continue to inspire and unite for many years to come.
On behalf of the committee, we extend our deepest gratitude to the editorial team—Emily Limón, Pete Ivey, Ian A. Stewart, J.R. Sheetz, Isabelle Guerin,
and the entire communications team of the Grand Lodge of California. Your
vision and dedication are the lifeblood of our publication. To the Masons of
California, thank you for making this magazine a reflection of your passion and
commitment to the craft.
Respectfully submitted,
Standing Committee
Russell E. Hennings, Chairman, Editor-in-Chief

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON 175TH ANNIVERSARY OF
THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
On April 17, 1850, in the city of Sacramento, a convention of Freemasons
was held for the purpose of organizing and constituting a Grand Lodge of Free
and Accepted Masons in the State of California.
The grand lodges represented at that convention the District of Columbia,
Missouri, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Louisiana. After due consideration of
the convention’s proposal, a constitution for a Grand Lodge in California was
adopted on the April 18 and the Grand Lodge of California opened for the first
time in ample form on the April 19, 1850.
Accordingly, our grand lodge will be celebrating its 175th anniversary in April
2025. A statewide celebration is planned for the evening of April 19, when we will
hold contemporaneous festive boards in Sacramento, San Francisco, Pasadena,
and San Diego. We will likewise hold celebrations at both our Masonic Homes
in the state. In addition, we will be inviting our lodges to honor a statewide
day of service to our communities on April 17 in celebration of our milestone
anniversary.
While more information on these celebrations will be forthcoming, I’d like
to invite our brethren to start this celebration by wearing our commemorative
175th anniversary pins, available from any committee member, or with these
beautiful coins, available for purchase in the exhibition hall.
We thank you, Most Worshipful, for our appointment to this committee
and will look forward to sharing more information with our craft about the
upcoming events.
Respectfully submitted,
Standing Committee
Steven L. Yeffa, Chair
Narbeh Bagdasarian
Jairo Gomez, Jr.
Russell E. Hennings

MUTUAL RECOGNITION WITH
FOREIGN GRAND LODGES 2024-2025
The Grand Lodge of California enjoys mutual recognition with grand
lodges in the United States and around the world. This includes some, but not
all, of the foreign grand lodges in the 2024 Acacia Book, as well as a number of
foreign grand lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign grand lodges that are recognized by the Grand Lodge
of California are listed below alphabetically by country. For those that are published in the 2024 Acacia Book, the corresponding page number is provided in
parentheses. Recognized grand lodges that are not published in the 2024 Acacia
Book are marked with an asterisk (*). The mutual recognition between our Grand
Lodge and those listed all include the right to intervisitation.
In some cases, the Grand Lodge of California has extended an offer of
recognition to a number of grand lodges where mutual recognition does not
yet exist. Those are found at end of this list.
The Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of California is responsible for all
correspondence with these grand lodges and the lodges under their jurisdiction.
Please contact this office for assistance.

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR'S REPORT
To the Board of Trustees
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California
Opinion
We have audited the accompanying consolidated financial statements of The Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the ''Organization''), which comprise the
consolidated statement of financial position as of October 31, 2024, and the related consolidated
statements of activities, functional expenses, and cash flows for the year then ended and the related notes
to the consolidated financial statements.
In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material
respects, the financial position of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California as of October 31, 2024, and the changes in their net assets and their cash flows for
the year then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America.
Basis for Opinion
We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America.
Our responsibilities under those standards are further described in the Auditor's
Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements section of our report. We are required to be
independent of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California and to meet our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with the relevant ethical
requirements relating to our audit. We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and
appropriate to provide a basis for our audit opinion.
Responsibilities of Management for the Financial Statements
Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these consolidated financial
statements in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America,
and for the design, implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and
fair presentation of consolidated financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether
due to fraud or error.
In preparing the consolidated financial statements, management is required to evaluate whether there are
conditions or events, considered in the aggregate, that raise substantial doubt about The Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California's ability to continue as a going
concern within one year after the date that the consolidated financial statements are available to be
issued.

1

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

449

Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements
Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the consolidated financial statements as
a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor's
report that includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but is not absolute
assurance and therefore is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with generally accepted
auditing standards will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. The risk of not detecting a
material misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may
involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control.
Misstatements, including omissions, are considered material if there is a substantial likelihood that,
individually or in the aggregate, they would influence the judgment made by a reasonable user based on
the consolidated financial statements.
In performing an audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards, we:


Exercise professional judgment and maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit.



Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated financial statements,
whether due to fraud or error, and design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks.
Such procedures include examining, on a test basis, evidence regarding the amounts and disclosures
in the consolidated financial statements.



Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures
that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the
effectiveness of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California's internal control. Accordingly, no such opinion is expressed.



Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of significant
accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluate the overall presentation of the
consolidated financial statements.



Conclude whether, in our judgment, there are conditions or events, considered in the aggregate, that
raise substantial doubt about The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period of time.
